countries.name: France
countries.tagline: The country that wrote the law of place into every bottle, from chalk in Champagne to galets in Châteauneuf.

stats.note: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026): vineyard area 740 kha (preliminary, -4.4% on 2024, second after Spain); production 36.1 mhl (second after Italy's 44.4 mhl); consumption 22.0 mhl; exports 12.5 mhl worth 11.2 bn EUR (first by value). Agreste estimate for the 2026 harvest (1 Oct 2026): about 35 mhl.

countries.overview:
France is the country every other wine nation measures itself against, and the reason is less about volume than about an idea: that a wine should taste of a named place, and that the place should be protected by law. Italy makes more wine and Spain has more vines, but France invented the modern grammar of wine. Bordeaux gave the world the blended red and the château as a brand. Burgundy taught it that a single walled field can be worth more than a whole valley. Champagne turned a cold-climate accident into the world's celebration drink. The Rhône, the Loire and Alsace defined what Syrah, Chenin Blanc and Riesling can say about stone and weather.

The numbers are large even in a shrinking market. The OIV put France's vineyard at 740,000 hectares in 2025, second in the world after Spain, after a 4.4 percent fall in a single year as growers in Bordeaux, the Languedoc and the Rhône pulled out vines under state-funded grubbing-up schemes. France made 36.1 million hectolitres of wine in 2025, second only to Italy and 16 percent below its five-year average, and the first official estimate for 2026 (about 35 million hectolitres in October 2026) points to another historically small crop after a hot, dry summer. France is still the world's largest exporter by value (11.2 billion euros in 2025) and its second-largest wine-drinking nation, though the French now drink far less than their grandparents did.

What makes France matter to a wine nerd is the density of difference. Within a few hours' drive you move from the chalk of Champagne to the Kimmeridgian marl of Chablis, from the limestone and clay mosaic of the Côte d'Or to the granite of Beaujolais and Hermitage, the galets roulés of Châteauneuf-du-Pape and the gravel croupes of the Médoc. Each of those soils sits under a different climate: Atlantic in Bordeaux and the Loire, semi-continental in Burgundy and Alsace, Alpine in Savoie and the Jura, Mediterranean in Provence, the Languedoc and the southern Rhône. The French word for the sum of all this is terroir, and the country's whole legal system is built to defend it.

That system was born of crisis. Phylloxera destroyed most of France's vineyards between the 1860s and 1890s, fraud and artificial wine flooded the market, and in 1907 hundreds of thousands of Languedoc growers marched in protest. The answer, worked out by lawmakers and growers such as Joseph Capus and Baron Pierre Le Roy de Boiseaumarié, was the 1935 law that created the appellation d'origine contrôlée and the body now called INAO. Today there are about 360 wine AOCs, each with a cahier des charges that fixes where the grapes grow, which varieties are allowed, how much each hectare may yield and how the wine is made.

The eastern half of the country holds many of the most coveted names. Burgundy runs from Chablis to the Mâconnais, with the Côte d'Or's 32 grand crus at its heart. Beaujolais shows what Gamay does on granite. The Rhône Valley falls from the steep schist and granite of Côte Rôtie and Hermitage to the sun-baked Grenache country around Châteauneuf-du-Pape. Alsace, French and German by turns, makes some of the world's great dry and sweet whites behind the Vosges. In the mountains the Jura ages wine under a veil of yeast to make vin jaune, while Savoie, Bugey and Lorraine keep alive grapes and styles found nowhere else.

The West holds Bordeaux and its classifications, the long string of Loire appellations, Cognac and Armagnac country, the varied Southwest, and then the Mediterranean arc of the Languedoc, Roussillon, Provence and Corsica. Climate change is now rewriting all of it: harvests in Burgundy and the Rhône start two to three weeks earlier than in the 1980s, alcohol levels have risen, frosts and hail are more destructive, and INAO has begun admitting heat-tolerant and disease-resistant varieties for trial within appellations. France's future will be decided by how well the 1935 idea of fixed places can adapt to a moving climate.

history.title: Greeks from Phocaea found Massalia
history.text: Greek settlers from Phocaea in Asia Minor founded Massalia (Marseille) around 600 BC and brought vines, amphorae and the habit of drinking wine with meals. From this trading port Greek wine and Greek drinking vessels moved up the Rhône corridor to the Celtic world, and the earliest vineyards of Provence and the lower Rhône trace back to this contact.

history.title: The Vix krater: Celtic princes drink Mediterranean wine
history.text: At Mont Lassois near Vix in northern Burgundy a Celtic noblewoman was buried around 510 BC with a bronze krater 1.64 m tall, the largest Greek wine-mixing vessel known. Found in 1953, it shows that wine was a status drink of the Gaulish elite long before anyone in Burgundy grew grapes, and that the trade route ran from Massalia up the Rhône and Saône.

history.title: Lattara: the oldest known winemaking in France
history.text: Excavations at the Etruscan and Gaulish trading port of Lattara (Lattes, near Montpellier) uncovered a limestone pressing platform dated to about 425 to 400 BC, along with Etruscan amphorae that had held wine. Chemical residue analysis published in 2013 made it the earliest firm evidence of grape wine being made on French soil, by Gauls who had learned the craft from Mediterranean traders.

history.title: Roman Gaul and the Allobrogica vine
history.text: After Rome conquered southern Gaul (Gallia Narbonensis, from 121 BC) vineyards spread north along the rivers. Pliny the Elder and Columella praised the wine of Vienne on the Rhône, made by the Allobroges from a cold-hardy vine they called Allobrogica, often linked to the ancestors of Syrah or Mondeuse. By the third and fourth centuries vines were planted around Bordeaux, in Burgundy (a speech to Constantine in 312 mentions old vineyards near Autun) and on the Moselle.

history.title: Cluny, Cîteaux and the walled Clos de Vougeot
history.text: The Benedictine abbey of Cluny (founded 910) and the Cistercian abbey of Cîteaux (founded 1098) became Burgundy's great landowners. Cistercian monks observed that different plots gave consistently different wines, built up the Clos de Vougeot vineyard from the early 1100s and had walled its 50 hectares by 1336. Their patient mapping of plots by quality is the ancestor of Burgundy's climats and of the whole French idea of terroir.

history.title: Eleanor of Aquitaine and the English claret trade
history.text: When Eleanor of Aquitaine married Henry Plantagenet in 1152, and he became Henry II of England two years later, Bordeaux and Gascony passed to the English crown for three centuries. Light red clairet shipped from Bordeaux became England's everyday wine, and privileges granted to Bordeaux merchants let them block upriver wines until their own had sold. The trade lasted until the French victory at Castillon in 1453 and left English a lasting word: claret.

history.title: The popes in Avignon
history.text: Clement V moved the papacy to Avignon in 1309, and his successor John XXII built a summer castle on the hill above a village that became Châteauneuf-du-Pape. The papal court's demand for wine raised the reputation of the southern Rhône and of Burgundy, whose reds the popes imported up the Saône and down the Rhône. The village took its present name in 1893.

history.title: Philip the Bold bans the 'disloyal' Gamay
history.text: Duke Philip the Bold of Burgundy issued an ordinance in 1395 ordering growers to uproot Gamay, which he called a very bad and disloyal plant, in favour of Pinot (then called Noirien). The decree, repeated by later dukes, is one of the first laws anywhere to regulate grape varieties for quality, and it explains why Pinot Noir rules the Côte d'Or while Gamay found its home in Beaujolais.

history.title: Dutch merchants reshape French wine
history.text: Dutch traders became the main buyers of French wine in the 1600s. They wanted cheap white wine to distill into brandewijn (brandy), which pushed the Charente and Armagnac toward spirits, and sweet wines from Sauternes, Monbazillac and the Loire. Dutch engineers also drained the marshes of the Médoc, opening the gravel banks where Bordeaux's great châteaux would later be planted.

history.title: The Bordeaux classification
history.text: For the Exposition Universelle in Paris, Napoleon III asked Bordeaux to present its best wines, and the city's brokers ranked the red châteaux of the Médoc (plus Haut-Brion) into five growths and the sweet wines of Sauternes and Barsac into their own classes, using prices achieved over many decades. The list has changed only once for the reds (Mouton Rothschild's promotion in 1973) and still shapes prices today.

history.title: Phylloxera arrives in the Gard
history.text: After oidium (powdery mildew) had cut yields in the 1850s, a far worse plague appeared: vines began dying at Pujaut in the Gard in 1863. In 1868 Jules-Émile Planchon identified the cause as an aphid-like insect from America, Phylloxera vastatrix. Over the next three decades it destroyed most of the French vineyard. The cure, grafting European vines onto resistant American rootstocks, was championed by scientists in Montpellier in the 1880s and remains universal practice.

history.title: The fraud law and the revolt of the Midi
history.text: Replanting after phylloxera, cheap Algerian imports and sugar-stretched or artificial wine caused a price collapse. A law of 1 August 1905 made fraud in food and wine a crime, but prices kept falling. In 1907 Languedoc growers led by Marcelin Albert of Argeliers staged mass rallies, reaching hundreds of thousands in Montpellier on 9 June. Troops fired on protesters in Narbonne and the 17th Infantry Regiment mutinied in Béziers. The crisis pushed France toward controlling origin and quality by law.

history.title: Le Roy, Capus and the birth of the AOC
history.text: Laws of 1919 let courts define appellations by local custom, which proved weak. In 1923 Baron Pierre Le Roy de Boiseaumarié of Château Fortia led Châteauneuf-du-Pape's growers to set their own rules on boundaries, grape varieties, minimum ripeness and sorting. With the Bordeaux senator Joseph Capus he pushed for a national system, achieved by the decree-law of 30 July 1935 that created appellations d'origine contrôlées and the national committee that became INAO in 1947. The first AOCs, including Arbois, Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Tavel, were decreed in 1936.

history.title: AOP, IGP, Vin de France and the Climats on the UNESCO list
history.text: EU wine reform in 2009 recast the French pyramid: AOCs became AOPs (protected designations of origin, though AOC may still be used), vins de pays became IGPs, and basic table wine became Vin de France, which may now show grape and vintage. In July 2015 UNESCO listed both the Climats of Burgundy and the Champagne hillsides, houses and cellars as World Heritage, recognising vineyard landscapes themselves as cultural monuments.

history.title: Heat, grubbing up and a shrinking vineyard
history.text: On 28 June 2019 Vérargues in the Hérault recorded 46.0°C, France's highest temperature ever, scorching vines across the Languedoc. Falling consumption, export troubles and repeated frost, hail and drought followed, and from 2023 the state funded the grubbing up of tens of thousands of hectares, especially in Bordeaux. The OIV recorded a 34,000 hectare drop in French vineyard area in 2025 alone, and the 2026 harvest was estimated at about 35 million hectolitres, one of the smallest in decades.

countries.classification:
France's wine law is a pyramid built on the idea that origin, not grape or brand, is the guarantee of character.

At the top sit about 360 Appellations d'Origine Contrôlées (AOC), called Appellations d'Origine Protégées (AOP) in EU language since 2009; labels may use either term. Each AOC has a cahier des charges approved by INAO (Institut national de l'origine et de la qualité) and the agriculture ministry. It defines the delimited area, often parcel by parcel, the permitted grape varieties and their proportions, minimum planting density, pruning and maximum yield, minimum natural ripeness, winemaking and ageing rules, and sometimes the bottle. Growers' unions (ODG) write and defend these rules, and independent bodies inspect and taste the wines. AOCs nest inside each other: a regional appellation such as Bourgogne covers hundreds of communes, a village appellation such as Gevrey-Chambertin a few, and a grand cru such as Chambertin a single named vineyard.

Below the AOCs come about 75 Indications Géographiques Protégées (IGP, the former vins de pays created in 1968 to 1979), such as IGP Pays d'Oc or Vin de Pays du Val de Loire, with looser rules and the freedom to name grape varieties. At the base is Vin de France, the 2009 successor to vin de table, which may show grape and vintage but no place smaller than France. Some of the country's most sought-after natural and experimental wines are bottled as Vin de France because their makers break appellation rules on grapes, style or yield.

Region-specific hierarchies sit on top of the AOC system. Burgundy ranks land itself: regional, village, premier cru and grand cru, with 33 grand crus that are each an AOC in their own right. Bordeaux ranks châteaux, not land, through the 1855 classification, the Graves list of 1953 to 1959, the Saint-Émilion classification revised roughly each decade, and the Crus Bourgeois and Crus Artisans. Alsace has 51 grand cru AOCs, Champagne divides villages into grand cru and premier cru, and the Rhône and Beaujolais ladder runs from regional wine through Villages to named crus. Labels can add a lieu-dit (a named place in the land register) or a climat where the rules allow, which is how single-vineyard names reach the bottle outside the formal classifications.

Why it matters: an AOC name tells you where the grapes grew, the varieties you can expect and a minimum style, but not quality on its own. The grower's name still counts, which is why French wine lovers learn both maps and producers.
countries.climate_soils:
France sits where four climate influences meet, which is why it can make both Chablis and Banyuls. The west is Atlantic: mild winters, frequent rain and long, temperate growing seasons in Bordeaux, Cognac and the Loire, where the ocean moderates heat but brings rot pressure. The northeast and centre are semi-continental: Champagne, Burgundy, Alsace and the Jura have cold winters, spring frost risk and warm summers, so vineyards cling to sheltered, sun-facing slopes. The Alps and the Jura mountains add altitude and short seasons in Savoie and Bugey. The south is Mediterranean: hot, dry summers, mild winters and strong winds such as the mistral in the Rhône and Provence and the tramontane in Roussillon, which dry the grapes and keep disease low but bring drought stress.

The rocks underneath are just as varied. Much of the northeast lies on Jurassic limestone and marl laid down in shallow seas: the Kimmeridgian marl of Chablis and Sancerre, the Bajocian and Bathonian limestones of the Côte d'Or, the marls of the Jura. Champagne grows on Cretaceous chalk. The old crystalline massifs supply granite and schist: the Vosges under parts of Alsace, the Massif Central's eastern edge in Beaujolais and the northern Rhône, and the schists of the Roussillon and Corsica. Great rivers have left gravel and pebble terraces: the Médoc's Garonne gravels and the quartzite galets roulés of the southern Rhône. Rift valleys and faults, such as the Saône graben below the Côte d'Or and the Rhine rift under Alsace, created the long fault-line slopes on which many of France's finest vineyards sit.

Climate change is moving the targets. Average growing-season temperatures in Burgundy and the Rhône have risen by well over 1°C since the 1980s, harvests start in August more often than in October, and wines carry more alcohol. Spring frosts after early budburst (2016, 2017, 2021) and summer heatwaves (2003, 2019, 2022, 2025) have become the main threats. Growers are responding with later pruning, higher trunks, cover crops, north-facing and higher sites, and new or rediscovered varieties.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.note: France's most planted grape; the backbone of Bordeaux's Right Bank and of most Bordeaux blends, also common in the Southwest and IGP Pays d'Oc.

grapes.name: Ugni Blanc
grapes.note: Italy's Trebuchino, planted mostly in Cognac and Armagnac country for distillation; high-acid, neutral and very productive.

grapes.name: Grenache
grapes.note: The leading red of the southern Rhône, Languedoc and Roussillon; the core of Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Gigondas and the vins doux naturels of Banyuls and Maury.

grapes.name: Syrah
grapes.note: Native to the northern Rhône (Côte Rôtie, Hermitage, Cornas), widely planted in the south as a blending partner for Grenache.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: Dominant on the Left Bank gravels of the Médoc and Graves, and widely planted in the Languedoc for varietal IGP wines.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: Burgundy's white grape from Chablis to the Mâconnais, a key Champagne grape, and important in the Jura and Languedoc (Limoux).

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.note: The red grape of Burgundy and the most planted grape in Champagne; also Alsace's only red and important in the Jura, Savoie and Sancerre.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.note: The red of the middle Loire (Chinon, Bourgueil, Saumur-Champigny) and a major Saint-Émilion and Pomerol partner.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.note: Loire classics Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé, white Bordeaux and Sauternes (with Sémillon), and Touraine.

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.note: Once the workhorse of the Midi; old bush vines now prized in Corbières, Faugères and Roussillon.

grapes.name: Gamay
grapes.note: The Beaujolais grape on granite and schist, also found in the Loire, Savoie and the Massif Central; banished from the Côte d'Or in 1395.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.note: The Loire's great white, dry to lusciously sweet and sparkling in Vouvray, Savennières, Anjou and Saumur.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.note: Alsace's noblest grape, made mostly dry on granite, limestone and volcanic grand crus.

grapes.name: Gewurztraminer
grapes.note: Alsace's aromatic speciality, often off-dry, and the main grape of many late-harvest wines.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre
grapes.note: Late-ripening star of Bandol and an important blender in Châteauneuf-du-Pape and the Languedoc.

grapes.name: Savagnin
grapes.note: The Jura's ancient white grape, aged under a veil of yeast to make vin jaune.

grapes.name: Melon de Bourgogne
grapes.note: The grape of Muscadet near Nantes, a Burgundian refugee.

grapes.name: Sémillon
grapes.note: The botrytis-prone partner of Sauvignon in Sauternes, Barsac and dry white Graves.

regions.name: Burgundy
regions.tagline: A 250 km ribbon of slopes where monks, dukes and growers spent a thousand years deciding which few rows make the best wine.
regions.summary:
Burgundy is the place where wine stopped being about grapes and started being about addresses. From Chablis in the north to the Mâconnais in the south, the region strings together about 30,000 hectares of vines, yet its reputation rests on a strip of hillside in the Côte d'Or barely 50 km long and often only a few hundred metres wide. There, two grapes do almost everything: Pinot Noir for reds and Chardonnay for whites, with Aligoté and Gamay in supporting roles.

What makes Burgundy unique is how finely the land is divided and ranked. The region has 84 appellations, from the broad regional AOC Bourgogne to village names such as Meursault, more than 600 premier cru climats and 33 grand crus. A single grand cru such as Clos de Vougeot can be split among about 80 owners, so the same vineyard yields wines of very different quality. That is why Burgundy lovers learn both the map and the grower, and why the market splits between domaines that farm and bottle their own grapes and négociant houses in Beaune and Nuits-Saint-Georges that buy grapes, must or wine.

Burgundy has swung from red to white. In 1983 output was roughly half red and half white; by 2022 the BIVB estimated 61 percent white, 28 percent red and 11 percent Crémant de Bourgogne. Prices have also detached from the rest of the wine world. Small crops in 2016, 2019, 2021 and 2024, global demand and a limited supply of land have pushed grand cru prices to levels where a hectare of Montrachet or Chambertin is worth tens of millions of euros.
regions.history:
Romans and Gauls planted vines here by the third century, but Burgundy's character was shaped by the church. The Benedictines of Cluny (910) and the Cistercians of Cîteaux (1098) gathered gifts of vineyard land, compared plots over generations and walled the best ones: Clos de Vougeot, Clos de Bèze, Clos de Tart. The Valois dukes of Burgundy, who ruled a state stretching to Flanders from 1363 to 1477, used wine as diplomacy; Philip the Bold's ordinance of 1395 ordered Gamay pulled up in favour of Pinot.

The French Revolution broke up church and noble estates from 1789 and sold them as biens nationaux, and Napoleonic inheritance law then divided holdings among all children. That is why Burgundy's grand crus are a patchwork of tiny parcels. In the nineteenth century villages hyphenated their names to their most famous vineyard (Gevrey added Chambertin in 1847, Chambolle added Musigny in 1878, Puligny and Chassagne added Montrachet in 1879), the railway reached Beaune and Dijon, and phylloxera arrived in 1878. Négociants dominated until the 1930s, when the depression, the AOC law of 1935 and pioneers such as the Marquis d'Angerville, Henri Gouges and Armand Rousseau began domaine bottling, a shift that became the norm after the 1980s.

In July 2015 UNESCO inscribed the Climats, terroirs of Burgundy on the World Heritage list: 1,247 named vineyard plots on the slopes from Dijon to the Maranges, together with the historic centres of Dijon and Beaune that governed and traded them.
regions.terroir:
Burgundy's slopes sit on Jurassic limestones and marls laid down 150 to 200 million years ago, tilted and broken when the Bresse plain collapsed along the Saône fault as the Alps rose. The Côte d'Or is that fault scarp: an east and southeast-facing escarpment whose middle slopes (about 250 to 350 m) combine thin, well-drained soil, morning sun and shelter from western weather. Above, the soil is too thin and cold; below, on the flat, it is deep, rich and frost-prone. That simple geometry explains most of the classification: grand crus sit mid-slope, premier crus beside and just above or below, village wine lower down, regional wine on the plain.

Differences in the rock explain the rest. In the Côte de Nuits, harder Bajocian and Bathonian limestones and marls give structured, long-lived reds. In the Côte de Beaune, Callovian and Oxfordian marls and softer limestones open the slope into gentler, broader hills where Chardonnay excels at Meursault, Puligny and Chassagne. Side valleys called combes funnel cool air and scree onto the vineyards below them, which is why sites such as Clos Saint-Jacques and Les Amoureuses are so distinct. Chablis grows on Kimmeridgian marl full of fossil oyster shells; the Mâconnais on limestone and marl ridges crowned by the cliffs of Solutré and Vergisson.

The climate is semi-continental: cold winters, warm summers, frequent hail and a long, cool ripening season that suits early-ripening Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Climate change has moved harvests from late September and October to late August and early September, increased frost risk after earlier budburst and favoured whites from cooler sites such as Saint-Aubin and the Hautes-Côtes.
regions.grapes: Pinot Noir (about 40 percent of plantings) makes almost all the reds of the Côte d'Or and Côte Chalonnaise and the light reds of Irancy and the Auxerrois. Chardonnay (about half the vineyard) dominates Chablis, the white villages of the Côte de Beaune and the Mâconnais. Aligoté, a sharper white grape, has its own regional AOC and the village AOC Bouzeron. Gamay is grown mainly in the Mâconnais for Mâcon rouge and Coteaux Bourguignons and blended with Pinot in Bourgogne Passe-tout-grains. Minor grapes include Sauvignon Blanc (only in Saint-Bris), César (a dark, tannic Irancy speciality), Pinot Gris (Pinot Beurot), Pinot Blanc and Melon de Bourgogne.
regions.styles: Still reds from Pinot Noir ranging from light, perfumed regional wines to dense, age-worthy grand crus; still whites from Chardonnay from steely Chablis to rich, oak-aged Meursault and Montrachet; Aligoté whites; small amounts of rosé (notably Marsannay); and Crémant de Bourgogne, traditional-method sparkling wine that now makes more than a tenth of Burgundy's output.
regions.classification: Burgundy ranks land, not producers, in four tiers. Regional appellations (Bourgogne, Bourgogne Aligoté, Coteaux Bourguignons, Crémant de Bourgogne, and named zones such as Bourgogne Hautes-Côtes de Nuits) make about half the wine. Forty-four village appellations, such as Pommard or Chablis, take their name from a commune or small group of communes. Within them, premier cru climats may add their name to the village (Volnay premier cru Clos des Ducs). At the top, 33 grand crus are appellations in their own right and carry only the vineyard name: Chambertin, Musigny, Montrachet, Corton and the seven climats of Chablis Grand Cru. A climat is a named, delimited plot with its own history; a lieu-dit is a named place in the land register, which may also appear on village-level labels. A monopole is a climat owned by a single domaine, such as Romanée-Conti or Clos de Tart.

regions.name: Chablis and the Grand Auxerrois
regions.tagline: Chardonnay grown on the fossil bed of an ancient sea, cold enough that growers light fires among the vines in April.
regions.summary: Chablis is Burgundy's northern outpost, about 130 km northwest of Beaune and closer to Champagne than to the Côte d'Or. Its Chardonnay is the archetype of cool, mineral white wine: pale, tense and lemony, with a saline, oyster-shell edge. Around Auxerre, the Grand Auxerrois keeps alive the remnants of a vineyard that once supplied Paris by river: Irancy for reds, Saint-Bris for Sauvignon Blanc, Vézelay for Chardonnay below the great basilica, and several Bourgogne zones such as Chitry, Coulanges-la-Vineuse, Côtes d'Auxerre, Épineuil, Tonnerre and Côte Saint-Jacques.
regions.history: Cistercian monks of Pontigny, founded in 1114, developed the Chablis vineyard, and the canons of Saint-Martin de Tours, who had fled the Vikings with the relics of Saint Martin in 877, built the cellar called the Obédiencerie in the town. Shipped down the Yonne and Seine, the wines of the Yonne were the everyday drink of medieval Paris, and the department carried about 40,000 hectares of vines before phylloxera. Railways bringing cheap southern wine, phylloxera and the First World War nearly wiped the area out; by the 1950s Chablis had only a few hundred hectares. Frost-fighting techniques (heaters from the 1960s, sprinkler systems from the 1970s) and a disputed 1978 extension onto Portlandian soils allowed it to grow back to more than 5,000 hectares.
regions.terroir: The key is Kimmeridgian marl: alternating beds of grey limestone and marl about 155 million years old, packed with the tiny comma-shaped fossil oyster Exogyra virgula. It gives the grand and premier crus their chalky, saline tension. The plateau tops are harder Portlandian limestone, where most Petit Chablis grows. The Serein river cuts the vineyard in two: the seven grand crus face southwest on a single slope above the town on the right bank. Winters are cold and spring frost is the great danger, so growers use heaters (bougies), wind machines and water sprinklers that coat buds in protective ice.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay only for Chablis. Pinot Noir and César in Irancy; Sauvignon Blanc and Sauvignon Gris in Saint-Bris; Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Aligoté for the Bourgogne zones; Aligoté and Sacy for Crémant de Bourgogne.
regions.styles: Dry whites from lean and saline (Petit Chablis) to powerful and age-worthy (grand cru, often partly barrel-fermented); light, peppery reds from Irancy and Épineuil; aromatic Sauvignon from Saint-Bris; Crémant de Bourgogne from Bailly and the co-ops.
regions.classification: Four levels: Petit Chablis (about 1,000 ha mostly on plateau soils), Chablis (the bulk), Chablis premier cru (about 40 climats grouped under 17 main names, about 750 to 800 ha in production) and Chablis Grand Cru (one AOC of about 100 ha split into seven climats: Blanchot, Bougros, Les Clos, Grenouilles, Preuses, Valmur and Vaudésir).

regions.name: Côte de Nuits
regions.tagline: Twenty kilometres of limestone that hold 24 of Burgundy's grand crus and almost all of its most expensive red wine.
regions.summary: The Côte de Nuits runs from the southern edge of Dijon to Corgoloin, a narrow east-facing slope rarely more than a kilometre wide. It is red wine country: Pinot Noir makes more than 90 percent of the wine, and 24 of the Côte d'Or's 32 grand crus lie here, from Chambertin in Gevrey to La Tâche and Romanée-Conti in Vosne. Each village has a recognisable personality: the rose-scented Marsannay, the muscular Gevrey-Chambertin, the bridge village of Morey-Saint-Denis, silky Chambolle-Musigny, the walled Clos de Vougeot, opulent Vosne-Romanée and the firmer, earthier Nuits-Saint-Georges.
regions.history: The slope was worked by the abbeys of Bèze, Cîteaux, Saint-Vivant de Vergy and the canons of Langres, who left walled clos such as Clos de Bèze, Clos de Vougeot and Clos de Tart. The Prince de Conti's purchase of La Romanée in 1760 and Napoleon's taste for Chambertin made these names famous. In the twentieth century growers such as Armand Rousseau and Henri Gouges pioneered domaine bottling, and later Henri Jayer's work at Cros Parantoux helped define the modern style of pure, ripe, destemmed Pinot Noir.
regions.terroir: The Côte de Nuits is steeper and narrower than the Côte de Beaune, and harder limestones (Comblanchien, Prémeaux and the Bajocian entroquite limestones full of crinoid fragments) lie close to the surface. Combes such as Lavaux at Gevrey and the Combe d'Orveau above Chambolle cut through the slope, spreading scree fans and cool night air. Marls appear at the foot of the slope and in places such as Bonnes-Mares and Clos de Vougeot, where the soil varies from top to bottom. Most grand crus sit at 250 to 300 m on the gentle middle slope just above the Route des Grands Crus.
regions.grapes: Pinot Noir dominates; Chardonnay and some Pinot Blanc make rare whites (Musigny blanc, Clos Blanc de Vougeot, Nuits-Saint-Georges blanc from Les Perrières and Clos de l'Arlot, Morey's Monts Luisants).
regions.styles: Reds above all, from light and early-drinking Côte de Nuits-Villages to long-lived grand crus; Marsannay rosé; small volumes of white.
regions.classification: Eight village appellations plus Côte de Nuits-Villages, numerous premier crus and 24 grand crus. Flagey-Échezeaux has no village appellation of its own: its village and premier cru land is sold as Vosne-Romanée, while Échezeaux and Grands-Échezeaux are grand crus in their own right.

regions.name: Côte de Beaune
regions.tagline: The southern half of the Côte d'Or, where Burgundy's great white wines are made and its red wine trade still has its headquarters.
regions.summary:
The Côte de Beaune runs about 25 km from the hill of Corton to the Maranges, and it is broader and gentler than the Côte de Nuits, with wider combes and more varied soils. That variety makes it Burgundy's most versatile slope: perfumed reds in Savigny, Beaune, Pommard and Volnay, and the world's benchmark Chardonnays in Meursault, Puligny-Montrachet and Chassagne-Montrachet. It has eight grand crus: the red and white Corton, the white Corton-Charlemagne and Charlemagne on the same hill, and the five Montrachets that straddle Puligny and Chassagne.

The town of Beaune is the commercial heart of Burgundy. Under its streets run kilometres of cellars belonging to négociant houses such as Bouchard Père et Fils, Joseph Drouhin, Louis Jadot, Louis Latour, Chanson, Champy and Albert Bichot, and every November the Hospices de Beaune charity auction sets the tone for the new vintage.
regions.history:
Beaune was a Gallo-Roman settlement and became the seat of the dukes of Burgundy before Dijon. In 1443 the chancellor Nicolas Rolin and his wife Guigone de Salins founded the Hôtel-Dieu, a hospital for the poor whose roof of glazed coloured tiles is now Burgundy's emblem. Over the centuries benefactors gave it vineyards, and since 1859 the Hospices has sold the wine of its roughly 60 ha domaine at an annual charity auction. Run by Christie's from 2005 to 2020 and by Sotheby's since 2021, the 165th sale on 16 November 2025 offered 552 barrels and raised about 18.8 million euros (about $21.5 million), with the Pièce des Présidents, a barrel of Pommard premier cru Les Rugiens, selling for around $460,000.

Many great white-wine domaines (Leflaive, Coche-Dury, Lafon, Roulot, Ramonet) grew from smallholdings in the twentieth century, while the négociants of Beaune kept the region's trade connected to the world. The Cité des Climats et vins de Bourgogne, opened in 2023, has its flagship in Beaune.
regions.terroir: The slope is a patchwork of Middle and Upper Jurassic rocks. Around Corton the hill is capped by hard limestone over Oxfordian marls, with whites on the upper marly slopes (Corton-Charlemagne) and reds on the iron-rich lower slopes. From Beaune to Volnay limestone dominates, giving fine, fragrant reds, while Pommard's heavier clays give more muscular ones. South of Volnay, at Meursault, the slope turns more southeast and the soils become marly and stony: ideal for Chardonnay. At Puligny the water table is high (cellars are shallow), and the Montrachet hill rises above the village on thin soil over hard limestone. Saint-Aubin, Saint-Romain and the Hautes-Côtes de Beaune sit higher in the hills and benefit from a cooler climate.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay for the great whites of Meursault, Puligny-Montrachet, Chassagne-Montrachet, Corton-Charlemagne and Saint-Aubin; Pinot Noir for the reds of Corton, Aloxe, Savigny, Beaune, Pommard, Volnay, Monthélie, Santenay and Maranges.
regions.styles: Red and white in almost every village; Volnay and Pommard are almost entirely red, Puligny almost entirely white. Crémant de Bourgogne and Aligoté come from the plain and the Hautes-Côtes.
regions.classification: Seventeen village appellations plus the Côte de Beaune and Côte de Beaune-Villages AOCs; many hundreds of premier cru climats; eight grand crus (Corton, Corton-Charlemagne, Charlemagne, Montrachet, Chevalier-Montrachet, Bâtard-Montrachet, Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet, Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet). Red wines from most villages may also be sold as Côte de Beaune-Villages.

regions.name: Côte Chalonnaise
regions.tagline: Burgundy's hidden middle: five villages making honest red and white Burgundy at a fraction of Côte d'Or prices.
regions.summary: South of Santenay the slope breaks up into a jumble of hills west of Chalon-sur-Saône, and the Côte Chalonnaise begins. Its five village appellations (Bouzeron, Rully, Mercurey, Givry and Montagny) and the regional Bourgogne Côte Chalonnaise make Pinot Noir and Chardonnay in the same styles as the Côte de Beaune, but lighter, firmer and much cheaper. Rully is the source of much Crémant de Bourgogne; Bouzeron is the only village appellation for Aligoté.
regions.history: Chalon-sur-Saône was a Roman river port, and Givry was said to be the favourite wine of King Henri IV. The Cistercians of La Ferté, the first daughter house of Cîteaux, and the abbey of Cluny farmed vines here. In the twentieth century the area rebuilt after phylloxera more slowly than the Côte d'Or, and négociants such as Faiveley (at Mercurey) and Antonin Rodet invested heavily. Aubert de Villaine of the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti has made wine at Bouzeron since 1973, which helped win Bouzeron its village AOC in 1997.
regions.terroir: Unlike the continuous Côte d'Or escarpment, the Chalonnaise is a series of separate limestone and marl hills with valleys between them, so vineyards face many directions and sit higher (250 to 400 m). The soils are similar Jurassic limestones and marls, with Triassic marls in places. The climate is a little warmer but more exposed, and wines are typically leaner and more mineral than in the Côte de Beaune.
regions.grapes: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; Aligoté at Bouzeron; Gamay for Passe-tout-grains and Coteaux Bourguignons.
regions.styles: Red and white still wines; much Crémant de Bourgogne around Rully.
regions.classification: Village appellations with premier crus in Rully, Mercurey, Givry and Montagny (Montagny is white only, Givry mostly red); no grand crus.

regions.name: Mâconnais
regions.tagline: Burgundy's sunny south, where limestone cliffs rise over Chardonnay country and the village of Chardonnay itself still stands.
regions.summary: The Mâconnais, between Tournus and the Beaujolais border, is Burgundy's largest white-wine area. Its rolling hills of limestone and marl make mostly Chardonnay, sold as Mâcon, Mâcon-Villages or one of 27 Mâcon village names, and its southern corner holds the region's best whites: Pouilly-Fuissé, Saint-Véran, Pouilly-Loché and Pouilly-Vinzelles, under the dramatic limestone cliffs of Solutré and Vergisson. Viré-Clessé in the north is the other village appellation. The wines are riper, rounder and more fruit-driven than Côte d'Or whites, from crisp co-op Mâcon to oak-aged single climats that can rival Meursault.
regions.history: The abbey of Cluny, founded in 910 in the hills west of Mâcon, was the most powerful monastery in Christendom and a major vineyard owner. The Roche de Solutré has given its name to the Solutrean culture of the Upper Palaeolithic (about 22,000 to 17,000 years ago), and thousands of horse bones were found at its foot. The region's co-operatives, starting with Chardonnay and Lugny in the 1920s, produce most of the volume. Since the 1980s a generation of growers such as Jean Thévenet, Guffens-Heynen and the Château de Fuissé has shown how good Mâconnais Chardonnay can be, and Pouilly-Fuissé won 22 premier crus in 2020.
regions.terroir: Parallel limestone ridges running north to south, separated by valleys, with marl and clay on the lower slopes. In the south the Jurassic limestone ends in the cliffs of Solutré and Vergisson, whose scree feeds the Pouilly-Fuissé slopes; to the south the limestone gives way to the granite of the Beaujolais, and Saint-Véran straddles both. The climate is warmer and sunnier than the Côte d'Or, with Mediterranean influences reaching up the Saône valley.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay dominates (more than 85 percent); Gamay and some Pinot Noir for Mâcon rouge.
regions.styles: Mostly dry white; some light red Mâcon and rosé; Crémant de Bourgogne.
regions.classification: Regional Mâcon, Mâcon-Villages and Mâcon plus a village name; five village appellations (Pouilly-Fuissé, Pouilly-Loché, Pouilly-Vinzelles, Saint-Véran, Viré-Clessé). Pouilly-Fuissé premier crus since the 2020 vintage, Pouilly-Loché and Pouilly-Vinzelles premier crus since 2024.

regions.name: Beaujolais
regions.tagline: Gamay on pink granite: the region that gave the world a party wine, then a cult of natural winemakers and ten serious crus.
regions.summary:
Beaujolais runs about 55 km from the southern edge of the Mâconnais to the outskirts of Lyon, on the eastern slopes of the Monts du Beaujolais. Almost all of it is Gamay Noir, which here, on granite and schist, makes wines of bright red fruit, low tannin and joyful freshness. The region is often grouped with Burgundy, and it shares the Bourgogne regional appellations, but its grape, soils and culture are its own.

Beaujolais has three main tiers. Beaujolais AOC covers the south and makes light reds, much of it once sold as Beaujolais Nouveau. Beaujolais-Villages covers 38 communes in the north. At the top, ten crus, each a separate AOC, sit in the granite hills of the north: Saint-Amour, Juliénas, Chénas, Moulin-à-Vent, Fleurie, Chiroubles, Morgon, Régnié, Brouilly and Côte de Brouilly. Their wines are anything but simple: Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent age for a decade or more.

The region has been through hard times. Its vineyard area has shrunk by roughly a third since the early 2000s as the Nouveau craze faded, and growers have pulled out vines in the south. Production is now about 400,000 to 500,000 hl a year. White Beaujolais, from Chardonnay, is only about 4 percent of production, and Inter Beaujolais aims to triple it.
regions.history:
The lords of Beaujeu gave the region its name in the tenth century, and its wine supplied Lyon by road and river: the saying goes that Lyon is watered by three rivers, the Rhône, the Saône and the Beaujolais. In the nineteenth century the Paris-Lyon railway opened Paris to it. Beaujolais Nouveau, the new wine of the year, was sold in Lyon's bouchons for centuries; after the Second World War rules allowed its early release, and from 1985 it went on sale on the third Thursday of November. Promoted by négociants such as Georges Duboeuf, it became a global event in the 1980s and 1990s.

As Nouveau's popularity faded, a different revolution grew. Jules Chauvet, a négociant and chemist in La Chapelle-de-Guinchay, argued for wine made without sulphur, chaptalisation or commercial yeasts. His disciples, Marcel Lapierre, Jean Foillard, Guy Breton and Jean-Paul Thévenet, called the Gang of Four by the American importer Kermit Lynch, made Morgon the cradle of the natural wine movement in the 1980s. Their success, and that of a new wave of growers since 2010, has given the crus a cult following.
regions.terroir: The Beaujolais sits at the eastern edge of the Massif Central. In the north the bedrock is mostly pink granite (the gore, a crumbly decomposed granite sand), with blue volcanic diorite at Brouilly, schist at Morgon's Côte du Py, and veins of manganese at Moulin-à-Vent. These acidic, poor, free-draining soils restrain Gamay's vigour and give the crus their structure. The south, the Pierres Dorées, has limestone and clay that give lighter, softer wine and some whites. Vines are trained in traditional gobelet bush form on the slopes, at 200 to 500 m. The climate is semi-continental with Mediterranean influence: warmer than the Mâconnais, with hail and drought as recent threats.
regions.grapes: Gamay Noir à Jus Blanc makes about 95 percent of the wine. Chardonnay (about 4 percent of production) makes Beaujolais blanc, mainly in the south and on the limestone of the north. A little Aligoté is also allowed.
regions.styles: Red Beaujolais from light primeur (Nouveau) to structured, age-worthy crus; Beaujolais rosé; white Beaujolais; Crémant de Bourgogne from the area; and Coteaux Bourguignons. Winemaking often uses whole-bunch semi-carbonic maceration, which gives Gamay its fruity, candied, banana-and-kirsch aroma, though many cru growers also destem and age in oak like Burgundy.
regions.classification: Beaujolais AOC (with 38 communes allowed to add their name, e.g. Beaujolais Lantignié, or to use Beaujolais-Villages); Beaujolais-Villages; ten cru appellations. The crus may also be sold as Bourgogne or Coteaux Bourguignons. There are no premier crus yet, but Fleurie's growers voted in 2023 for a premier cru application covering seven lieux-dits, and other crus have mapped their climats.

regions.name: Rhône Valley
regions.tagline: From the granite cliffs of Côte Rôtie to the pebble-strewn plateau of Châteauneuf-du-Pape: Syrah in the north, Grenache in the south, one river between them.
regions.summary:
The Rhône Valley vineyards run about 250 km from Vienne, just south of Lyon, to Avignon and the Costières de Nîmes, and they form France's second-largest region for appellation wine. Inter Rhône counted 60,223 ha of AOC vineyards in 2025 (excluding Châteauneuf-du-Pape, which reports separately), producing about 2 million hectolitres, three quarters of it red.

The region is really two. The Northern Rhône is a narrow corridor of steep, terraced granite and schist slopes where Syrah is the only red grape and Viognier, Marsanne and Roussanne make the whites: Côte Rôtie, Condrieu, Hermitage, Cornas, Saint-Joseph, Crozes-Hermitage and Saint-Péray. It makes less than 10 percent of the region's wine. After a gap of about 50 km with few vines, the Southern Rhône opens out into a broad, sunny, Mediterranean landscape of garrigue and pebbles where Grenache leads blends with Syrah, Mourvèdre, Cinsault and many others: Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Gigondas, Vacqueyras, Rasteau, Cairanne, Lirac, Tavel and the oceans of Côtes du Rhône. In the hills to the east, the Diois makes sparkling Clairette de Die.

The hierarchy runs from Côtes du Rhône through Côtes du Rhône Villages (with or without one of about 20 village names) to 18 named crus, the latest of which, Laudun, was promoted in 2024.
regions.history:
Vienne was a capital of the Allobroges and later of Roman Gaul, and its wine, vinum picatum with a resinous taste, was praised by Pliny, Martial and Plutarch. The popes in Avignon (1309 to 1377) made the southern vineyards fashionable. In 1650 a ruling in Roquemaure set rules for the wines of the Gard bank of the river, and by 1737 royal edict required casks from that bank to be branded C.D.R. (Côte du Rhône), a very early appellation idea. The name moved to both banks in the nineteenth century.

In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries Hermitage was among the most expensive wines in France, often used to beef up Bordeaux (hermitagé claret). Phylloxera, found at Pujaut near Avignon in 1863, and the decline of the hillside terraces nearly killed the north: by the 1970s Côte Rôtie had barely 70 ha. Marcel Guigal's single-vineyard Côte Rôties from the late 1970s, Gérard Chave in Hermitage, Auguste Clape in Cornas and Georges Vernay in Condrieu helped restore the north's reputation. In the south, Baron Le Roy's 1923 rules for Châteauneuf-du-Pape became the model for France's 1935 appellation law.
regions.terroir:
North of Valence, the Rhône cuts through the eastern edge of the Massif Central, and the vineyards cling to granite, gneiss and schist on the west bank (Côte Rôtie, Condrieu, Saint-Joseph, Cornas) and to the granite outcrop of Hermitage, an old piece of the Massif Central stranded on the east bank when the river changed course. Terraces held by dry-stone walls (chaillées) make farming laborious. The climate is semi-continental, with cold, dry north winds.

South of Montélimar the valley widens into a basin of limestone hills, ancient river terraces and sediments. The Rhône and Durance spread layers of rounded quartzite pebbles (galets roulés) from the Alps over red clay in places such as Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Lirac and the Plan de Dieu; elsewhere there are sands, sandstone (safres), limestone and marl. The Mediterranean climate brings more than 2,500 hours of sun, dry summers and the mistral, a cold north wind that can blow at more than 100 km/h, drying the vines and protecting them from disease but stunting growth. Grenache thrives here, and bush vines (gobelet) still dominate old vineyards.
regions.grapes: Syrah is the sole red grape of the north (Côte Rôtie may co-ferment up to 20 percent Viognier, Hermitage and Crozes up to 15 percent Marsanne and Roussanne, Saint-Joseph 10 percent). Viognier makes Condrieu and Château-Grillet; Marsanne and Roussanne make white Hermitage, Crozes, Saint-Joseph and Saint-Péray. In the south, Grenache is king, blended with Syrah, Mourvèdre, Cinsault, Carignan, Counoise, Vaccarèse, Terret Noir, Muscardin and others; whites come from Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Bourboulenc, Roussanne, Viognier and Picpoul. Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains makes the sweet Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise and the sparkling Clairette de Die Tradition.
regions.styles: Mostly red (about 73 percent), with rosé (14 percent, led by Tavel) and white (13 percent). Styles range from the perfumed, savoury Syrahs of the north and the generous, spicy Grenache blends of the south to sweet fortified Muscat and Grenache (vins doux naturels of Beaumes-de-Venise and Rasteau) and sparkling wines from Die and Saint-Péray.
regions.classification: Four tiers. Côtes du Rhône (regional, about 26,800 ha in 2025); Côtes du Rhône Villages (about 2,700 ha without a village name and 5,300 ha with one); 18 named crus, from Côte Rôtie to Laudun; plus satellite appellations such as Ventoux, Luberon, Grignan-les-Adhémar, Costières de Nîmes, Duché d'Uzès, Côtes du Vivarais and the Diois appellations. Within the crus, lieux-dits may appear on labels (Côte Rôtie and Hermitage are informally mapped into famous sites), but there are no official premier or grand crus.

regions.name: Northern Rhône
regions.tagline: Syrah and Viognier on terraces so steep that vines are tied to wooden stakes, one by one.
regions.summary: The Northern Rhône stretches from Vienne to Valence and contains eight crus on about 4,600 ha (2025). Syrah reaches its classic expression here: smoky, peppery, floral and savoury, from the perfumed Côte Rôtie to the massive, long-lived Hermitage and the wild, tannic Cornas. Viognier, once nearly extinct, makes the opulent Condrieu and Château-Grillet.
regions.history: The Roman city of Vienne made the region famous for wine in the first century AD. Hermitage's name comes from a legend of a knight, Gaspard de Stérimberg, who retired to the hill as a hermit in 1224 after the Albigensian crusade. In the nineteenth century the hill's wine fetched prices close to the best Bordeaux. After decades of neglect, the revival began with Guigal, Chave, Jaboulet and Chapoutier in the 1980s, and land prices on the steepest slopes now rival Burgundy's.
regions.terroir: Granite and gneiss dominate, with mica-schist in Côte Brune, decomposed granite (gore) and loess in places. Slopes of up to 60 percent require terraces and hand work; vines are trained on single stakes (échalas) in Côte Rôtie and Cornas. The climate is continental with Mediterranean hints; the cold north wind (la bise) keeps grapes healthy.
regions.styles: Red Syrah, sometimes co-fermented with white grapes; dry whites; sparkling Saint-Péray.
regions.classification: Eight crus with no further official hierarchy; informal lieux-dits.

regions.name: Southern Rhône
regions.tagline: Grenache country: garrigue, mistral and pebbles, with Châteauneuf-du-Pape at its heart.
regions.summary: The Southern Rhône is a wide plain and hill country from Montélimar to Avignon and across the river into the Gard. It makes more than 90 percent of Rhône wine, mostly Grenache-based blends. Its crus are Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Gigondas, Vacqueyras, Beaumes de Venise, Rasteau, Cairanne, Vinsobres, Lirac, Tavel and Laudun, surrounded by Côtes du Rhône and Côtes du Rhône Villages and, to the east and south, Ventoux, Luberon, Grignan-les-Adhémar, Costières de Nîmes and Duché d'Uzès.
regions.history: The Romans planted along the Rhône and around Vaison-la-Romaine and Orange. The Avignon papacy (1309 to 1377) and its successors made the region's wines fashionable, and the papal enclave of the Comtat Venaissin lasted until 1791. In the twentieth century co-operatives such as those of Cairanne, Rasteau and Tain dominated, but since the 1980s a wave of growers has made Gigondas, Rasteau, Cairanne and Vinsobres into crus in their own right.
regions.terroir: Mediterranean climate with dry summers and the mistral. Soils include ancient Rhône terraces covered with galets roulés over red clay, sands and safres (Miocene sandstones), limestone and marl, and the Jurassic limestone spires of the Dentelles de Montmirail.
regions.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Cinsault, Carignan; whites from Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Bourboulenc, Roussanne, Viognier; Muscat for VDN.
regions.styles: Generous red blends, rosé (Tavel), whites, and vins doux naturels.
regions.classification: Côtes du Rhône, Côtes du Rhône Villages (named and unnamed), ten southern crus.

regions.name: Diois
regions.tagline: Mountain valley sparkling wine from Muscat, made by a method older than Champagne's.
regions.summary: The Diois is the valley of the Drôme river around the town of Die, east of the Rhône in the foothills of the Vercors. Its 1,400 ha make Clairette de Die, a gently sweet, Muscat-scented sparkling wine made by the ancestral method (méthode dioise), plus Crémant de Die, still Coteaux de Die and the reds and whites of Châtillon-en-Diois.
regions.history: Pliny the Elder described a naturally sweet sparkling wine made by the Voconces tribe of the area, whose capital was Dea Augusta (Die), and the Diois claims it as the ancestor of Clairette de Die. AOC status came in 1942.
regions.terroir: Mountain vineyards at 200 to 700 m, among the highest in France, on limestone scree and marls, with cool nights and late harvests.
regions.grapes: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, Clairette; Aligoté and Chardonnay; Gamay, Pinot Noir and Syrah for Châtillon-en-Diois.
regions.styles: Sparkling (ancestral and traditional method) and light still wines.
regions.classification: Four AOCs: Clairette de Die, Crémant de Die, Coteaux de Die, Châtillon-en-Diois.

regions.name: Alsace
regions.tagline: A ribbon of vineyards in the rain shadow of the Vosges, French and German by turns, making some of the world's great Rieslings in tall green flutes.
regions.summary:
Alsace's vineyards form a narrow band about 120 km long on the lower slopes of the Vosges mountains, from Marlenheim west of Strasbourg to Thann near Mulhouse, looking east across the Rhine plain to Germany's Black Forest. CIVA counted 15,529 ha in 2022. It is white-wine country: about 90 percent of the wine is white, and unlike most French regions, it is labelled by grape variety. Four grapes are considered noble, Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat, and only they (plus a few exceptions) may carry a grand cru name. Pinot Blanc and Auxerrois, Sylvaner, Chasselas and Pinot Noir (the only red) make up the rest.

The region has three appellations by name, plus the 51 grand crus, each an AOC in its own right since 2011. AOC Alsace (or Vin d'Alsace) covers most of the volume and may add one of 13 village or area names (such as Alsace Bergheim or Alsace Côtes de Barr) or a lieu-dit. Crémant d'Alsace, created in 1976, is traditional-method sparkling wine, and it has been the region's main growth category in the 2020s as still-wine sales fell. Alsace Grand Cru is the top tier.

Alsace's style ranges from bone-dry, steely Riesling to rich, off-dry Pinot Gris and the lusciously sweet Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles. The region's winemakers have argued for decades about sweetness on labels; since 2021 a sweetness indication (sec, demi-sec, moelleux or doux) has been required on still Alsace wines.
regions.history:
Romans planted vines in Alsace, and by the Middle Ages it was one of Europe's most prized wine regions, shipping wine down the Rhine to Germany, the Netherlands, Scandinavia and England from more than 160 villages. The Thirty Years' War (1618 to 1648) ruined it. After Alsace became French in stages from 1648, its vineyards recovered, but phylloxera and the German annexation after the Franco-Prussian War (1871 to 1918) pushed growers toward high-yielding hybrid varieties and bulk wine for blending in German cellars.

When Alsace returned to France in 1918, growers chose quality: they pulled up hybrids and built the system of varietal labelling and dry, aromatic wines that defines the region today. The Nazi de facto annexation (1940 to 1944) and fighting in the Colmar Pocket in the winter of 1944 to 1945 devastated villages such as Ammerschwihr, Bennwihr, Kientzheim and Sigolsheim. An ordinance of 2 November 1945 created the Alsace appellation; the appellation contrôlée mention became mandatory in 1962, a 1972 law required all Alsace wine to be bottled in the region in the tall flûte bottle, the grand cru AOC followed in 1975, Crémant d'Alsace in 1976 and the Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles mentions in 1984. The Route des Vins d'Alsace, opened in 1953, is one of the oldest wine routes in France.

Family houses such as Hugel (in Riquewihr since 1639), Trimbach (founded 1626), Dopff, Léon Beyer and Faller (Domaine Weinbach) shaped the region's reputation abroad, while co-operatives make a large share of the wine. Alsace was an early centre of biodynamic farming: Eugène Meyer of Bergholtz converted in 1969, and Zind-Humbrecht, Ostertag, Marcel Deiss and Kreydenweiss followed.
regions.terroir:
The Vosges mountains block westerly rain, so Colmar receives only about 600 mm of rain a year, one of the driest places in France, and the growing season is sunny, dry and long, with cool nights that keep acidity. The vineyards run along the Vosges foothills at about 200 to 400 m, facing east, southeast and south.

Geologically Alsace is a fault zone: when the Rhine rift valley sank 30 to 50 million years ago, the edge of the Vosges broke into a mosaic of fractured blocks. That is why Alsace has more soil types in a small space than almost any other wine region: granite (Brand, Schlossberg, Sommerberg), gneiss, schist (Kastelberg), volcanic rock (Rangen), pink Vosges sandstone (Kessler, Kitterlé), limestone and marl (Hengst, Pfersigberg, Zinnkoepflé), gypsum-rich Keuper marl (Schoenenbourg), loess and alluvial plains. Each grand cru is defined by one dominant soil, and growers such as Olivier Humbrecht and Marcel Deiss argue that terroir, not variety, should lead.
regions.grapes: Riesling (about a fifth of the vineyard), Pinot Blanc and Auxerrois, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir (about a tenth and rising), Sylvaner, Muscat (Muscat d'Alsace and Muscat Ottonel), Chasselas and the local Klevener de Heiligenstein (Savagnin Rose). Chardonnay is allowed only for Crémant. Since 2022 Pinot Noir has been permitted in three grands crus: Hengst, Kirchberg de Barr and Vorbourg.
regions.styles: Dry and off-dry varietal whites; blends (Edelzwicker, Gentil); Pinot Noir reds and rosés; Crémant d'Alsace; and late-harvest sweet wines, Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles (botrytised), from the four noble grapes.
regions.classification: Three levels: AOC Alsace (with optional variety, 13 dénominations géographiques complémentaires and lieu-dit names), Crémant d'Alsace, and 51 Alsace grand cru AOCs, each restricted mostly to Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat at lower yields. Exceptions: Zotzenberg allows Sylvaner, Altenberg de Bergheim and Kaefferkopf allow blends, and Hengst, Kirchberg de Barr and Vorbourg allow Pinot Noir. A premier cru tier for the best lieux-dits has been discussed by growers for more than a decade (a proposal led by Olivier Humbrecht MW was presented around 2016), but as of October 2026 no Alsace premier cru has been recognised: INAO's parcel file of 19 October 2026 lists none, the June 2025 revision of the Alsace rules does not mention it, and the authorities have repeatedly warned that the term may not be used. Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles require higher minimum sugar levels, and chaptalisation is forbidden for them.

regions.name: Jura
regions.tagline: A small, stubborn vineyard between Burgundy and Switzerland that ages white wine under a veil of yeast and taught Pasteur how fermentation works.
regions.summary:
The Jura's vineyards form a thin strip about 80 km long on the western slopes of the Jura mountains, between Burgundy's Bresse plain and the Swiss border, centred on the towns of Arbois, Poligny and Lons-le-Saunier. With only about 1,850 ha, it is one of France's smallest wine regions, yet it has seven AOCs, five local grapes and a range of styles found nowhere else.

Its signature is vin jaune, yellow wine made from Savagnin and aged for at least six years and three months in barrels that are never topped up. A film of yeast called the voile (veil) forms on the surface, protecting the wine from oxidation while giving it its nutty, curry-spice and walnut flavours. It is sold in a squat 62 cl bottle, the clavelin, said to represent what remains of a litre after the long ageing. Other Jura wines include ouillé (topped-up) Chardonnay and Savagnin, oxidative whites aged sous voile for shorter periods, the pale reds of Poulsard and Trousseau, vin de paille made from grapes dried for months, Macvin (a fortified grape must) and Crémant du Jura.

Since the 2000s the Jura has become a darling of sommeliers and natural-wine lovers, led by growers such as Pierre Overnoy, Stéphane Tissot, Jean-François Ganevat and the Puffeney, Macle and Labet families.
regions.history: Vines have grown here since Roman times, and the abbey of Château-Chalon, founded in the seventh century, was famous for its yellow wine; its noble canonesses guarded the tradition. In the nineteenth century the Jura had about 20,000 ha of vines. Louis Pasteur, who grew up in Arbois, studied wine fermentation and spoilage here in the 1860s; the small vineyard at Rosières near Arbois that he bought for his experiments now belongs to the Académie des Sciences. Phylloxera and the First World War cut the vineyard to a fraction. Arbois was in the first batch of AOCs decreed in France, on 15 May 1936. Since 1997 the Percée du Vin Jaune festival, held each February in a different village, has celebrated the release of the vin jaune of six years before.
regions.terroir: The vineyard sits at 250 to 450 m on the transition between the Bresse plain and the Jura plateau, on steep, faulted slopes. Soils are mostly Triassic and Liassic marls (grey, blue and red), with limestone scree on the upper slopes. Savagnin likes the grey marls, Poulsard the red and blue marls, Trousseau the warmer gravelly soils around Arbois. The climate is continental: cold winters, wet springs with frost risk, and hot summers. The unheated cellars, cold in winter and warm in summer, are essential to the voile.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay (about half the vineyard), Savagnin (about a fifth), Poulsard or Ploussard (a thin-skinned, pale red grape), Trousseau (a darker, spicier red, the Bastardo of Portugal) and Pinot Noir.
regions.styles: Vin jaune; ouillé and sous-voile whites; light reds and rosés; vin de paille; Macvin du Jura (vin de liqueur); Crémant du Jura; Marc du Jura (spirit).
regions.classification: Four geographic AOCs (Arbois, Château-Chalon, Côtes du Jura, L'Étoile) and three product AOCs (Crémant du Jura, Macvin du Jura, Marc du Jura). Arbois may add Pupillin. Vin jaune and vin de paille are styles within the geographic appellations; Château-Chalon is for vin jaune only.

regions.name: Savoie
regions.tagline: Alpine vineyards under limestone cliffs and glaciers, home to Jacquère, Altesse and Mondeuse.
regions.summary:
Savoie's vineyards are scattered across about 2,000 ha of the French Alps, from the shores of Lake Geneva to the Combe de Savoie south of Chambéry, in Savoie, Haute-Savoie, Ain and Isère. They grow mostly on slopes facing south and southeast, often under limestone cliffs, and they make light, fresh, mountain wines that match the region's cheeses and fondues. Jacquère makes most of the whites; Altesse (Roussette) the finest; Bergeron (Roussanne) the richest; and Mondeuse the region's dark, peppery red.

The main appellation is Vin de Savoie (or Savoie), which can add one of 16 cru names, such as Apremont, Abymes, Chignin, Chignin-Bergeron, Arbin, Cruet, Jongieux and Crépy. Roussette de Savoie is for Altesse whites, with four crus. Seyssel, on the Rhône, is for still and sparkling Altesse and Molette.
regions.history: Vines in Savoie go back to the Allobroges and the Romans. In the Middle Ages the House of Savoy and its monasteries developed the vineyards. On the night of 24 to 25 November 1248, part of Mont Granier collapsed, burying several villages and killing perhaps thousands of people; the rubble field became the vineyards of Apremont and Les Abymes. Savoie became French only in 1860. Phylloxera, emigration and the boom of skiing tourism shaped the modern vineyard, which sells most of its wine locally. The Vin de Savoie AOC dates from 1973, and since 2015 sparkling Vin de Savoie may be labelled Crémant de Savoie. The Crépy appellation was absorbed into Vin de Savoie as a cru in the 2010s.
regions.terroir: Glacial moraines, limestone scree from cliff falls (Apremont, Abymes, Chignin), molasse and marl. Most vineyards lie at 250 to 500 m on south and southeast slopes, often near lakes (Bourget, Geneva) that moderate temperatures. The climate is Alpine, with cold winters, warm summers and the Föhn wind.
regions.grapes: Jacquère (about half the vineyard), Altesse (Roussette), Roussanne (Bergeron), Chasselas (near Lake Geneva), Gringet (unique to Ayze), Mondeuse Noire, Gamay, Pinot Noir and the rare Persan.
regions.styles: Light, crisp white wines; fragrant Altesse; rich Chignin-Bergeron; peppery Mondeuse reds; Crémant de Savoie and the sparkling wines of Ayze and Seyssel.
regions.classification: Vin de Savoie with 16 crus, Roussette de Savoie with four crus (Frangy, Marestel, Monterminod, Monthoux), and Seyssel. A crémant mention has existed since 2015.

regions.name: Bugey
regions.tagline: A pocket of mountain vineyards in the Ain, best known for Cerdon, a pink, sweet, gently sparkling wine.
regions.summary: Bugey is a scattered collection of about 500 ha of vineyards in the southern Ain department, between the Jura and Savoie, in the hills along the Rhône and the Ain. It makes light wines from Chardonnay, Altesse, Jacquère, Gamay, Pinot Noir, Mondeuse and Poulsard. Its signature is Bugey Cerdon, a pink, low-alcohol (about 8 percent), off-dry sparkling wine made from Gamay and Poulsard by the ancestral method. The gastronome Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin was born in Belley, Bugey's capital, in 1755.
regions.history: Bugey was a VDQS from 1958 and became an AOC, along with Roussette du Bugey, in 2009. The vineyard once covered several thousand hectares supplying Lyon but declined with phylloxera and rural exodus.
regions.terroir: Limestone scree and marl on slopes at 200 to 500 m, often steep and terraced, under the cliffs of the southern Jura mountains.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Altesse (Roussette), Jacquère, Mondeuse Blanche; Gamay, Pinot Noir, Mondeuse Noire and Poulsard for reds, rosés and sparkling.
regions.styles: Still white, red and rosé; méthode ancestrale Cerdon; traditional-method sparkling (Bugey mousseux) and Montagnieu.
regions.classification: Bugey AOC (with three crus: Cerdon, Manicle and Montagnieu) and Roussette du Bugey (with two crus: Montagnieu and Virieu-le-Grand).

regions.name: Lorraine
regions.tagline: The remains of a once-great vineyard, now known for vin gris and Auxerrois.
regions.summary: Lorraine's two small appellations, Côtes de Toul and Moselle, are the survivors of a vineyard that covered tens of thousands of hectares before the twentieth century. Côtes de Toul is famous for vin gris, a very pale rosé from Gamay and Pinot Noir; Moselle makes light whites from Auxerrois and Müller-Thurgau and some Pinot Noir. Together they cover only about 200 ha. Wines from the hills of the Meuse further west are sold as IGP Côtes de Meuse.
regions.history: In the nineteenth century Lorraine had more than 30,000 ha of vines supplying Nancy, Metz and the garrisons of the east. Railways bringing cheap southern wine, phylloxera, the First World War, which ravaged the area, and the 1927 delimitation of Champagne that excluded Lorraine growers all destroyed the trade. A handful of growers replanted with grafted vines from the 1930s, and the Côtes de Toul became a VDQS in 1951 and an AOC in 1998; Moselle followed as AOC in 2010.
regions.terroir: Côtes de Toul grows on the east-facing limestone and marl escarpment west of Toul. Moselle's vineyards are scattered in three zones: south of Metz, around Sierck-les-Bains and Contz-les-Bains near Luxembourg, and around Vic-sur-Seille. The climate is cool and continental.
regions.grapes: Gamay, Pinot Noir and Auxerrois at Toul; Auxerrois, Müller-Thurgau, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir and Gamay in Moselle.
regions.styles: Vin gris (pale rosé), light reds, crisp whites, and some traditional-method sparkling wine.
regions.classification: Two AOCs: Côtes de Toul (1998) and Moselle (2010).

appellations.name: Chablis
appellations.summary:
Chablis is one of the most imitated wine names in the world and one of the most distinctive white wines in France. The AOC covers about 3,800 ha of Chardonnay across Chablis and 19 surrounding communes along the Serein valley, and includes the premier cru climats, which carry the village name followed by their own: Chablis premier cru Montée de Tonnerre, Chablis premier cru Vaillons.

Village Chablis is pale, dry and taut, with green apple, lemon and a chalky, sometimes saline finish often compared with oyster shell. It is usually fermented and aged in stainless steel, which keeps the focus on acidity and stone, though many good growers use some old oak. Premier crus add depth and a longer life: Montée de Tonnerre and Mont de Milieu on the warmer right bank give fuller, more structured wines, while left-bank Vaillons, Montmains and Les Forêts are finer and more mineral. Good premier crus improve for 10 years or more and develop notes of hazelnut, honey and wet stone.
appellations.terroir: Kimmeridgian marl and limestone on both banks of the Serein, 130 to 300 m; the premier crus mostly face southeast or southwest on the side valleys. Cold winters and spring frost; harvests in mid-September.
appellations.nerd_note: INAO's parcel file registers only some premier cru names (Fourchaume, Mont de Milieu, Vosgros, Vaucoupin and others) as separate denominations; famous names such as Montée de Tonnerre, Vaillons and Montmains are grouping names that can legally cover several smaller climats, such as Chapelot and Pied d'Aloup under Montée de Tonnerre.

appellations.name: Chablis Grand Cru
appellations.summary:
Chablis Grand Cru is a single appellation of about 107 ha on one southwest-facing hillside across the Serein from the town of Chablis, divided into seven climats that appear on the label: Bougros, Preuses, Vaudésir, Grenouilles, Valmur, Les Clos and Blanchot. It is the 33rd grand cru of Burgundy and the only one outside the Côte d'Or.

The wines are richer, riper and far longer-lived than other Chablis, but still keep the region's nervy acidity and chalk. Many growers ferment or age them partly in oak, and the best need five to ten years to show their depth of honey, smoke, citrus peel and iodine. Les Clos, the largest, is the most powerful and slow-developing; Blanchot, facing southeast, is the most floral and delicate; Valmur and Vaudésir sit in a fold of the hill and show both power and finesse; Preuses is round and open; Bougros, at the western end, is the most rustic and earthy; Grenouilles, the smallest at the foot of the slope by the river, is dominated by the La Chablisienne co-op's Château Grenouilles.
appellations.terroir: Kimmeridgian marl, steep slopes between about 130 and 250 m, sheltered and facing the afternoon sun; the warmest site in Chablis, which is why it ripens fully every year.
appellations.nerd_note: La Moutonne, a 2.35 ha monopole of Domaine Long-Depaquit lying mostly in Vaudésir with a strip in Preuses, is often called the eighth grand cru. It is not a separate climat in law but may appear on the label alongside the grand cru name.

appellations.name: Petit Chablis
appellations.summary: Petit Chablis is the entry level of Chablis: Chardonnay grown mostly on the higher plateaus and Portlandian limestone that surround the Kimmeridgian slopes. It now covers roughly 1,000 ha and has grown fast since the 1990s as frost protection improved. The wines are light, crisp and citrusy, made to be drunk within two or three years, and are some of the best-value white Burgundies. The name says small, but in warm vintages good growers make Petit Chablis that tastes like village Chablis.
appellations.terroir: Portlandian limestone, slightly younger and harder than Kimmeridgian, on exposed plateau tops; more wind and frost.
appellations.nerd_note: The Kimmeridgian versus Portlandian argument split Chablis in the 1970s: traditionalists such as William Fèvre fought expansion onto Portlandian soils, while others argued exposure mattered more than rock.

appellations.name: Irancy
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir with up to 10% César
appellations.summary: Irancy is the red-wine village of the Auxerrois, a natural amphitheatre of slopes 15 km southwest of Chablis that became a village AOC in 1999. Pinot Noir dominates, but growers may add up to 10 percent César, an old, dark and tannic local grape. The wines are fresh, red-fruited and peppery, with more grip than most regional Burgundy, and from good growers they age for a decade. Cherry orchards share the slopes, and the village celebrates them as much as its wine.
appellations.terroir: Kimmeridgian marls and limestone on south and southeast-facing slopes; the Côte de Palotte and Les Mazelots are its best-known climats.
appellations.nerd_note: César, thought to be a cross of Pinot Noir and Argant, survives almost only here; Domaine Colinot is known for rare pure César bottlings sold as Bourgogne.

appellations.name: Saint-Bris
appellations.summary: Saint-Bris is Burgundy's odd one out: the only appellation in the region for Sauvignon Blanc. Grown around the villages of Saint-Bris-le-Vineux, Chitry, Irancy and Quenne south of Auxerre, it was a VDQS called Sauvignon de Saint-Bris before becoming an AOC in 2003. The wines are crisp and grassy like a Loire Sauvignon but with a chalky, Burgundian texture. Sauvignon Gris may be added for extra weight.
appellations.terroir: Kimmeridgian and Portlandian limestones and marls; the village of Saint-Bris sits on a maze of medieval cellars dug into the rock.
appellations.nerd_note: The Goisot family, biodynamic since 2002, bottles single-site Saint-Bris such as Exogyra Virgula, named after the fossil oyster in the soil.

appellations.name: Vézelay
appellations.summary: Vézelay is Burgundy's newest village appellation, promoted from Bourgogne Vézelay to its own AOC in 2017. Its Chardonnay vineyards climb the hills around the hilltop basilica of Sainte-Marie-Madeleine, a UNESCO World Heritage site and the starting point of a pilgrim route to Santiago de Compostela. The wines are light, floral and racy, closer to Chablis than to the Côte d'Or, and the vineyard was largely replanted from the 1970s after a century of abandonment.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl slopes at 200 to 300 m in the Cure valley; cool, late-ripening sites.
appellations.nerd_note: Vézelay grows on four communes: Vézelay, Saint-Père, Asquins and Tharoiseau.

appellations.name: Marsannay
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay (rosé from Pinot Noir)
appellations.summary:
Marsannay, at the northern gate of the Côte de Nuits on the outskirts of Dijon, is the only village appellation in the Côte d'Or that can be red, white and rosé. Covering Couchey, Marsannay-la-Côte and Chenôve, it was long Dijon's source of everyday wine and became famous after 1919 for rosé (Clair de Marsannay), which earned the appellation status before the reds. Since 1987 it has been a full village AOC.

Today the reds are the story: perfumed, crunchy Pinot Noir from climats such as Clos du Roy, Les Longeroies and Au Champ Salomon, which growers have been pushing for premier cru status. They are lighter than Gevrey's but often among the best-value reds in Burgundy.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl slopes facing east and southeast, cooled by air from the Combe de Fixin and the Ouche valley; some vines on alluvial fans.
appellations.nerd_note: Marsannay's growers have applied for premier cru status for about 14 climats, including Clos du Roy and Les Longeroies; INAO's parcel register of October 2026 still lists no Marsannay premier cru.

appellations.name: Fixin
appellations.summary: Fixin is a small village just north of Gevrey-Chambertin whose reds are firm, dark and earthy, like a slightly rustic Gevrey. Most wine is red, from premier crus such as Clos de la Perrière, Clos Napoléon, Les Hervelets, Les Arvelets and Clos du Chapitre. Wines from neighbouring Brochon may be sold as Fixin or Côte de Nuits-Villages. Fixin also has a link to Napoleon: Claude Noisot, an officer of his Imperial Guard, built a park and commissioned a statue of the emperor awakening to immortality by François Rude in 1847.
appellations.terroir: Steep slopes of limestone and marl; Clos de la Perrière sits on an old quarry at the top of the village.
appellations.nerd_note: Clos de la Perrière, a monopole of the Joliet family, was ranked as a tête de cuvée, alongside Chambertin, in Dr Jules Lavalle's 1855 classification of Burgundy.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin
appellations.summary:
Gevrey-Chambertin is the largest red village of the Côte d'Or and the home of nine grand crus, more than any other commune. In 1847 the village of Gevrey added the name of its most famous vineyard, Chambertin, starting a fashion that spread down the Côte. Its reds are the most powerful and structured of the Côte de Nuits: dark fruit, spice, earth and firm tannin, built to age.

The appellation spreads unusually far onto flatter land east of the main road, and village-level quality varies widely. The best premier crus lie on two slopes. North of the Combe de Lavaux, the southeast-facing Côte Saint-Jacques holds Clos Saint-Jacques, Lavaut Saint-Jacques, Les Cazetiers and Combe au Moine, often as fine as the grand crus. South of the village, a continuous band of grand crus runs from Mazis-Chambertin and Ruchottes past Chambertin and Clos de Bèze to Latricières and Mazoyères at the Morey border. Gevrey's growers range from historic names such as Armand Rousseau to modern stars such as Denis Mortet, Fourrier, Claude Dugat and Duroché.
appellations.terroir: Bajocian and Bathonian limestones with marls; the Combe de Lavaux spreads a cone of scree and gravel that gives the village land unusual depth. Slopes face east and southeast at 250 to 380 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Some Gevrey-Chambertin village wine legally comes from Brochon, which shares a strip of the appellation.

appellations.name: Morey-Saint-Denis
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir (some Chardonnay and Pinot Blanc)
appellations.summary:
Morey-Saint-Denis is the small village between Gevrey-Chambertin and Chambolle-Musigny, and its wines sit between them in style: the structure of Gevrey with some of Chambolle's perfume. It holds four complete grand crus (Clos de la Roche, Clos Saint-Denis, Clos des Lambrays and Clos de Tart) and a slice of Bonnes-Mares. For decades its growers sold the village wine under the names of its more famous neighbours, which kept Morey relatively obscure and good value.
