Premier crus such as Les Ruchots, Clos de la Bussière, Les Monts Luisants, Clos Sorbè and Les Millandes give sappy, earthy reds. Les Monts Luisants is also the source of one of Burgundy's rarest whites: Domaine Ponsot's Clos des Monts Luisants was planted with Aligoté in 1911.
appellations.terroir: Limestone over marl; the gravelly scree of the Combe Grisard and Combe de la Roche feeds the lower slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: The village added Saint-Denis to its name in 1927, after its grand cru Clos Saint-Denis.

appellations.name: Chambolle-Musigny
appellations.summary:
Chambolle-Musigny makes the most perfumed and silky reds of the Côte de Nuits, wines often described as the iron fist in a velvet glove. The village sits at the mouth of the Combe d'Ambin, and its vineyards hold two grand crus at either end: Bonnes-Mares to the north and Musigny to the south.

Between them, the premier crus are among the most sought-after in Burgundy, led by Les Amoureuses, which touches Musigny and costs as much as many grand crus. Les Charmes, Les Cras, Les Sentiers, Les Fuées, Les Baudes, La Combe d'Orveau and Derrière la Grange are also outstanding. The wines are lighter in colour than Gevrey's but extraordinarily aromatic (violet, rose, raspberry) and fine-grained, and age for decades.
appellations.terroir: More active limestone and less clay than its neighbours, with thin soils that drain fast; the Combe d'Ambin and Combe d'Orveau bring cool air.
appellations.nerd_note: Chambolle added Musigny to its name in 1878. Its premier cru Les Amoureuses, about 5.3 ha, often sells above grand crus such as Clos de Vougeot.

appellations.name: Vougeot
appellations.summary: Vougeot is Burgundy's smallest village appellation once you take away its grand cru: the 50 ha Clos de Vougeot fills most of the commune's vineyard, leaving only about 16 ha for village and premier cru wine. The premier crus Les Petits Vougeots, Les Cras, Clos de la Perrière and Le Clos Blanc lie just above and north of the Clos, against Chambolle-Musigny. Le Clos Blanc de Vougeot, a Chardonnay vineyard planted by the Cistercians in 1110 and now a monopole of Domaine de la Vougeraie, is one of the Côte de Nuits' rare great whites.
appellations.terroir: Limestone slopes north of the Clos with the brown soils of the Combe d'Orveau fan.
appellations.nerd_note: The village premier crus are among the least known in Burgundy because almost all attention goes to the Clos.

appellations.name: Vosne-Romanée
appellations.summary:
Vosne-Romanée is the most famous wine village in the world. Its grand crus (Romanée-Conti, La Tâche, Richebourg, La Romanée, Romanée-Saint-Vivant and La Grande Rue) together cover only about 27 ha, yet they make the most expensive red wines anywhere. Next door, Échezeaux and Grands-Échezeaux in the commune of Flagey-Échezeaux are worked largely by Vosne growers, and Flagey's village and premier cru land is sold as Vosne-Romanée.

The style is rich and exotic: dark cherry, spice, rose and orange peel over silky, velvety tannins, with a density that sets it apart from Chambolle's lightness and Nuits's firmness. The premier crus are worth their own pilgrimage: Cros Parantoux, made famous by Henri Jayer; Aux Malconsorts, which touches La Tâche; Les Suchots and Aux Brûlées, close to Richebourg and Romanée-Saint-Vivant; Les Beaux Monts high on the slope. The village is home to Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, Domaine Leroy, Méo-Camuzet, Grivot, Cathiard, Liger-Belair, Arnoux-Lachaux and the Gros family.
appellations.terroir: Brown limestone soils with clay over Bathonian and Bajocian rock; the grand crus sit on a smooth, gently sloping band at 260 to 300 m facing east.
appellations.nerd_note: Dr Morelot wrote in 1831 that there were no common wines in Vosne, a line still quoted by every grower in the village.

appellations.name: Nuits-Saint-Georges
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir (some Chardonnay and Pinot Blanc)
appellations.summary:
Nuits-Saint-Georges is the commercial town that gave the Côte de Nuits its name, and, after Gevrey-Chambertin, the largest appellation of the Côte de Nuits, extending south into Premeaux-Prissey. It has no grand crus but 41 premier crus, more than any other Côte de Nuits village. The reds are the firmest and most earthy of the côte: dark fruit, spice, iron and tannin that need time.

The appellation falls into three parts. North of the town, next to Vosne-Romanée, Aux Boudots, Aux Cras, Aux Murgers, Les Damodes and Aux Chaignots give finer, more Vosne-like wines. South of the town, Les Saints-Georges, Les Vaucrains, Les Cailles, Les Pruliers and Les Porrets give deeper, more structured wine. Further south in Premeaux, walled monopoles such as Clos de la Maréchale, Clos des Forêts Saint-Georges, Clos de l'Arlot and Clos des Corvées round it off. Les Saints-Georges, whose name the town added in 1892, has long been proposed for grand cru status; the growers' application was still under study at INAO in 2026.
appellations.terroir: Varied: limestone, marl and alluvial fans from the Meuzin valley; the southern slope is steeper and stonier.
appellations.nerd_note: The white Nuits-Saint-Georges premier cru Les Perrières from Domaine Henri Gouges comes from a mutant Pinot Noir that turned white, propagated by Henri Gouges in the 1930s and sometimes called Pinot Gouges.

appellations.name: Côte de Nuits-Villages
match: Côte de Nuits-Villages / Vins fins de la Côte de Nuits
Côte de Nuits-Villages ou Vins fins de la Côte de Nuits
Vins fins de la Côte de Nuits
appellations.summary: Côte de Nuits-Villages covers the edges of the Côte de Nuits: Fixin and Brochon in the north, and Premeaux-Prissey (outside the Nuits-Saint-Georges limits), Comblanchien and Corgoloin in the south. The southern villages are famous for the pink Comblanchien limestone quarried for the Paris Opéra floor and Orly airport. The wines are mostly lighter reds with typical Côte de Nuits structure and can be excellent value from good growers.
appellations.terroir: Thin soils over Comblanchien limestone at the narrowest point of the Côte, where the slope is barely 200 m wide.
appellations.nerd_note: Its official alternative name, Vins fins de la Côte de Nuits, is almost never used on labels.

appellations.name: Chambertin
appellations.summary:
Chambertin is the king of Gevrey and one of the two or three most famous red vineyards in Burgundy. About 12.9 ha of gentle east-facing slope above the Route des Grands Crus, it takes its name from the field of a man called Bertin, who, legend says, planted it to copy his neighbours the monks of Bèze. Napoleon drank it diluted with water on campaign, and it was Burgundy's most celebrated red through the nineteenth century.

Great Chambertin combines power and depth with polish: black cherry, liquorice, game and earth, firm but fine tannin, and a long life of 20 to 40 years. Ownership is divided among about 25 producers, and quality has varied, but Armand Rousseau (2.15 ha), Trapet, Rossignol-Trapet, Denis Mortet, Leroy, Dugat-Py and Bouchard set the standard.
appellations.terroir: Brown limestone soils with marl and clay over Bathonian and Bajocian limestone, at about 275 to 300 m; a wood above protects it from cold air and erosion.
appellations.nerd_note: Wine from Chambertin-Clos de Bèze may be sold as Chambertin, but never the reverse; INAO's parcel file therefore draws the Chambertin AOC at 28.2 ha, enclosing both vineyards.

appellations.name: Chambertin-Clos de Bèze
appellations.summary:
Clos de Bèze is the oldest documented great vineyard of Burgundy. In 630 Duke Amalgaire gave land here to the abbey of Bèze, whose monks cleared and enclosed it; their walled vineyard became the model for Chambertin next door. Today about 15.4 ha, it lies just north of Chambertin, and the two are rivals for the title of Gevrey's finest wine.

Clos de Bèze tends to be slightly more aromatic and refined than Chambertin, with silky, sometimes spicy black fruit and great length. The wine may also be labelled Chambertin, but most owners prefer the older name. About 18 producers share it, including Armand Rousseau, Bruno Clair, Faiveley, Drouhin-Laroze, Prieuré-Roch and Louis Jadot.
appellations.terroir: Slightly stonier and with more limestone than Chambertin, east-facing at 275 to 300 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Rousseau's 1.42 ha and the Damoy family's large holding (about 5.4 ha) make them the biggest names in the Clos.

appellations.name: Chapelle-Chambertin
appellations.summary: Chapelle-Chambertin, about 5.5 ha below Clos de Bèze, takes its name from a chapel built in 1155 by the monks of Bèze, destroyed during the Revolution. Its soil is thin and stony over limestone, giving one of the lighter and more delicate Gevrey grand crus, fragrant and red-fruited rather than massive. Rossignol-Trapet, Trapet, Drouhin-Laroze, Pierre Damoy and Louis Jadot are leading names.
appellations.terroir: Shallow soil on hard limestone, just below the Route des Grands Crus.
appellations.nerd_note: Chapelle includes the climats En la Chapelle and Les Gemeaux.

appellations.name: Charmes-Chambertin
appellations.summary: Charmes-Chambertin, about 12.2 ha below Chambertin and Latricières, is the most accessible Gevrey grand cru, partly because wine from neighbouring Mazoyères-Chambertin (about 18.6 ha) may also be sold as Charmes, giving about 31 ha in all. The name probably comes from chaume, a clearing of scrub, not charm, though the wine is indeed charming: soft, round, fruit-forward Pinot Noir that is approachable young. Dozens of producers make it, from Armand Rousseau, Dugat-Py and Claude Dugat to Taupenot-Merme and Perrot-Minot.
appellations.terroir: Deeper soil on the lower part of the grand cru band, at about 260 to 280 m.
appellations.nerd_note: INAO's parcel file delimits Charmes-Chambertin and Mazoyères-Chambertin as one 30.9 ha area because Mazoyères may be sold under the Charmes name.

appellations.name: Mazoyères-Chambertin
appellations.summary: Mazoyères-Chambertin, about 18.6 ha south of Charmes at the Morey border, is a grand cru that hardly anyone puts on a label because its wine may legally be sold as Charmes-Chambertin, a better-known name. A handful of growers, such as Camus, Perrot-Minot and Taupenot-Merme, insist on the original name. The wines are often a little firmer and more structured than Charmes, from slightly cooler soils.
appellations.terroir: Limestone with more clay at the southern end of Gevrey's grand cru belt, next to Clos de la Roche in Morey.
appellations.nerd_note: The spelling varies: Mazoyères and Mazoyères-Chambertin are both seen; the name is thought to come from mas, a farmhouse.

appellations.name: Griotte-Chambertin
appellations.summary: Griotte-Chambertin, about 2.7 ha in a slight hollow below Chambertin, is the smallest of Gevrey's grand crus. Its name is often linked to griotte (sour cherry), which suits the wine's bright red-cherry fruit, though it may come from criot, a stony place. The wines are aromatic and fleshy, with a lovely freshness. Ponsot, Fourrier, Claude Dugat, Joseph Drouhin and Chézeaux are among a small group of owners.
appellations.terroir: A shallow bowl of stony soil over limestone that traps heat; just below Chambertin.
appellations.nerd_note: With so little land, a whole year's Griotte-Chambertin is often barely a thousand cases for the whole world.

appellations.name: Latricières-Chambertin
appellations.summary: Latricières-Chambertin, about 7.4 ha directly south of Chambertin, is cooled by air flowing from the Combe Grisard at the Morey border, which gives it a fresh, sometimes austere style with fine minerality and spice. Its soil is thin and its rock hard. Leroy, Trapet, Rossignol-Trapet, Faiveley, Drouhin-Laroze and Arnoux-Lachaux make it.
appellations.terroir: Shallow, stony soil over hard limestone; cool air from the Combe Grisard.
appellations.nerd_note: The name probably derives from tricière, a poor soil fit only for scrub.

appellations.name: Mazis-Chambertin
appellations.summary: Mazis-Chambertin, about 9.1 ha at the northern end of Gevrey's grand cru belt below Ruchottes, combines Mazis-Haut, close to Clos de Bèze in quality, and Mazis-Bas, on deeper soil. The wines are dense and deeply coloured with dark fruit and a wild, gamey edge. Armand Rousseau, Faiveley, Bernard Dugat-Py, Harmand-Geoffroy and the Hospices de Beaune (cuvée Madeleine Collignon) are notable sources.
appellations.terroir: Brown limestone soils with more clay and depth on the lower part.
appellations.nerd_note: The Hospices de Beaune's Mazis-Chambertin cuvée Madeleine Collignon is one of the auction's most expensive red lots.

appellations.name: Ruchottes-Chambertin
appellations.summary: Ruchottes-Chambertin, about 3.3 ha above Mazis, is the highest and stoniest Gevrey grand cru. Its name may come from rochers, rocks, and its thin soil gives a lean, mineral, finely etched wine that can be austere young. Armand Rousseau's 1.06 ha Clos des Ruchottes monopole, Domaine Georges Roumier (made from the Michel Bonnefond parcel) and Mugneret-Gibourg are the references.
appellations.terroir: Very thin soil over hard Bathonian limestone, high on the slope.
appellations.nerd_note: Ruchottes-Chambertin is divided between Ruchottes du Dessus and Ruchottes du Bas.

appellations.name: Clos de la Roche
appellations.summary: Clos de la Roche is the largest and usually the finest grand cru of Morey-Saint-Denis, about 16.9 ha that grew in 1971 when several neighbouring climats were added. Its name refers to a large stone thought to have been used for Celtic rituals. The wines are deep, firm and savoury, with dark fruit and a stony, almost Chambertin-like power. Ponsot, Dujac, Armand Rousseau, Hubert Lignier, Leroy and Arlaud are its leading growers.
appellations.terroir: Thin soil on hard limestone that comes to the surface in places; one of the stoniest grand crus.
appellations.nerd_note: Domaine Ponsot's Clos de la Roche Cuvée Vieilles Vignes comes from vines planted in the 1950s and is famous for being made without new oak.

appellations.name: Clos Saint-Denis
appellations.summary: Clos Saint-Denis, about 6.6 ha south of Clos de la Roche, gave its name to the village of Morey in 1927. It is named after the collegiate church of Saint-Denis de Vergy, founded in 1023, whose canons owned it. The wines are fragrant and elegant, with red fruit and spice, lighter than Clos de la Roche. Dujac's version, made with whole clusters, is the benchmark, alongside Ponsot, Bertagna and Arlaud.
appellations.terroir: Limestone with a little more clay than Clos de la Roche, gently sloping at about 270 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Despite the name, Clos Saint-Denis has had no walls for centuries.

appellations.name: Clos des Lambrays
appellations.summary: Clos des Lambrays, about 8.8 ha in Morey-Saint-Denis, was promoted to grand cru only in 1981, the first change to the list since the 1930s. Apart from a tiny strip owned by Domaine Taupenot-Merme, it is the monopole of Domaine des Lambrays, which LVMH bought in 2014. Its rows run across a slope that faces east and then northeast, giving wines that are sappy, silky and finely aromatic. Whole-cluster fermentation has long been part of its style.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl with a varied exposure that turns slightly northeast at the top; vines planted down the slope.
appellations.nerd_note: The domaine also makes two rare white premier crus in Puligny-Montrachet, Les Folatières and Clos du Cailleret.

appellations.name: Clos de Tart
appellations.summary:
Clos de Tart is a walled 7.5 ha monopole in Morey-Saint-Denis owned by only three proprietors in almost 900 years: the Bernardine nuns of Notre-Dame de Tart from 1141, the Marey-Monge family from 1791 and the Mommessin family from 1932, until François Pinault's Artémis group bought it in 2017. Unusually, its rows run north to south across the slope, which slows erosion and lets every row see different soils.

The wine is deep, spicy and structured, among the most powerful in Morey, and its old cellars are among the deepest in the Côte. It touches Bonnes-Mares at its southern edge.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl with six distinct soil zones mapped by the estate; the rows cross the contour lines.
appellations.nerd_note: Clos de Tart was valued at more than 250 million euros when Artémis bought it in 2017, the highest price per hectare ever recorded for a Burgundy vineyard.

appellations.name: Bonnes-Mares
appellations.summary:
Bonnes-Mares, about 15 ha, straddles the Morey-Chambolle border, with most of it (about 13.5 ha) in Chambolle-Musigny. Its name may come from marer, to plough, or from the 'good mothers', the nuns of Tart who owned it. A diagonal line divides it: the northern terres rouges on iron-rich clay give firm, structured wine; the southern terres blanches on white marl give a more aromatic, mineral style. Most growers blend both.

Bonnes-Mares is the most powerful wine of Chambolle, darker and more tannic than Musigny, and ages for decades. Comte Georges de Vogüé (2.7 ha), Georges Roumier, Domaine Dujac, Robert Groffier, Drouhin-Laroze and Fougeray de Beauclair make it.
appellations.terroir: Two soils: red clay over limestone in the north (terres rouges) and white Bathonian marl in the south (terres blanches).
appellations.nerd_note: The Morey part (about 1.5 ha) is mostly owned by Clos de Tart, which bottles a Morey Bonnes-Mares.

appellations.name: Musigny
appellations.summary:
Musigny is the grand cru for those who believe the greatest red Burgundy should be about grace rather than power. About 10.9 ha at the southern end of Chambolle-Musigny, just above Clos de Vougeot, it combines Les Musigny and Les Petits Musigny with part of La Combe d'Orveau. The wine is famous for its silky texture and haunting perfume of violets, roses and red fruit, yet it lasts for decades.

Comte Georges de Vogüé owns about 7.1 ha, two thirds of the vineyard, and is the only producer of Musigny blanc, a rare Chardonnay replanted in the 1990s and sold as Bourgogne blanc until 2015 while the vines matured. Jacques-Frédéric Mugnier, Georges Roumier (a tiny parcel), Leroy, Joseph Drouhin, Jacques Prieur, Faiveley and Louis Jadot also make it.
appellations.terroir: Steeper than its neighbours, with little topsoil over hard limestone and some red clay; facing east at 260 to 300 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Musigny is the only grand cru in the Côte de Nuits allowed to produce both red and white wine.

appellations.name: Clos de Vougeot
match: Clos de Vougeot ou Clos Vougeot
appellations.summary:
Clos de Vougeot is Burgundy's great monument: a single walled vineyard of about 50 ha, created by the Cistercian monks of Cîteaux from 1110 onward and completely enclosed by 1336. The monks used it as a laboratory, separating the wine of different parts of the slope; their cuvée of the upper vineyard was the abbey's gift to popes and kings. Confiscated in 1789, it was sold intact, but it has since been divided among about 80 owners.

Because it runs from the top of the slope (next to Musigny and Grands-Échezeaux) down to the flat land by the road, quality and style vary. The best wines come from the upper and middle parts and from serious growers: dense, spicy, dark-fruited Pinot Noir with firm tannins. The Château du Clos de Vougeot in the middle of the vineyard, with its twelfth-century press house and sixteenth-century Renaissance building, belongs to the Confrérie des Chevaliers du Tastevin.
appellations.terroir: Upper part on light limestone soils, middle on limestone with clay, lowest part on deeper alluvial clay; rows run down the slope from about 240 to 270 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Château de la Tour, with about 5.5 ha, is the largest owner and the only one making wine inside the walls.

appellations.name: Echezeaux
appellations.summary:
Échezeaux, in the commune of Flagey-Échezeaux, is the second-largest grand cru of the Côte de Nuits at about 37.7 ha, made up of 11 lieux-dits stretched from the Clos de Vougeot wall up toward the woods. The size and the mix of soils mean that Échezeaux is the most variable of the Vosne grand crus. The upper parts, such as Les Échezeaux du Dessus, Les Poulaillères and En Orveaux, give the most refined wine.

At its best Échezeaux is fragrant, spicy and supple, more approachable than Grands-Échezeaux. Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, Emmanuel Rouget (from Henri Jayer's vines), Mongeard-Mugneret, Arnoux-Lachaux, Dujac, Anne Gros, Grivot and Georges Noëllat are among about 80 owners.
appellations.terroir: Brown limestone and marl, deeper at the bottom near the Clos de Vougeot wall, thinner and stonier at the top under the woods.
appellations.nerd_note: The name comes from chesaux, an old word for a group of houses; the official register spells it without an accent.

appellations.name: Grands-Echezeaux
appellations.summary: Grands-Échezeaux, about 9.1 ha on flatter land next to the top wall of Clos de Vougeot and just below Musigny, is considered the finer and more consistent of the two Échezeaux grand crus. Its wines are dense, structured and deeply aromatic, with the power of Vosne and some of Musigny's perfume. Domaine de la Romanée-Conti owns about 3.5 ha, and Mongeard-Mugneret, Joseph Drouhin, Gros Frère et Sœur and Lamarche share most of the rest.
appellations.terroir: Deeper, flatter brown limestone soils with clay, at about 260 m.
appellations.nerd_note: The Cistercian monks of Cîteaux owned and worked Grands-Échezeaux alongside the Clos de Vougeot.

appellations.name: Richebourg
appellations.summary: Richebourg, about 8 ha north of Romanée-Conti, is the most opulent of Vosne's grand crus: rich, velvety and sensuous, with dark fruit, spice and a fleshy weight. It comprises Les Richebourg and Les Véroilles, which faces slightly northeast. Domaine de la Romanée-Conti owns about 3.5 ha; other owners include Leroy, Méo-Camuzet (from Henri Jayer's family vines), Grivot, Anne Gros, Gros Frère et Sœur, Mongeard-Mugneret and Hudelot-Noëllat.
appellations.terroir: Brown limestone with more clay than Romanée-Conti; the lower part benefits from a slight hollow.
appellations.nerd_note: The name probably means 'rich town', and the wine was praised as early as the eighteenth century.

appellations.name: Romanée-Conti
appellations.summary:
Romanée-Conti is the most famous vineyard in the world and its wine the most expensive red. A plot of only 1.81 ha, it is the monopole of Domaine de la Romanée-Conti and produces about 5,000 to 6,000 bottles a year. It was called Cros des Cloux when the monks of Saint-Vivant de Vergy owned it; by 1651 it was La Romanée. In 1760 Louis-François de Bourbon, Prince de Conti, outbid Madame de Pompadour to buy it and added his name. After the Revolution it passed through several owners until Jacques-Marie Duvault-Blochet bought it in 1869; his descendants, the de Villaine family, now share the domaine with the Leroy family heirs.

Romanée-Conti was the last vineyard in the Côte d'Or to be pulled up after phylloxera, in 1945. The wine is not the most powerful in Vosne but the most complete: layered, spicy and ethereal, with roses, oriental spice and a finish that seems to go on forever. Aubert de Villaine co-directed the domaine for nearly five decades from 1974; Perrine Fenal and Bertrand de Villaine now lead it.
appellations.terroir: A gentle 6 percent slope facing east-southeast at about 270 m, on brown limestone soil with clay and some iron, over Bajocian and Bathonian rock; good natural drainage.
appellations.nerd_note: The domaine pulled up the ungrafted vines after the 1945 harvest and replanted from its own cuttings in 1947, so no Romanée-Conti was made from 1946 to 1951.

appellations.name: La Romanée
appellations.summary: La Romanée, about 0.85 ha just above Romanée-Conti, is France's smallest appellation. It is a monopole of the Comte Liger-Belair family, who bought it in 1815. For decades the wine was made and sold by négociants such as Bouchard Père et Fils; since the 2002 vintage Louis-Michel Liger-Belair has made all of it himself. The wine is concentrated and finely structured, with dark fruit and a firm, mineral line, and needs long ageing.
appellations.terroir: Steeper than Romanée-Conti, with thin soil over limestone; rows run across the slope in the upper part.
appellations.nerd_note: La Romanée is the smallest AOC in France at 0.84 ha in INAO's parcel file.

appellations.name: La Tâche
appellations.summary: La Tâche, about 6.06 ha south of Romanée-Conti, is the other great monopole of Domaine de la Romanée-Conti. The domaine bought the original La Tâche in 1933 and merged it with the adjoining Les Gaudichots, expanding the grand cru to its current size. The wine is darker, more exuberant and spicier than Romanée-Conti, often more impressive young, and ages for decades.
appellations.terroir: Varied exposure from east to southeast, with steeper upper slopes; brown limestone with clay over limestone and marl.
appellations.nerd_note: Tâche means a task or piece of work, perhaps a plot worked by a sharecropper.

appellations.name: Romanée-Saint-Vivant
appellations.summary: Romanée-Saint-Vivant, about 9.4 ha below Romanée-Conti and Richebourg and just above the village of Vosne, takes its name from the Benedictine priory of Saint-Vivant de Vergy, which owned it for centuries. It gives the most delicate and feminine of Vosne's grand crus: silky, spicy and fragrant, with a gentle tannic touch. Domaine de la Romanée-Conti farms about 5.3 ha, mostly the former Clos des Quatre Journaux of the Marey-Monge family. Leroy, Sylvain Cathiard, Arnoux-Lachaux, Hudelot-Noëllat and Follin-Arbelet also make it.
appellations.terroir: Deeper soil with more clay on the gentle lower slope near the village.
appellations.nerd_note: The ruins of the Saint-Vivant abbey are in the Hautes-Côtes above Curtil-Vergy, restored by an association with support from the DRC.

appellations.name: La Grande Rue
appellations.summary: La Grande Rue, a 1.65 ha strip between Romanée-Conti and La Tâche, is the monopole of Domaine François Lamarche. It was left as a premier cru in the 1930s, reportedly because the family did not apply for grand cru status, and was only promoted in 1992. The wine is fine and elegant with red fruit and spice; quality has improved markedly under Nicole Lamarche since the 2000s.
appellations.terroir: Same brown limestone as its neighbours, on a narrow strip running up the slope.
appellations.nerd_note: Its narrowness means the rows run the full height of the slope, so each row sees the whole range of soils.

appellations.name: Bourgogne Hautes Côtes de Nuits
appellations.summary: The Hautes-Côtes de Nuits is the high country behind the Côte de Nuits: a plateau of combes, woods and hamlets at 300 to 450 m, where vines alternate with blackcurrant fields for crème de cassis. It is a named zone (dénomination géographique) of the Bourgogne AOC, not an AOC of its own. Long considered too cold for good ripening, it has become one of the winners of climate change: its Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are fresh, aromatic and increasingly sought out, and several Côte d'Or domaines have bought land here.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl plateaus and combes at altitude; later ripening and cooler nights than the main slope.
appellations.nerd_note: The Hautes-Côtes were replanted after the 1950s, encouraged by the founding of the Caves des Hautes-Côtes co-operative in 1968.

appellations.name: Ladoix
appellations.summary: Ladoix (officially the commune of Ladoix-Serrigny) is the northern gateway to the Côte de Beaune and the least known of the villages around the hill of Corton, even though part of its land is classified as Corton and Corton-Charlemagne grand cru. Its village and premier cru wines, such as Les Joyeuses, La Micaude, Le Bois Roussot and Les Grêchons, are supple, fruity reds and bright whites that offer some of the best prices in the Côte d'Or. Many growers here also sell wine as Côte de Beaune-Villages or under the Aloxe-Corton name, which shares some of Ladoix's slopes.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl at the eastern foot of the Corton hill, with some Côte de Nuits-style rocks at Buisson where the two côtes meet.
appellations.nerd_note: Ladoix sits at the boundary between the Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune: the hamlet of Buisson marks where Comblanchien limestone gives way to Beaune's marls.

appellations.name: Aloxe-Corton
appellations.summary: Aloxe-Corton is the village at the foot of the hill of Corton, and most of its best land is classified as grand cru: Corton for reds, Corton-Charlemagne for whites. The village and premier cru wines below are mostly red, firm and dark-fruited with an earthy note, a step down in intensity from Corton but often good value. Premier crus such as Les Valozières, Les Fournières, Les Vercots and Les Maréchaudes lie on the lower slopes toward Ladoix and Chorey. The village is dominated by the glazed-tile roof of Château Corton C (Domaine Corton-André), one of the region's postcard images.
appellations.terroir: Iron-rich brown limestone soils on the lower Corton slope, turning more alluvial toward the plain.
appellations.nerd_note: Louis Latour has run its winery at Château Corton Grancey in Aloxe since 1891, and the house's Corton-Grancey is a blend of several Corton climats.

appellations.name: Pernand-Vergelesses
appellations.summary: Pernand-Vergelesses is tucked into a side valley behind the hill of Corton, and its steep west-facing slopes include a large part of Corton-Charlemagne, the En Charlemagne climat. The village wines are now best known for their whites: lively, citrusy Chardonnay grown higher and cooler than in Meursault, which benefits in hot years. The reds come mostly from premier crus such as Île des Vergelesses (opposite Savigny's Les Vergelesses), Les Fichots and Creux de la Net, and are fresh, spicy and fine.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl on cool, steep slopes at up to 350 m, some facing west; the village lies in a combe sheltered from the main slope.
appellations.nerd_note: Bonneau du Martray, Pernand's most famous estate and one of Corton-Charlemagne's largest owners, was bought by Stan Kroenke (owner of Screaming Eagle) in 2017.

appellations.name: Savigny-lès-Beaune
appellations.summary: Savigny-lès-Beaune lies where the valley of the Rhoin opens onto the plain just north of Beaune, and it is one of the Côte de Beaune's largest red-wine villages. The valley creates two slopes: the north side, facing south and southeast, has premier crus such as Les Lavières, Aux Serpentières, Aux Guettes and Les Vergelesses next to Pernand, while the south side, facing northeast toward Beaune, includes Les Marconnets, Les Narbantons, Les Peuillets and La Dominode. The reds are fresh, light to medium-bodied and fragrant, with red berry fruit and a gentle tannic grip.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and gravelly scree brought down by the Rhoin; sandier soils near the valley floor.
appellations.nerd_note: The Château de Savigny-lès-Beaune houses a museum of motorcycles, racing cars and fighter jets in its grounds.

appellations.name: Chorey-lès-Beaune
appellations.summary: Chorey-lès-Beaune is the only Côte de Beaune village that sits entirely on the flat land east of the main road, and for that reason it has no premier crus. Its soft, fruity reds are some of the most approachable and affordable in the Côte d'Or, especially from Tollot-Beaut, whose wines are a benchmark for good Pinot Noir from the plain. A village AOC only since 1970, it was previously sold as Côte de Beaune-Villages.
appellations.terroir: Alluvial gravel, sand and clay on the flat, with deeper soil and more frost risk than the slope.
appellations.nerd_note: Château de Chorey, a seventeenth-century moated house, belongs to the Germain family and is now partly a guesthouse.

appellations.name: Beaune
appellations.summary:
Beaune is both Burgundy's wine capital and one of its largest village appellations, and it has more premier crus by area than any other commune: about 320 ha of the roughly 410 ha in production are premier cru, and there are no grand crus. Much of the slope is owned by the big négociants of the town, and their premier crus are flagship wines: Bouchard Père et Fils's Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus (in Les Grèves), Louis Jadot's Clos des Ursules (in Les Vignes Franches) and Joseph Drouhin's Clos des Mouches.

Beaune's reds are medium-bodied, fragrant and red-fruited, softer and earlier-maturing than Côte de Nuits wines. The best premier crus run in a continuous band along the slope: Les Marconnets and Clos du Roi near Savigny, Les Bressandes, Les Grèves, Les Teurons and Les Cents Vignes in the middle, and Les Avaux, Clos des Mouches and Les Vignes Franches to the south toward Pommard. Some climats, notably Clos des Mouches and Les Aigrots, also make excellent whites.
appellations.terroir: Limestone with marl and gravel; the middle slope has stony soils (Les Grèves takes its name from gravel), while the southern end has more clay.
appellations.nerd_note: Bouchard Père et Fils's L'Enfant Jésus, a 4 ha parcel in Les Grèves once owned by Carmelite nuns, takes its name from the order's devotion to the Infant Jesus of Beaune.

appellations.name: Côte de Beaune
appellations.summary: Côte de Beaune is a confusing name. Beyond being the name of the whole southern half of the Côte d'Or, it is also a small appellation of its own: about 50 ha of vines on the upper slopes and plateau of the Montagne de Beaune, above the Beaune premier crus. The wines, red and white, are fresh and light, with more acidity than Beaune village wine; Joseph Drouhin and Domaine des Croix make good examples.
appellations.terroir: Higher, cooler limestone slopes and plateau above Beaune, at 300 to 350 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Do not confuse it with Côte de Beaune-Villages, a red-only appellation that covers 16 villages.

appellations.name: Pommard
appellations.summary:
Pommard is the most famous red-only village of the Côte de Beaune and the source of its most powerful wine: deep in colour, firm, earthy and long-lived, often compared to the Côte de Nuits. Its name was one of the most widely known in the world in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, which encouraged imitation and fraud before the AOC era.

Pommard has no grand crus, but two premier crus are often proposed for promotion. Les Rugiens, next to Volnay, is split into Rugiens Bas, the finer lower part with red, iron-rich soil, and Rugiens Hauts. Les Grands Épenots and Les Petits Épenots, toward Beaune, give more elegant and aromatic wine; within them the Comte Armand domaine's Clos des Épeneaux monopole is a classic. Other notable climats include Les Pézerolles, Les Jarolières and Les Charmots.
appellations.terroir: Heavier brown clay over limestone, more clay than Volnay, with red iron-rich soils in Les Rugiens; the village sits at the mouth of a broad combe.
appellations.nerd_note: The Pièce des Présidents of the 2025 Hospices de Beaune auction, a barrel of Pommard premier cru Les Rugiens, sold for around $460,000.

appellations.name: Volnay
appellations.summary:
Volnay is the most delicate and perfumed red wine of the Côte de Beaune, often called the Chambolle-Musigny of the south. Its vineyards climb to a village perched high on the slope, and more than half the appellation is premier cru. The reds are bright, silky and floral, with red cherry and violet and fine tannin, yet the best age for decades.

The great premier crus include Les Caillerets, Clos des Chênes, Taillepieds, Champans and Les Santenots (which lie in Meursault but are sold as Volnay when red). Several walled clos are monopoles of historic domaines: Marquis d'Angerville's Clos des Ducs, which belonged to the dukes of Burgundy, and Domaine de la Pousse d'Or's Clos de la Bousse d'Or. The Marquis d'Angerville was a pioneer of estate bottling in the 1920s and fought fraud with Henri Gouges, and Volnay's reputation owes much to that independence.
appellations.terroir: Thin soils on hard limestone with less clay than Pommard; the higher slope has whiter, stonier soil, and the slope turns southeast.
appellations.nerd_note: Red wines from the Santenots climats in Meursault are sold as Volnay premier cru Santenots, while white wines from the same plots are sold as Meursault.

appellations.name: Monthélie
appellations.summary: Monthélie lies just above Meursault next to Volnay, and its best slopes are a continuation of Volnay's: premier crus such as Sur la Velle, Les Champs Fulliots and Les Duresses give light, fragrant reds that resemble a rustic Volnay at a lower price. A few growers also make fresh whites. The village is one of the smallest and least known in the Côte de Beaune, which makes it a happy hunting ground for value.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl on south and southeast slopes, some facing Volnay; higher sites on the hill toward Auxey.
appellations.nerd_note: The name is often written without an accent, Monthelie; the official register uses Monthélie.

appellations.name: Auxey-Duresses
appellations.summary: Auxey-Duresses lies in the valley that runs west from Meursault toward Saint-Romain, and it makes both reds and whites. The reds come mostly from the southeast-facing slope opposite Monthélie, including the premier crus Les Duresses and Climat du Val; the whites from the cooler slopes facing Meursault. Both are leaner and fresher than their famous neighbours' wines. Lalou Bize-Leroy's Maison Leroy has its headquarters in the village.
appellations.terroir: Marl and limestone in a narrow valley; the Montagne du Bourdon faces southeast and holds the premier crus.
appellations.nerd_note: Leroy's cellars in Auxey hold one of the largest stocks of old Burgundy in the world, much of it from the négociant era.

appellations.name: Saint-Romain
appellations.summary: Saint-Romain is the highest village of the Côte de Beaune, set among cliffs and woods 400 m up where the Auxey valley meets the Hautes-Côtes. Long considered too cool for great wine, it makes crisp, mineral whites and light reds that have gained from warmer summers. It has no premier crus. The village is also the home of the tonnellerie François Frères, one of Burgundy's most famous barrel makers, and of Domaine d'Auvenay, Lalou Bize-Leroy's private estate.
appellations.terroir: Marl and limestone at 300 to 400 m below limestone cliffs; late ripening and cool nights.
appellations.nerd_note: François Frères, founded in 1910 in Saint-Romain, supplies barrels to many of Burgundy's top domaines, including the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti.

appellations.name: Meursault
appellations.summary:
Meursault is the largest white-wine village of the Côte d'Or and the one that defines rich, round, nutty Chardonnay: butter, hazelnut, toast and ripe orchard fruit over a backbone of acidity. It has no grand crus, but its premier crus rival them. Les Perrières, on stony soil high in the south, is the most mineral and is often called a grand cru in waiting; Les Genevrières is floral and fine; Les Charmes is the broadest and most generous; and Les Gouttes d'Or, Le Porusot, Les Bouchères and Blagny add more nuances.

Meursault also excels in single-lieu-dit village wines. Climats such as Les Tessons, Les Narvaux, Les Luchets, Le Clos de la Barre, Les Rougeots and Les Tillets are bottled separately by growers such as Coche-Dury, Roulot and Lafon and command premier cru prices. Meursault's cellars, cut deep into the limestone, allow long, slow ageing on the lees. The Paulée de Meursault, a harvest feast revived by Count Jules Lafon in 1923, is the last of the Trois Glorieuses.
appellations.terroir: Marl and limestone with more stone on the upper slopes; the premier crus lie south toward Puligny, facing east and southeast at 230 to 300 m.
appellations.nerd_note: A small amount of red Meursault is made, but the Santenots climats sell their red as Volnay; Blagny's red is sold as Blagny.

appellations.name: Blagny
match: Blagny ou Blagny Côte de Beaune
appellations.summary: Blagny is a hamlet high on the hill between Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet, and its appellation is one of Burgundy's oddities: the Blagny AOC is for red wine only. Its whites, from the same slopes, are sold as Meursault premier cru Blagny or Puligny-Montrachet premier cru. The reds are firm, rustic and earthy, and only a handful of growers still make them, as the whites are more profitable.
appellations.terroir: Marl and limestone at about 350 m, high above Meursault and Puligny, cooler than the slope below.
appellations.nerd_note: The hamlet once belonged to the Cistercians of Maizières, whose wine house is now owned by Domaine Martelet de Cherisey.

appellations.name: Puligny-Montrachet
appellations.summary:
Puligny-Montrachet is the white-wine village par excellence. It added the name of its most famous vineyard, Le Montrachet, in 1879, and it shares Montrachet and Bâtard-Montrachet with Chassagne while holding Chevalier-Montrachet and Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet alone. Its wines are the most precise, finely chiselled whites of the Côte: white flowers, citrus and stone fruit, a steely line and a long mineral finish, less buttery than Meursault.

The premier crus run north from the grand crus: Le Cailleret and Les Pucelles beside them; Les Folatières, Clavaillon and the Champ Canet higher up; Les Combettes, Les Perrières and Les Referts against Meursault. Puligny's water table is high, so cellars are shallow, which is why many growers bottle earlier than in Meursault. Domaine Leflaive, run by Anne-Claude Leflaive from 1990 until her death in 2015, made Puligny's name in biodynamics and is still its reference.
appellations.terroir: Limestone with marls and clay; a high water table means few underground cellars. The grand crus sit at 250 to 280 m on thin soil over hard limestone.
appellations.nerd_note: Puligny's water table was blamed for its lack of cellars until the 1990s, when growers such as Leflaive found that shallow cellars still allowed slow lees ageing.

appellations.name: Chassagne-Montrachet
appellations.summary:
Chassagne-Montrachet, at the southern end of the Côte de Beaune's great white zone, makes both reds and whites in quantity. Until the 1980s it was mostly red, but rising demand for Chardonnay has replanted many slopes with white. Its whites are rounder and more floral than Puligny's, with a hazelnut richness; its reds are firm, earthy and good value.

Chassagne shares Montrachet and Bâtard-Montrachet with Puligny and holds Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet alone. Its premier cru map is complicated, with about 55 named climats: Les Caillerets, La Romanée, Les Ruchottes, Les Chaumées and Les Vergers on the upper slopes north of the village; Morgeot, a large area with an abbey cellar, to the south; and En Remilly and Blanchot Dessus against Saint-Aubin and the Montrachet. Pink Comblanchien-like stone was quarried here for buildings across Burgundy.
appellations.terroir: Limestone, marl and clay; pink and white stone quarries above the village; the reds come mostly from the heavier soils toward Santenay.
appellations.nerd_note: Domaine Ramonet's founder Pierre Ramonet built the estate from 1920s smallholdings and bought his first Montrachet parcel in 1978.

appellations.name: Saint-Aubin
appellations.summary: Saint-Aubin is Burgundy's rising white star. Its village and the hamlet of Gamay sit in a side valley behind Puligny and Chassagne, and its best premier crus, En Remilly and Les Murgers des Dents de Chien, touch the Montrachet hill directly. About two thirds of its vineyard is premier cru. The wines are leaner and more mineral than Puligny's, with crisp acidity and a chalky texture, and they have gained from warm vintages.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl at 300 to 350 m with steep southeast slopes; cooler than the main côte.
appellations.nerd_note: The hamlet of Gamay is often claimed as the namesake of the Gamay grape.

appellations.name: Santenay
appellations.summary: Santenay is the last major village of the Côte de Beaune and makes mostly red wine: sturdy, dark-fruited and earthy, more structured than Volnay and less polished than Pommard. Premier crus such as Les Gravières, La Comme, Clos Rousseau and Clos de Tavannes lie on varied soils, and a few whites, such as the premier cru Clos des Mouches, are excellent. Santenay is also a spa town with hot springs and a casino, and its castle once belonged to Philip the Bold.
appellations.terroir: Complex geology with faults; limestone and marl with gravel; the slope turns southwest toward the Maranges.
appellations.nerd_note: The Château de Santenay, also called Château Philippe le Hardi, is famous for its roof of glazed tiles and its large vineyard estate.

appellations.name: Maranges
appellations.summary: Maranges is the southernmost appellation of the Côte de Beaune, a 1989 merger of three villages in Saône-et-Loire (Cheilly-, Dezize- and Sampigny-lès-Maranges) whose wines were previously sold as Côte de Beaune-Villages. It makes sturdy, rustic, red-fruited reds that are among the best values in the Côte d'Or. Its premier crus, such as La Fussière and Le Clos des Loyères, lie on south-facing slopes.
appellations.terroir: Marl and limestone on a south-facing hill; slightly warmer than the rest of the Côte.
appellations.nerd_note: Maranges was the first appellation of the Côte de Beaune created by merging villages rather than recognising one.

appellations.name: Côte de Beaune-Villages
appellations.summary: Côte de Beaune-Villages is a red-only appellation that can be used by 16 villages of the Côte de Beaune (not Aloxe-Corton, Beaune, Pommard or Volnay). Most is a blend from several communes, sold by négociants; growers in small villages also use it for wine from young vines or less favoured plots. It is soft and early-drinking, a step up from regional Bourgogne rouge.
appellations.terroir: Varied; any of the participating villages' red-wine land.
appellations.nerd_note: Each participating village may also add its own name, e.g. Chorey-lès-Beaune Côte de Beaune.

appellations.name: Corton
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir; Chardonnay and Pinot Blanc for white
appellations.summary:
Corton is the largest grand cru of Burgundy and the only one of the Côte de Beaune for red wine. The appellation covers about 160 ha around the hill of Corton, across Aloxe-Corton, Ladoix-Serrigny and Pernand-Vergelesses, but the vineyard in production is closer to 100 ha, and its wines vary greatly. Most labels add the climat name, such as Corton Bressandes. The 28 climats include Le Corton at the top of the hill, Les Bressandes, Le Clos du Roi, Les Renardes, Les Pougets, Les Perrières, Les Grèves, Le Rognet and Les Maréchaudes.

Red Corton is firm, earthy and slow to open, often austere young but long-lived; Le Clos du Roi and Les Bressandes are the most refined, Les Renardes the most wild and gamey. A small amount of white Corton, from Chardonnay and Pinot Blanc, also exists. The hill is crowned by the Bois de Corton.
appellations.terroir: A hill of Bathonian limestone capped with woods; reds come from the lower and middle slopes on iron-rich, reddish brown marls and limestone, east, southeast and south-facing, from 250 to 330 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Domaine de la Romanée-Conti began leasing vines in Bressandes, Clos du Roi and Renardes from the Prince de Mérode in 2009 and has made a Corton ever since.

appellations.name: Corton-Charlemagne
appellations.summary:
Corton-Charlemagne is one of the world's great white wines and, with about 72 ha, the largest white grand cru of the Côte d'Or. It covers the upper slopes of the hill of Corton facing southwest and west, in Pernand-Vergelesses and Aloxe-Corton, plus a sliver in Ladoix. Legend says the Emperor Charlemagne owned vines here and, when his white beard became stained by red wine, ordered white grapes planted; he did give vineyards here to the abbey of Saulieu in 775.

The wine is powerful and mineral, slower to open than Montrachet and more austere when young, with citrus, flint and spice that need a decade to unwind. Bonneau du Martray (about 9.5 ha), Coche-Dury, Louis Latour, Bouchard Père et Fils, Rapet, Roumier and the Hospices de Beaune (cuvée François de Salins) are among its best sources.
appellations.terroir: Marly limestone and Oxfordian marls on the upper hill under the wood, at 280 to 330 m; cool, windy slopes, many facing west.
appellations.nerd_note: Wines from Corton-Charlemagne may in theory include Aligoté, a historical tolerance, though nobody uses it today.

appellations.name: Charlemagne
appellations.summary: Charlemagne is a grand cru appellation that exists almost entirely on paper. It covers the lieux-dits En Charlemagne in Pernand-Vergelesses and Le Charlemagne in Aloxe-Corton, the historic heart of Corton-Charlemagne, and its wines are virtually always sold under the better-known Corton-Charlemagne name. A handful of growers have occasionally used it to make a point.
appellations.terroir: The same marly limestone slopes as Corton-Charlemagne under the Bois de Corton.
appellations.nerd_note: Charlemagne is the least-used of Burgundy's 33 grand crus; on most maps it is shown as part of Corton-Charlemagne.

appellations.name: Montrachet
appellations.summary:
Le Montrachet is the most famous white wine vineyard in the world: about 8 ha split almost equally between Puligny-Montrachet and Chassagne-Montrachet. Its name, from mont rachet (bald hill), describes the scrubby slope above it, and its fame was already established in the eighteenth century. Montrachet combines richness and mineral tension like no other site: a dense, layered texture, aromas of citrus, honey, nuts and smoke, and a finish that lasts for minutes. It can age for decades.

About 18 owners share it. The Marquis de Laguiche family (about 2 ha, made by Joseph Drouhin), Bouchard Père et Fils, Domaine de la Romanée-Conti (0.68 ha), Domaine des Comtes Lafon, Domaine Leflaive, Ramonet, Jacques Prieur and Baron Thénard are among them.
appellations.terroir: A gentle 3 percent slope facing east-southeast at 250 to 270 m, on thin brown limestone soil over hard Bathonian limestone; it catches sun from dawn to dusk and drains perfectly.
appellations.nerd_note: Alexandre Dumas is said to have written that Montrachet should be drunk kneeling with head bared.

appellations.name: Chevalier-Montrachet
appellations.summary: Chevalier-Montrachet, about 7.6 ha directly above Le Montrachet in Puligny, is steeper, stonier and higher, and its wines are leaner and more mineral, with less flesh but great finesse and age-worthiness. Domaine Leflaive (about 2 ha), Bouchard Père et Fils (2.5 ha), Louis Jadot (Les Demoiselles), Louis Latour (Les Demoiselles) and Domaine d'Auvenay are among its owners.
appellations.terroir: Thin, stony soil over hard limestone on a steeper slope above Montrachet, at 265 to 290 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Les Demoiselles, a section of Chevalier owned by Jadot and Latour, was added to the grand cru in 1939.

appellations.name: Bâtard-Montrachet
appellations.summary: Bâtard-Montrachet, about 11.9 ha directly below Le Montrachet and divided between Puligny and Chassagne, is the richest and most opulent of the Montrachet family: broad, honeyed and powerful, with more weight than Chevalier and less finesse than Montrachet. Its name means bastard, and folklore spins tales of a medieval knight's illegitimate son, though it more likely refers to a lesser piece of land. Leflaive, Ramonet, Pierre-Yves Colin-Morey, Jean-Noël Gagnard, Bernard Morey and the Hospices de Beaune make it.
appellations.terroir: Deeper brown soils with more clay on the lower slope below the Route des Grands Crus, at 240 to 255 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Bâtard is the largest of the five Montrachet grand crus.

appellations.name: Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet
appellations.summary: Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet, about 3.7 ha in the northeast corner of Bâtard-Montrachet entirely in Puligny, gives a slightly lighter, more elegant and earlier-approachable wine than Bâtard. The name, 'welcome', may refer to a gift of land. Domaine Leflaive is the largest owner (about 1.15 ha), followed by Ramonet, Paul Pernot, Faiveley and Vincent Girardin.
appellations.terroir: Brown limestone soil at the lowest, most northerly part of the Bâtard slope.
appellations.nerd_note: Wine from Bienvenues may legally be sold as Bâtard-Montrachet.

appellations.name: Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet
appellations.summary: Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet, about 1.6 ha south of Bâtard entirely in Chassagne, is the smallest and rarest of the Montrachet family. Its stony soil (criots probably means a place full of stones) gives a fine, mineral wine. Only a handful of producers bottle it: Blain-Gagnard, Fontaine-Gagnard, Roger Belland, Joseph Drouhin and Hubert Lamy.
appellations.terroir: Stony, thin soil on a small slope south of Bâtard at about 240 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Total annual production is typically under 10,000 bottles, the smallest output of the five Montrachet grand crus.

appellations.name: Bourgogne Hautes Côtes de Beaune
appellations.summary: The Hautes-Côtes de Beaune is the hill country behind the Côte de Beaune, from Échevronne to the Couchois, with vineyards at 300 to 450 m among woods and pastures. Like its Nuits counterpart it is a named zone of the Bourgogne AOC. Its fresh reds and crisp whites have become far more consistent with warmer summers, and the village of La Rochepot with its castle is the area's landmark.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl plateaus and valleys; cooler and windier than the côte below.
appellations.nerd_note: Many Côte d'Or domaines source Aligoté and Bourgogne blanc from the Hautes-Côtes.

appellations.name: Bouzeron
appellations.summary: Bouzeron is the only village appellation in Burgundy dedicated to Aligoté, the region's other white grape. Promoted from Bourgogne Aligoté Bouzeron in 1997, it requires the golden-berried Aligoté doré rather than the more productive green Aligoté vert. The wines are fresher and more floral than Chardonnay, with lemon, white flowers and a salty bite, and age better than most people expect. Domaine A. et P. de Villaine, founded by Aubert de Villaine of the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti in 1973 and now run by his nephew Pierre de Benoist, is the appellation's ambassador.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl slopes at 270 to 350 m in a narrow valley just north of Rully.
producers: Domaine A. et P. de Villaine
appellations.nerd_note: Bouzeron's red and Chardonnay wines are sold as Bourgogne Côte Chalonnaise; only Aligoté may carry the village name.

appellations.name: Rully
appellations.summary: Rully, the northernmost village of the Côte Chalonnaise, is mostly white and has long been the heart of Burgundy's sparkling wine industry: many crémant houses were founded here in the nineteenth century. Its still Chardonnay is bright and fresh with citrus and apple, and its reds are light and fruity. There are 23 premier crus, such as Grésigny, La Pucelle, Les Cloux and Rabourcé.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl hills facing east and southeast, around 230 to 350 m, with the twelfth-century Château de Rully on the slope.
appellations.nerd_note: The twelfth-century Château de Rully has passed down through the same family line for centuries and overlooks its own vineyards.

appellations.name: Mercurey
appellations.summary: Mercurey is the largest and best-known village of the Côte Chalonnaise, making mostly red wine with more structure and depth than its neighbours: dark cherry, earth and firm tannin. It has about 32 premier crus, among them Clos des Myglands, Clos du Roy, Clos l'Évêque and Clos des Barraults, and some of Burgundy's best value reds come from producers such as Faiveley, which built a large estate here, the Château de Chamirey and Domaine François Raquillet.
appellations.terroir: Limestone with clay and marl; the premier crus lie on the slopes north and west of the village.
appellations.nerd_note: Mercurey is believed to take its name from a Roman temple to Mercury on the old road between Chalon and Autun.

appellations.name: Givry
appellations.summary: Givry, south of Mercurey, is a red-wine village whose fame dates to King Henri IV, who is said to have favoured it (and a mistress who lived here). Its 37 premier crus include Clos Salomon, Clos du Cellier aux Moines and Clos Jus. The reds are fragrant, light-bodied and fresh; the whites are crisp and stony.
appellations.terroir: Limestone slopes and combes, with stony white soils on the upper slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: Clos du Cellier aux Moines was a Cistercian vineyard of the abbey of La Ferté from 1130; its cellar still stands.

appellations.name: Montagny
appellations.summary: Montagny is the white-only appellation at the southern end of the Côte Chalonnaise, covering Montagny-lès-Buxy, Buxy, Jully-lès-Buxy and Saint-Vallerin. It has about 49 premier crus, and more than half the appellation is classified premier cru, a legacy of an old rule based on alcohol rather than site that was reformed in 1989. The Cave des Vignerons de Buxy dominates production; the wines are crisp, nutty and dry.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl hills at 250 to 400 m, cooler than the northern Chalonnaise.
appellations.nerd_note: For decades any Montagny reaching 11.5 percent alcohol could be called premier cru; a reform in 1989 tied the title to named climats instead.

appellations.name: Bourgogne Côte Chalonnaise
appellations.summary: Bourgogne Côte Chalonnaise is the regional Bourgogne zone for the 44 communes of the Côte Chalonnaise, used for wines from outside the village appellations or from young vines. It is light, fresh and easy, often excellent value from good village growers.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl hills west of Chalon-sur-Saône.
producers: Domaine A. et P. de Villaine

appellations.name: Bourgogne Côtes du Couchois
appellations.summary: The Côtes du Couchois is a small, red-only Bourgogne zone around Couches, west of the Maranges, on granite and sandstone hills that are unusual for Burgundy. Light, peppery reds are its speciality.
appellations.terroir: Triassic sandstone, granite and marl on hills around Couches.

appellations.name: Mâcon
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay; Gamay and Pinot Noir for reds
appellations.summary: Mâcon is the umbrella appellation of the Mâconnais and its three tiers: plain Mâcon (red, white and rosé), Mâcon-Villages (white only, from a list of villages) and Mâcon followed by one of 27 village names, such as Mâcon-Lugny, Mâcon-Azé, Mâcon-Milly-Lamartine, Mâcon-Chardonnay, Mâcon-Uchizy, Mâcon-Fuissé or Mâcon-Pierreclos. Some village names may also be used for reds. The whites are fresh, ripe and unoaked, with apple, pear and white flowers; at their best, from growers such as Héritiers du Comte Lafon (Milly-Lamartine) or Guillot-Broux (Cruzille), they are serious and long-lived. The reds, mostly Gamay, are light and fruity.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl ridges running north to south across the Mâconnais, with clay valleys and some granite in the south and west.
appellations.nerd_note: The village of Chardonnay near Tournus gives its name to the Mâcon-Chardonnay appellation; whether the grape takes its name from the village or vice versa is still debated.

appellations.name: Pouilly-Fuissé
appellations.summary:
Pouilly-Fuissé is the leading white appellation of the Mâconnais, about 800 ha delimited across four communes (Fuissé, Solutré-Pouilly, Vergisson and Chaintré) beneath the limestone cliffs of Solutré and Vergisson. The wines are richer and riper than Mâcon, often barrel-fermented, with citrus, peach, hazelnut and a firm mineral finish, and the best age for a decade or more.

After a 13-year campaign led by growers' union president Frédéric-Marc Burrier, 22 climats were promoted to premier cru from the 2020 vintage, covering about 194 ha, roughly a quarter of the appellation. They include Sur la Roche and Les Crays under Vergisson, Le Clos de Solutré and En Servy at Solutré, Les Ménétrières, Le Clos and Les Brûlés at Fuissé, and Aux Quarts, Le Clos Reyssier and Les Chevrières at Chaintré. They were the Mâconnais's first premier crus.
appellations.terroir: Jurassic limestone and marl on steep slopes and scree fans below the cliffs of Solutré and Vergisson, at 200 to 400 m; facing east and south. Chaintré, further south, has warmer, clay-rich soils.
appellations.nerd_note: The 22 premier crus were approved in late 2020 for that vintage; they were the first premier crus anywhere in the Mâconnais.

appellations.name: Pouilly-Loché
appellations.summary: Pouilly-Loché is the smallest of the Pouilly appellations, about 35 ha in the commune of Loché just south of Pouilly-Fuissé. Its whites are lighter and fresher than Pouilly-Fuissé, and may also be sold as Pouilly-Vinzelles. Since the 2024 vintage one climat, Les Mûres (about 7 ha), has been classified premier cru, approved on 18 November 2024. The Cave des Grands Crus Blancs co-operative makes much of the wine.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and clay on gentle east-facing slopes near the Saône plain.
appellations.nerd_note: Wines from Pouilly-Loché may legally be sold as Pouilly-Vinzelles, but the reverse is not allowed.

appellations.name: Pouilly-Vinzelles
appellations.summary: Pouilly-Vinzelles covers about 70 ha around Vinzelles and Loché, between Pouilly-Fuissé and the Saône. Its whites are similar to Pouilly-Fuissé but a little lighter. Three premier crus were recognised from the 2024 vintage: Les Quarts (about 12.5 ha, on the same slope as Pouilly-Fuissé's Aux Quarts), Les Longeays and Les Pétaux.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl with some granite-derived sands, on east-facing slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: The Bret brothers of La Soufrandière were key advocates of the 2024 premier cru promotion.

appellations.name: Saint-Véran
appellations.summary: Saint-Véran, created in 1971, wraps around Pouilly-Fuissé in two separate parts: Davayé and Prissé to the north, and Chânes, Chasselas, Leynes and Saint-Vérand to the south, on the border with the Beaujolais. It was created partly to give the white wines of Beaujolais villages a proper Burgundian name. The wines are fresh and fruity in the south on granite and clay, and more mineral in the north on limestone. They are some of the best-value whites in Burgundy.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl in Davayé and Prissé; granite, sandy clay and limestone patches in the southern villages near the Beaujolais.
appellations.nerd_note: Saint-Véran is spelled without the final d of the village of Saint-Vérand, a quirk of its 1971 creation.

appellations.name: Viré-Clessé
appellations.summary: Viré-Clessé, created in 1999 from two former Mâcon village appellations, covers Viré, Clessé, Laizé and Montbellet in the northern Mâconnais. Its whites are rich and ripe, sometimes with a touch of residual sugar from botrytis-affected grapes, a style championed by Jean Thévenet of Domaine de la Bongran, whose late-harvested wines were initially refused the appellation. The rules were later changed to allow them.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and clay with white marl, on gentle slopes at 200 to 300 m.
appellations.nerd_note: The rules now provide for late-harvested wines with residual sugar, which may carry the traditional local mention levroutée.

appellations.name: Bourgogne
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; also Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc, César (Yonne), Gamay in the Beaujolais crus
appellations.summary:
Bourgogne is the regional appellation of Burgundy, covering about 40,000 ha across 264 communes in four departments, from the Yonne to the Beaujolais crus. Red Bourgogne is mostly Pinot Noir and white mostly Chardonnay. Many good domaines make their Bourgogne from village-quality vines just below the appellation line, which makes it one of the best introductions to their style.

Fourteen named zones (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) may follow the name: Côte d'Or (created 2017), Hautes Côtes de Nuits, Hautes Côtes de Beaune, Côte Chalonnaise, Côtes du Couchois, Chitry, Coulanges-la-Vineuse, Côtes d'Auxerre, Épineuil, Tonnerre, Côte Saint-Jacques, La Chapelle Notre-Dame, Le Chapitre and Montrecul. Since 2011 the crus of Beaujolais have also been allowed to declare Pinot Noir and Gamay as Bourgogne rouge, a controversial rule.
appellations.terroir: From Kimmeridgian marl in the Yonne to the limestones of the Côte d'Or and the granite of the Beaujolais crus.
appellations.nerd_note: Bourgogne Côte d'Or, created in 2017, can be used only for wines from the 40 communes of the Côte d'Or slope, letting growers distinguish their regional wine from that of the wider region.

appellations.name: Bourgogne aligoté
appellations.grapes: Aligoté (up to 15% Chardonnay historically, now 100% Aligoté)
appellations.summary: Bourgogne Aligoté is the regional appellation for Aligoté, Burgundy's second white grape, a natural cross of Pinot and Gouais Blanc. Long dismissed as a sharp wine to mix with crème de cassis (the kir, named after Canon Félix Kir, mayor of Dijon), it is now taken seriously by growers who plant it on good slopes and keep old vines: Ponsot, d'Auvenay, de Villaine, Sylvain Pataille and Roulot. A movement called Les Aligoteurs promotes it.
appellations.terroir: Grown across Burgundy, best on limestone slopes of the Côte d'Or and Hautes-Côtes.
producers: Domaine A. et P. de Villaine
appellations.nerd_note: The kir was popularised by Canon Kir after the Second World War; the original mix used Bourgogne Aligoté and crème de cassis from Dijon.

appellations.name: Bourgogne Passe-tout-grains
appellations.grapes: Gamay with at least 30% Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Bourgogne Passe-tout-grains is Burgundy's traditional field blend of Pinot Noir and Gamay, co-fermented, with at least 30 percent Pinot Noir and 15 percent Gamay. Once the growers' everyday red, it has been shrinking as Coteaux Bourguignons replaced it, but a few domaines such as Lafarge, Rossignol and Henri Jayer's heirs keep it as a light, joyful, cherry-fruited wine.
appellations.terroir: Grown across Burgundy, mostly on plain and plateau sites.
appellations.nerd_note: Its name means 'all grapes go in', a reminder that most old Burgundian vineyards were mixed plantings.

appellations.name: Coteaux Bourguignons
match: Coteaux Bourguignons / Bourgogne grand ordinaire / Bourgogne ordinaire
Coteaux Bourguignons ou Bourgogne grand ordinaire ou Bourgogne ordinaire
appellations.grapes: Gamay, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Aligoté, Melon de Bourgogne, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris
appellations.summary: Coteaux Bourguignons replaced the old Bourgogne Grand Ordinaire in 2011 as the broadest regional appellation of Burgundy, and it extends into the Beaujolais. It lets producers blend Gamay and Pinot Noir in any proportion and makes a lot of simple, easy-drinking red from Beaujolais Gamay, as well as white from Chardonnay, Aligoté and Melon de Bourgogne. The old name may still be used.
appellations.terroir: Any land of the Burgundy and Beaujolais regional areas.
appellations.nerd_note: Bourgogne grand ordinaire remains a legal synonym, though almost no one uses it now.

appellations.name: Crémant de Bourgogne
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Aligoté, Gamay (max 20%), Melon de Bourgogne, Sacy
appellations.summary: Crémant de Bourgogne is Burgundy's traditional-method sparkling wine, created in 1975 to replace Bourgogne mousseux. It is made mostly from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, with second fermentation in bottle and at least 9 months on the lees (24 months for Éminent and 36 for Grand Éminent, two quality tiers introduced in 2016). It now accounts for more than 10 percent of Burgundy's production, and much of it comes from the Châtillonnais in the north, the Auxerrois, Rully and the Mâconnais. Houses such as Bailly-Lapierre, Louis Bouillot, Veuve Ambal and Simonnet-Febvre are the big names.
appellations.terroir: Grown across Burgundy, especially the cooler Châtillonnais (on limestone like that of Champagne's Côte des Bar) and the Auxerrois.
appellations.nerd_note: The cellars of Bailly-Lapierre are dug into an old underground quarry on the Yonne that once supplied stone for Paris monuments.

appellations.name: Bourgogne mousseux
appellations.summary: Bourgogne mousseux is now reserved for sparkling red Burgundy, a nineteenth-century speciality once popular in Britain and America. Since Crémant de Bourgogne was created in 1975, white and rosé sparkling wines go under that name instead, leaving Bourgogne mousseux as a tiny, almost forgotten red style.
appellations.terroir: Burgundy regional area.
appellations.nerd_note: Sparkling red Burgundy was a Victorian fashion; a few houses still make it for curiosity.

appellations.name: Beaujolais
appellations.summary: Beaujolais AOC is the regional appellation, covering about 40,000 ha delimited (though far less is planted today) across 88 communes, mostly in the south of the region on limestone and clay around the golden-stone villages of the Pierres Dorées. It is the source of most Beaujolais Nouveau, released on the third Thursday of November, a few weeks after harvest, and of light, fruity reds for drinking within a year or two. Beaujolais blanc from Chardonnay is a growing niche. Some 38 communes in the north may add their name to Beaujolais or sell as Beaujolais-Villages.
appellations.terroir: Limestone, clay and sandstone in the south (Pierres Dorées), granite in the north.
appellations.nerd_note: Jean-Paul Brun of Domaine des Terres Dorées makes his reds with indigenous yeasts and destemming, Burgundy-style, rather than carbonic maceration, and was sometimes refused the appellation in tastings for being atypical.

appellations.name: Beaujolais-Villages
appellations.summary: Beaujolais-Villages covers 38 communes in the northern hills of the region, between and around the ten crus. On granite and schist soils, its Gamay is deeper and more structured than plain Beaujolais, though still fresh and fruity, and it can be made as Nouveau. Villages such as Lantignié, Quincié and Lancié are well known to fans for their quality.
appellations.terroir: Granite and schist slopes of the northern Beaujolais at 200 to 450 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Many cru growers bottle their younger vines as Beaujolais-Villages, which makes it one of the best bargains in French red wine.

appellations.name: Saint-Amour
appellations.summary: Saint-Amour is the northernmost of the ten crus and the only one lying entirely in Saône-et-Loire, on the border with the Mâconnais. Its name, from a Roman soldier who became a saint, has made it the wine of Valentine's Day, and it sells much of its wine around 14 February. The wines are supple and fruity with red berries and spice, and the mix of granite, schist and limestone soils gives some structure.
appellations.terroir: Granite, schist and some limestone and clay on east-facing hills, bordering the Saint-Véran appellation.
appellations.nerd_note: Saint-Amour is the only cru lying entirely in Burgundy's Saône-et-Loire department; Moulin-à-Vent (Romanèche-Thorins) and Chénas (La Chapelle-de-Guinchay) straddle it and the Rhône.

appellations.name: Juliénas
appellations.summary: Juliénas, named after Julius Caesar, is one of the most rustic and firmly structured crus. Its wines are dense and spicy with dark red fruit and need a year or two in bottle. The village's Cellier de la Vieille Église, a deconsecrated church turned tasting room, is decorated with Bacchic scenes.
appellations.terroir: Granite in the west, older schist and alluvium in the east; slopes facing east and southeast at 250 to 400 m.
appellations.nerd_note: The Château de Juliénas has one of the longest cellars in the Beaujolais.

appellations.name: Chénas
appellations.summary: Chénas is the smallest cru and the least known, partly because much of its land lies in the Moulin-à-Vent appellation. Its name comes from the oak forests (chênes) that once covered the slopes. The wines are deep and spicy with floral notes and can age; they are some of the best values among the crus.
appellations.terroir: Pink granite on the high western slopes, with alluvial sands lower down.
appellations.nerd_note: Paul-Henri Thillardon, a young Chénas grower, has become a symbol of the cru's revival since 2008.

appellations.name: Moulin-à-Vent
appellations.summary:
Moulin-à-Vent is the king of Beaujolais: the most structured and age-worthy of the crus, often compared to Burgundy and aged in oak. The appellation covers Romanèche-Thorins and Chénas and takes its name from a sixteenth-century windmill that still stands among the vines, a listed historic monument. Its pink granite is shot through with veins of manganese, credited with the wines' depth and their ability to age for 10 to 20 years.

The best climats, such as Les Thorins, Champ de Cour, La Rochelle, Les Carquelins and Rochegrès, are bottled separately by producers such as Château des Jacques (Louis Jadot), Richard Rottiers, Yvon Métras and Paul Janin. Old Moulin-à-Vent takes on truffle, spice and cherry notes that can confuse blind tasters into guessing Pinot Noir.
appellations.terroir: Pink granite with manganese veins, decomposed into sandy gore; gentle slopes at 250 to 300 m around the windmill.
appellations.nerd_note: The wine was once called Romanèche-Thorins; the windmill's name was adopted when the appellation was created in 1936.

appellations.name: Fleurie
appellations.summary: Fleurie is the most popular cru and, as its name suggests, the most floral: violet, iris and red berries over a silky, elegant texture. Its slopes of pure pink granite surround a village crowned by the chapel of La Madone, built in the 1870s on the hilltop above the vines. In 2023 more than 85 percent of Fleurie's growers voted to apply for premier cru status for seven lieux-dits (Les Moriers, Poncié, Les Garants, La Madone, La Roilette, Grille Midi and La Chapelle des Bois), about 27 percent of the appellation; INAO's decision is expected to take years.
appellations.terroir: A single granite massif with sandy gore; La Roilette next to Moulin-à-Vent has more clay and gives fuller wine.
appellations.nerd_note: The Cave de Fleurie co-operative, long led by Marguerite Chabert, popularised the cru in Lyon and Paris after the Second World War.

appellations.name: Chiroubles
appellations.summary: Chiroubles is the highest cru, with vineyards up to 400 to 450 m in a natural amphitheatre of granite. Its wines are the lightest and most delicate of the crus, fragrant and fresh, and in warm years the altitude is now an advantage. The village honours Victor Pulliat, a nineteenth-century ampelographer from Chiroubles who championed grafting to fight phylloxera.
appellations.terroir: Steep slopes of pink granite at the highest altitude of any cru, mostly facing east and southeast.
appellations.nerd_note: Victor Pulliat (1827 to 1896) planted a collection of more than 2,000 grape varieties in Chiroubles and helped save the region from phylloxera.

appellations.name: Morgon
appellations.summary:
Morgon is the second-largest cru and, with Moulin-à-Vent, the most powerful and age-worthy. Its wines are so distinctive that the locals have a verb for them: a Morgon that has aged into notes of kirsch, cherry and earth is said to morgonner. The appellation surrounds the village of Villié-Morgon, and its six climats (Côte du Py, Corcelette, Les Charmes, Grand Cras, Douby and Les Micouds) are often bottled separately.

Morgon is also the birthplace of natural wine: Marcel Lapierre and Jean Foillard, inspired by Jules Chauvet, began making unsulphured, wild-yeast Gamay here in the early 1980s. Their wines, along with Guy Breton's and those of a younger wave (Jean-Claude Lapalu, Mathieu Lapierre, Jean-Louis Dutraive, Julie Balagny), made Morgon a byword for vibrant, honest wine.
appellations.terroir: Granite in the west, but the famous Côte du Py, an extinct volcanic hill, has blue schist and pyrite-rich rock called roche pourrie (rotten rock) that gives Morgon its distinctive mineral character. Gravel and clay in Grand Cras and Les Charmes.
appellations.nerd_note: INAO's parcel file delimits Morgon at about 1,340 ha in the single commune of Villié-Morgon.

appellations.name: Régnié
appellations.summary: Régnié became the tenth cru in 1988, the newest of the group. It lies between Morgon and Brouilly on rolling granite hills around Régnié-Durette, whose church has two distinctive towers. The wines are lighter and fruity, with raspberry and red currant, and some growers such as Charly Thévenet and Julien Sunier have shown its potential.
appellations.terroir: Pink granite sand on rounded hills between 300 and 400 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Régnié's promotion in 1988 ended a long campaign; it was previously sold as Beaujolais-Villages.

appellations.name: Brouilly
appellations.summary: Brouilly is the largest and southernmost cru, encircling Mont Brouilly across six communes (Odenas, Saint-Lager, Cercié, Charentay, Quincié and Saint-Étienne-la-Varenne). Its wines are generous, fruity and approachable, the most typical of easy-drinking cru Beaujolais, with Pierreux and Les Brouilly among its best lieux-dits. Every September the Fête des Vins de Brouilly ends with a pilgrimage to the hilltop chapel.
appellations.terroir: Pink granite, sand and alluvial soils on the lower slopes and plains around Mont Brouilly.
appellations.nerd_note: Château de la Chaize, built from 1676 for the brother of Louis XIV's confessor Père La Chaize, was long the largest single estate in Brouilly.

appellations.name: Côte de Brouilly
appellations.summary: Côte de Brouilly covers the steep upper slopes of Mont Brouilly, an extinct volcano rising to 484 m, inside the larger Brouilly appellation. Its blue diorite rock, called blue stone (pierre bleue) or cornes vertes, gives deeper, more mineral and more concentrated wines than Brouilly. Château Thivin, the oldest estate on the hill, is the reference. The chapel of Notre-Dame-aux-Raisins on the summit, built in 1857 to ask for protection from oidium, hosts an annual winegrowers' pilgrimage.
appellations.terroir: Blue diorite (an old volcanic rock) and andesite on very steep slopes of all exposures around the hill.
appellations.nerd_note: Château Thivin has been in the Geoffray family since 1877; Claude Geoffray was one of the founders of the appellation.

appellations.name: Coteaux du Lyonnais
appellations.grapes: Gamay; Chardonnay and Aligoté for white
appellations.summary: Coteaux du Lyonnais is a small AOC on the hills west and southwest of Lyon, continuing the Beaujolais to the south. Its light Gamay reds and fresh Chardonnay whites are the house wines of Lyon's bouchons, and the area has shrunk to a few hundred hectares in production under pressure from the city's suburbs.
appellations.terroir: Granite, gneiss and some limestone and loess on hills from the Monts d'Or to the Monts du Lyonnais.
appellations.nerd_note: Coteaux du Lyonnais was a VDQS from 1952 and became an AOC in 1984.

appellations.name: Côte Rôtie
appellations.summary:
Côte Rôtie, the roasted slope, is the northernmost cru of the Rhône and one of the world's great Syrahs: perfumed with violet, black olive, bacon fat and pepper, silky yet structured, and capable of ageing for 20 years. Its 342 ha (2025) of vines climb terraces so steep, up to 60 percent, that every task is done by hand and each vine is tied to its own stake. Growers may co-ferment up to 20 percent Viognier, which fixes colour and lifts the aroma, though most use far less.
