The slope is divided into many lieux-dits, traditionally summed up as Côte Brune north of Ampuis, with darker, iron-rich schist that gives firmer, more tannic wines, and Côte Blonde to the south, with paler granite and gneiss that gives softer, more perfumed wine. Marcel Guigal's three single-site wines, La Mouline (first vintage 1966), La Landonne (1978) and La Turque (1985), known as the La La's, became cult wines from the 1980s and transformed the appellation, which had shrunk to about 70 ha in the 1970s. Today growers such as Jamet, Rostaing, Gilles Barge, Stéphane Ogier, Clusel-Roch, Bernard Levet and Jean-Michel Stephan bottle individual lieux-dits.
appellations.terroir: Mica-schist and gneiss in the north (Côte Brune), granite and leucogranite in the south (Côte Blonde and Condrieu side); southeast-facing terraces along the right bank of the Rhône from Saint-Cyr to Tupin-et-Semons, at 180 to 325 m. The plateau above, added in the 1960s delimitation, is debated.
appellations.nerd_note: Côte Rôtie's 1940 decree allowed some plateau land above the slopes; growers have long debated tightening it, and a 2025 to 2026 discussion in the trade press asked whether a Burgundy-style cru system could work here.

appellations.name: Condrieu
appellations.summary: Condrieu is the birthplace of Viognier and its finest expression: a dry white of apricot, peach blossom, honeysuckle and musk, rich and oily but with a mineral finish, best drunk within a few years. The appellation runs about 20 km south of Côte Rôtie on steep granite terraces across seven communes in three departments. By the late 1960s it was down to roughly a dozen hectares and Viognier was close to extinction; Georges Vernay, the 'pope of Condrieu', led its revival, and today 216 ha (2025) are planted. A few growers make a late-harvest sweet style, and the Vernay family's Coteau de Vernon is the most famous single site.
appellations.terroir: Granite with a sandy, mica-rich topsoil called arzelle, on steep terraces facing south and southeast at 150 to 300 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Condrieu's name is said to come from coin du ruisseau (corner of the stream), the confluence of streams at the village.

appellations.name: Château-Grillet
appellations.summary: Château-Grillet is one of France's smallest appellations and one of the few that consists of a single estate: about 3.8 ha of Viognier in a sun-trap amphitheatre of terraces above the Rhône at Vérin and Saint-Michel-sur-Rhône, completely enclosed by Condrieu. The Neyret-Gachet family owned it from 1830 until 2011, when François Pinault's Artémis group bought it. Since then the wine, sold in a distinctive brown flute bottle, has been made with more precision, with a second wine from younger vines. Château-Grillet is more restrained and longer-lived than most Condrieu.
appellations.terroir: A natural amphitheatre of granite terraces facing south and southeast, sheltered from the wind, at about 150 to 250 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Château-Grillet produces only about 10,000 bottles a year, and the INAO parcel file delimits 3.79 ha.

appellations.name: Saint-Joseph
appellations.grapes: Syrah (up to 10% Marsanne and Roussanne); Marsanne and Roussanne for white
appellations.summary: Saint-Joseph is the long, thin appellation of the right bank, running about 60 km from Chavanay to Guilherand-Granges opposite Valence across 26 communes in the Ardèche and Loire. It began in 1956 around Tournon and Mauves, where the slopes facing Hermitage were known as the Côte de Saint-Joseph after a Jesuit vineyard, and was expanded in 1969 to include flat land; a 1992 revision moved much of it back to the slopes. With 1,504 ha (2025), its reds range from light and peppery to dense and age-worthy. The best come from the original heart around Mauves, Tournon and Saint-Jean-de-Muzols, and from growers such as Jean-Louis Chave, Gonon, Coursodon and Faury. White Saint-Joseph from Marsanne and Roussanne is rich and nutty.
appellations.terroir: Granite and gneiss terraces, with some loess and sandy soils in the north; the best sites face southeast over the Rhône.
appellations.nerd_note: Chave's Saint-Joseph Clos Florentin, a walled parcel replanted on the terraces above Mauves, is one of the appellation's flagship wines.

appellations.name: Crozes-Hermitage
appellations.grapes: Syrah (up to 15% Marsanne and Roussanne); Marsanne and Roussanne for white
appellations.summary: Crozes-Hermitage is the largest appellation of the Northern Rhône (2,139 ha in 2025, still growing) and surrounds the hill of Hermitage on the east bank across 11 communes. Most is on flatter terraces and gentle hills, and the wines are fresh, fruity, peppery Syrah to drink young; the best, from the granite hills of the north around Gervans and Larnage or the pebbly terraces of Les Chassis to the south, approach Hermitage. The Cave de Tain co-operative makes a large share. Growers such as Alain Graillot (whose domaine his sons continue), Yann Chave, Combier, Domaine des Entrefaux and Dard et Ribo built its modern reputation.
appellations.terroir: Granite hills in the north (Gervans, Erôme, Serves), loess and clay around Mercurol and Larnage, and glacial pebble terraces of Les Chassis and Les Sept Chemins in the south.
appellations.nerd_note: Jaboulet's Domaine de Thalabert, first bottled separately in the 1960s, was the first Crozes-Hermitage to be taken seriously by critics.

appellations.name: Hermitage
match: Hermitage ou Ermitage ou l'Hermitage ou l'Ermitage
appellations.grapes: Syrah (up to 15% Marsanne and Roussanne); Marsanne and Roussanne for white
appellations.summary:
Hermitage is a single south-facing hill of 137 ha (2025) rising above Tain-l'Hermitage on the east bank of the Rhône, and it has been one of France's most famous wines for three centuries. Legend says a knight, Gaspard de Stérimberg, returned wounded from the crusade against the Albigensians in 1224 and was granted the hill by Queen Blanche of Castile to live as a hermit; the chapel of Saint-Christophe at the top recalls him. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries Hermitage sold for prices close to Lafite, and some Bordeaux was 'hermitagé', strengthened with Hermitage.

Red Hermitage is a powerful, dense, long-lived Syrah: black fruit, smoke, leather and spice that need 10 to 30 years. About a third of the hill makes white Hermitage, mostly Marsanne, which can age for decades into honeyed, nutty depths, and a little vin de paille. Traditionally the wines are blended from several of the hill's lieux-dits (Les Bessards, L'Hermite, Le Méal, Les Greffieux, Péléat, Les Rocoules, Les Diognières, Les Murets, Beaume), each adding a different element; Jean-Louis Chave's Hermitage is the model of this approach, while Chapoutier bottles single sites.
appellations.terroir: A granite block in the west (Les Bessards, Varogne) that the Rhône detached from the Massif Central; further east, loess, clay, alpine pebbles and limestone deposits (Le Méal, Les Greffieux, Les Murets). Terraces at 120 to 340 m, facing due south.
appellations.nerd_note: Hermitage may legally be spelled Ermitage, and Chapoutier uses that spelling for its single-site 'Ermitage' wines such as Le Pavillon and L'Ermite.

appellations.name: Cornas
appellations.summary: Cornas, 162 ha (2025) of steep granite in a single commune opposite Valence, makes the most rustic, tannic and wild Syrah of the Northern Rhône. Its name comes from the Celtic for burnt earth: an amphitheatre of terraces facing southeast, sheltered from the north wind, makes it one of the warmest spots in the north. Unlike its neighbours, Cornas must be 100 percent Syrah, with no white grapes. Auguste Clape kept the traditional style alive when others gave up, and today Thierry Allemand, Franck Balthazar, Vincent Paris, Guillaume Gilles, Domaine du Coulet and Alain Voge make cult wines. The best lieux-dits include Reynard, Chaillot, Sabarotte, Les Eygas, La Geynale and Patou.
appellations.terroir: Decomposed granite (gore) on steep terraces with some limestone and clay at the foot; a south-facing bowl that ripens early.
appellations.nerd_note: Thierry Allemand started with almost nothing in 1982, renting terraces nobody else wanted; his Reynard and Chaillot are now among the most sought-after Rhône wines.

appellations.name: Saint-Péray
appellations.summary: Saint-Péray, at the southern end of the Northern Rhône opposite Valence, is a white-only appellation of 128 ha (2025) that was once famous for sparkling wine: in the nineteenth century its traditional-method Marsanne was compared with Champagne, and Wagner is said to have ordered it. Sparkling Saint-Péray is now rare, and growers concentrate on still whites from Marsanne and Roussanne with surprising freshness from the area's limestone. Domaine Alain Voge, Chapoutier, Bernard Gripa and Vincent Paris are among the producers.
appellations.terroir: Granite in the west and a limestone outcrop around the ruined Château de Crussol, which gives Saint-Péray its distinctive freshness.
appellations.nerd_note: Sparkling Saint-Péray dates to 1829, when the Faure family applied the Champagne method to Marsanne.

appellations.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
appellations.grapes: 13 grape varieties (18 counting colour variants): Grenache Noir, Gris and Blanc, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Cinsault, Counoise, Vaccarèse, Terret Noir, Muscardin, Clairette, Clairette Rose, Bourboulenc, Roussanne, Picpoul Noir, Gris and Blanc, Picardan
appellations.summary:
Châteauneuf-du-Pape is the most famous wine of the Southern Rhône and the birthplace of French appellation law. Some 300 growers declared 3,122 ha for the 2025 vintage (3,738 ha are delimited in INAO's parcel file) in Châteauneuf-du-Pape and parts of Orange, Courthézon, Bédarrides and Sorgues, between Orange and Avignon. The 2025 crop was 88,271 hl, an average of only 28 hl/ha.

The village takes its name from the summer castle built by Pope John XXII in the 1320s; only one wall of the keep survived the Wars of Religion and a German demolition in 1944. In 1923 Baron Pierre Le Roy de Boiseaumarié of Château Fortia drew up rules with the growers: a delimited area based on where lavender and thyme grew, a list of grape varieties, a minimum alcohol of 12.5 percent, a ban on rosé, and the triage (sorting out of 5 to 20 percent of the harvest). Recognised by the courts in 1933, they became the model for the 1935 AOC law, and Châteauneuf was among the first AOCs decreed in 1936. In 1954 the village council even banned flying saucers from landing in its vineyards.

The red, about 93 percent of production, is usually a Grenache-led blend with Syrah, Mourvèdre and Cinsault, though some estates use all the permitted varieties (Beaucastel) or pure Grenache (Rayas). It is generous and spicy, with kirsch, garrigue herbs, leather and liquorice, often above 15 percent alcohol, and ages for 20 years or more in good vintages. Whites from Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Roussanne and Bourboulenc are rich and honeyed. Most bottles carry the papal coat of arms embossed in the glass.
appellations.terroir: The appellation is famous for its galets roulés, rounded quartzite pebbles carried by the ancient Rhône from the Alps and laid on red clay terraces, notably on the plateau of La Crau (Vieux Télégraphe) and around Mont-Redon and Cabrières. They store heat and reflect sun. But the soils are far more varied: sand in the northeast (Rayas, Pignan, Charvin), giving finer, more perfumed Grenache; safres (Miocene sandstone and sand) in the east; and Urgonian limestone in the west near the château. The mistral blows more than 100 days a year. Bush vines (gobelet), some more than 100 years old, are the norm.
appellations.nerd_note: Châteauneuf's maximum yield of 35 hl/ha is one of the lowest of any French AOC, and the rules still require growers to discard part of the harvest in the vineyard (le rapé).

appellations.name: Gigondas
appellations.grapes: Grenache (max 80%) with at least 15% Syrah and/or Mourvèdre; whites from Clairette from 2022
appellations.summary: Gigondas sits under the jagged limestone spires of the Dentelles de Montmirail, and its vineyards climb from 100 to more than 500 m, among the highest in the Southern Rhône. It was the first village to break away from the Côtes du Rhône Villages and become a cru in 1971. The reds are powerful, spicy and structured, with dark fruit, garrigue and a fresh edge from altitude, often compared to a more rustic Châteauneuf. A small amount of rosé is made, and since September 2022 white Gigondas, based on Clairette, has also been allowed. The appellation had 1,184 ha in 2025.
appellations.terroir: Triassic and Jurassic limestone and marl under the Dentelles, with sandy and clay terraces lower down; the higher sites (Les Hautes Garrigues, Le Colombier) give the freshest wines.
appellations.nerd_note: Château de Saint-Cosme's cellars include Gallo-Roman fermentation vats cut into the rock.

appellations.name: Vacqueyras
appellations.grapes: Grenache with Syrah and/or Mourvèdre; whites from Clairette, Grenache Blanc, Bourboulenc, Roussanne
appellations.summary: Vacqueyras, between Gigondas and Beaumes-de-Venise, became a cru in 1990. Its 1,421 ha (2025) spread over Vacqueyras and Sarrians on flatter terraces below the Dentelles, and its reds are generous, spicy and dark, slightly softer than Gigondas and good value. A little white and rosé is made. The twelfth-century troubadour Raimbaut de Vaqueiras was born here.
appellations.terroir: Pebbly terraces with red clay (like Châteauneuf) and sandy-limestone soils toward the Dentelles.
appellations.nerd_note: Vacqueyras is the only Rhône cru whose name is also that of a medieval troubadour; the Le Sang des Cailloux domaine names its cuvées after local saints and family members.

appellations.name: Beaumes de Venise
appellations.summary: Beaumes de Venise became a cru for its red wines in 2005, separate from the older Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise. Its 738 ha (2025) of Grenache and Syrah grow at the southern foot of the Dentelles de Montmirail on unusually diverse soils, and the reds are fresh and spicy with a firm line. The name refers to the caves (baumes) in the hillside and to the Comtat Venaissin, the papal territory.
appellations.terroir: Triassic gypsum and marl, Jurassic limestone and sandy soils, sometimes within a single estate; vineyards up to 400 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Venise has nothing to do with Venice: it derives from the Comtat Venaissin.

appellations.name: Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise
appellations.grapes: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains (and Muscat à Petits Grains Rouge)
appellations.summary: Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise is a vin doux naturel: Muscat grapes partly fermented and then fortified with grape spirit to keep their sweetness, at about 15 percent alcohol and at least 110 g/l of sugar. The wine is golden, floral and grapey, with orange blossom, apricot and lychee, best drunk young and chilled. Pliny mentioned the Muscat of the area, and the AOC dates from 1945. Planted area has fallen to 227 ha (2025) as demand for sweet wine declined.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and sandy marl slopes around Beaumes-de-Venise and Aubignan.
appellations.nerd_note: Some growers make pink or red-tinged versions from the red-berried Muscat à Petits Grains Rouge.

appellations.name: Rasteau
appellations.grapes: Grenache (min 50%), Syrah, Mourvèdre; Grenache for VDN
appellations.summary: Rasteau has two appellations. The older is a vin doux naturel, recognised in 1944: fortified Grenache made in red (and amber or rancio) styles, rich and port-like. The newer, since 2010, is a cru for dry red wine, Grenache-led blends that are among the most powerful and ripe of the Southern Rhône, from 861 ha (2025) of south-facing slopes. The village was formerly a Côtes du Rhône Villages.
appellations.terroir: Marl and clay with some pebbles and sand on south-facing amphitheatre slopes above the Ouvèze; one of the warmest sites in the south.
appellations.nerd_note: Rasteau vin doux naturel is now tiny (18 ha in 2025) while the dry red is one of the fastest-growing crus.

appellations.name: Cairanne
appellations.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre; whites from Clairette, Grenache Blanc, Roussanne
appellations.summary: Cairanne, on a hill north of Rasteau, was promoted from Côtes du Rhône Villages to cru in 2015 after a long campaign by its growers. With 886 ha (2025), it makes sumptuous, spicy reds and a small amount of rich white. Rosé is not allowed under the cru. Marcel Richaud, Oratoire Saint-Martin and the Cave de Cairanne are its leading producers.
appellations.terroir: Ancient terraces with pebbles, red clay and limestone (Garrigues des Plateaux), and sandy-clay soils on the slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: Marcel Richaud pioneered estate bottling in Cairanne in the 1970s and campaigned for decades for its promotion.

appellations.name: Vinsobres
appellations.summary: Vinsobres, in the Drôme near Nyons, became the first cru of the Drôme provençale in 2006. Its 559 ha (2025) lie at 200 to 500 m among olive groves, and its reds, mostly Grenache with plenty of Syrah, are fresher and more structured than those of lower crus. The name is often traced to Vinum Sobrium, and a seventeenth-century bishop of Vaison is said to have advised drinking it soberly.
appellations.terroir: Limestone, marl and pebble terraces on hillsides at altitude, with cooler nights.
appellations.nerd_note: Vinsobres was the first cru of the Drôme department's southern Rhône vineyards.

appellations.name: Lirac
appellations.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Cinsault; whites from Clairette, Grenache Blanc, Bourboulenc
appellations.summary: Lirac lies on the Gard bank of the Rhône opposite Châteauneuf-du-Pape, across Lirac, Roquemaure, Saint-Laurent-des-Arbres and Saint-Geniès-de-Comolas. It makes red, white and rosé from 848 ha (2025). Its reds have become far more serious since the 2000s, when Châteauneuf estates such as Mordorée and Pegau, and growers like Domaine de la Rocalière, raised the bar. Roquemaure's port shipped wine branded CdR under a 1737 royal edict, one of the earliest regulated origins in France.
appellations.terroir: Galets roulés on the eastern terraces facing Châteauneuf, sands and limestone garrigues to the west.
appellations.nerd_note: Saint Valentine's relics are said to have been brought to Roquemaure in 1868, and the town holds a Valentine's festival.

appellations.name: Tavel
appellations.grapes: Grenache (max 60%), Cinsault, Clairette, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Bourboulenc, Picpoul, Calitor, Carignan
appellations.summary: Tavel is the only Rhône appellation and one of the few in France devoted entirely to rosé, made since the Middle Ages and loved by the popes of Avignon, Louis XIV and Ernest Hemingway. Its 781 ha (2025) in Tavel and Roquemaure make a deeply coloured, structured rosé, more like a light red, with red fruit, spice and a vinous texture, which pairs with food and even ages. It was among the first AOCs in 1936. Tavel has suffered as fashion turned to pale Provence rosé; some producers now make paler versions, and its area fell by about a fifth between 2020 and 2024.
appellations.terroir: Three terroirs: galets roulés over red clay, sand and pebbles, and limestone slabs (lauzes) on the plateau.
appellations.nerd_note: Tavel's colour comes from several days of maceration, longer than most rosés, which is why it has tannin and ages.

appellations.name: Laudun
appellations.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre; whites from Clairette, Grenache Blanc, Roussanne, Viognier
appellations.summary: Laudun became the 18th cru of the Rhône Valley when INAO's national committee approved its promotion on 11 September 2024, with effect from the 2024 vintage. A Côtes du Rhône Villages with its own name since 1967, it covers about 512 ha (2025) in Laudun-l'Ardoise, Saint-Victor-la-Coste and Tresques on the Gard bank. Laudun is unusual for its whites, about 30 percent of production, which are fresh and floral from limestone and sand; rosé is no longer allowed under the cru name. Its reds are spicy and medium-bodied.
appellations.terroir: Three soils: sandy sandstone (safres), pebble terraces on the plateau of the Camp de César, and limestone slopes; Roman remains on the plateau show ancient settlement.
appellations.nerd_note: Laudun's promotion came 57 years after it gained a village name, and the cru excluded rosé even though the village was once known for it.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône
appellations.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre (red, together at least 70%) plus many others
appellations.summary:
Côtes du Rhône is the regional appellation of the whole valley, covering 26,777 ha in production in 2025 (down from more than 31,000 ha in 2020) across 167 communes in six departments. It is one of France's largest AOCs; the 2025 harvest was about 920,000 hectolitres of mostly red wine, typically Grenache-based blends from the south. Quality ranges from co-operative bulk wine to excellent bottlings such as Château de Fonsalette (from Rayas), Coudoulet de Beaucastel and Guigal's Côtes du Rhône. The northern Rhône's growers can also use it for declassified Syrah and Viognier.

A few lieux-dits may be added, and Brézème, a small hill of about 30 ha at Livron-sur-Drôme between the north and south, is the only place permitted to put its own name with the Côtes du Rhône name, for mostly pure Syrah.
appellations.terroir: Every soil of the valley, from northern granite to southern pebble terraces, sands and limestone.
appellations.nerd_note: Côtes du Rhône lost about 4,400 ha between 2020 and 2025 as growers pulled out vines under France's grubbing-up scheme.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages
appellations.summary: Côtes du Rhône Villages is the middle tier of the Rhône hierarchy: 8,019 ha in 2025, of which about 2,700 ha are sold under the plain Villages name and about 5,300 ha add one of the named villages. Yields are lower and grape rules stricter than for Côtes du Rhône. The cahier des charges under review by INAO in June 2026 lists 21 named villages: Chusclan, Gadagne, Massif d'Uchaux, Nyons, Plan de Dieu, Puyméras, Roaix, Rochegude, Rousset-les-Vignes, Sablet, Saint-Andéol, Saint-Gervais, Saint-Maurice, Saint-Pantaléon-les-Vignes, Sainte-Cécile, Séguret, Signargues, Suze-la-Rousse, Vaison-la-Romaine, Valréas and Visan. Nyons (2020) is the newest. Many former named villages, from Gigondas (1971) to Cairanne (2015) and Laudun (2024), have graduated to cru.
appellations.terroir: Varied: pebble terraces of the Plan de Dieu, limestone hills of Séguret and Sablet, sands of the Massif d'Uchaux and Sainte-Cécile, marl and limestone of the Drôme villages.
appellations.nerd_note: Ten of the named villages (Gadagne, Massif d'Uchaux, Nyons, Plan de Dieu, Puyméras, Saint-Andéol, Sainte-Cécile, Signargues, Suze-la-Rousse and Vaison-la-Romaine) cannot use their name on rosé.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Chusclan
appellations.summary: Gard-bank villages around Chusclan and Bagnols-sur-Cèze north of Laudun, long known for rosé; a named village since 1967. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Gadagne
appellations.summary: Five communes east of Avignon around Châteauneuf-de-Gadagne, on pebble terraces like Châteauneuf's; a named village since 2012. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Massif d'Uchaux
match: Côtes du Rhône Villages Massif d'Uchaux
appellations.summary: A wooded massif of sandstone and sand north of Orange, recognised in 2005; red only, known for fine, perfumed Grenache from estates such as Château Saint-Estève and Domaine de la Guicharde. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Nyons
appellations.summary: Olive capital of the Drôme provençale, recognised in 2020, with limestone hills at altitude giving fresh reds. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Plan de Dieu
match: Côtes du Rhône Villages Plan de Dieu
appellations.summary: A flat plateau of pebble-strewn garrigue between Orange and Vaison, once Templar land, making ripe, powerful Grenache-based reds. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Puyméras
appellations.summary: Hill vineyards in Puyméras, Faucon and Mérindol-les-Oliviers near Vaison-la-Romaine at up to 400 m, giving fresh, spicy reds. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Roaix
appellations.summary: A small village between Rasteau and Séguret with limestone and marl slopes; a named village since 1967. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Rochegude
appellations.summary: A village with a medieval château north of Orange, on pebble and sand terraces. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Rousset-les-Vignes
appellations.summary: A high village in the Drôme provençale on limestone, recognised in 1969, making fresh reds. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Sablet
appellations.summary: A village below the Dentelles near Gigondas on sandy soils (its name means sand), known for fine reds and some of the best whites of the Villages. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Saint-Andéol
appellations.summary: Four Ardèche communes around Saint-Marcel-d'Ardèche and Bourg-Saint-Andéol on the right bank, the only named village in the Ardèche. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Saint-Gervais
appellations.summary: A Gard village on a terrace above the Cèze, recognised in 1974; Domaine Sainte-Anne put it on the map. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Saint-Maurice
appellations.summary: Saint-Maurice-sur-Eygues in the Drôme, recognised in 1967, with pebble terraces along the Eygues. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Saint-Pantaléon-les-Vignes
appellations.summary: A Drôme village near Valréas, recognised in 1969, with sandy and limestone soils. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Sainte-Cécile
appellations.summary: Sainte-Cécile-les-Vignes and neighbours north of Orange, recognised in 2016, on pebble and sand terraces. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Séguret
appellations.summary: A perched medieval village below the Dentelles, with limestone slopes giving structured reds and fine whites. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Signargues
appellations.summary: Four Gard communes west of Avignon on pebble terraces, recognised in 2005; red only. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Suze-la-Rousse
appellations.summary: Villages around the castle of Suze-la-Rousse, home of the Université du Vin, recognised in 2016. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Vaison-la-Romaine
appellations.summary: Vineyards in Buisson and Villedieu near the Roman town of Vaison, recognised in 2016. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Valréas
appellations.summary: The largest named village, in the papal enclave (Enclave des Papes) of the Vaucluse surrounded by the Drôme, recognised in 1967. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Visan
appellations.summary: Visan, in the Vaucluse next to the Enclave des Papes, has been a named village of the Côtes du Rhône Villages since the 1960s, with pebbly terraces and limestone hills giving generous reds and some whites. It is listed in the cahier des charges but not drawn as a separate area in INAO's October 2026 parcel file, so its boundary may be missing from the map.

appellations.name: Côtes du Rhône Brézème
appellations.grapes: Syrah; Marsanne, Roussanne, Viognier for white
appellations.summary: Brézème is a 30 ha hill of terraced limestone and marl at Livron-sur-Drôme, where the Drôme meets the Rhône, halfway between the Northern and Southern Rhône. It is the only lieu-dit allowed to put its own name before Côtes du Rhône on the label. Mostly planted with Syrah, it makes northern-style reds; Jean-Marie Lombard revived it in the 1970s, and the Perrin family now farms Domaine de Bréseyme here.
appellations.terroir: Limestone marl terraces held by dry-stone walls on a south-facing hill.
appellations.nerd_note: Brézème shows that the line between the Northern and Southern Rhône is not absolute: its Syrah tastes far more northern than its latitude suggests.

appellations.name: Ventoux
appellations.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Cinsault, Mourvèdre, Carignan; whites from Clairette, Bourboulenc, Grenache Blanc, Roussanne
appellations.summary: Ventoux (Côtes du Ventoux until 2009) spreads across the foothills of Mont Ventoux, the 1,910 m giant of Provence, from Vaison-la-Romaine to Apt. Its 4,987 ha (2025) make fresh, fruity reds and rosés with a cooler character than the Rhône plain, thanks to altitude and cold air from the mountain. Château Pesquié, Domaine de Fondrèche and Perrin's La Vieille Ferme are well-known names.
appellations.terroir: Limestone, sandy and clay foothills at 200 to 500 m; big day-night temperature swings.
appellations.nerd_note: Ventoux lost about 12 percent of its area between 2020 and 2025.

appellations.name: Luberon
appellations.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Cinsault; whites from Vermentino, Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Roussanne, Ugni Blanc
appellations.summary: Luberon (Côtes du Luberon until 2009) covers the slopes on both sides of the Luberon mountains between Cavaillon and Manosque, in the regional nature park. Its 2,781 ha (2025) make mostly rosé and fresh whites, with Provençal character, and some reds. Château La Canorgue (setting of the film A Good Year), Château Val Joanis and the Marrenon co-operative are known producers.
appellations.terroir: Limestone, marl and sandy soils at 200 to 450 m; cooler and drier than the Rhône plain.
appellations.nerd_note: Luberon is an Inter Rhône appellation even though it is geographically in Provence.

appellations.name: Grignan-les-Adhémar
appellations.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Cinsault, Mourvèdre, Carignan; whites from Viognier, Marsanne, Roussanne, Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Bourboulenc
appellations.summary: Grignan-les-Adhémar was called Coteaux du Tricastin until 2010, when growers changed its name to escape association with the Tricastin nuclear plant after a uranium leak in 2008. It covers hills and plateaux of the Drôme provençale around the château of Grignan, where Madame de Sévigné's daughter lived. Its 971 ha (2025, down from 1,270 in 2020) make light, fruity reds and some fresh whites.
appellations.terroir: Limestone, sandy and pebbly soils on plateaux and hills, with mistral exposure.
appellations.nerd_note: The name honours the Adhémar family, lords of Grignan whose Renaissance château dominates the town.

appellations.name: Costières de Nîmes
appellations.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Carignan, Cinsault; whites from Grenache Blanc, Roussanne, Marsanne, Clairette, Vermentino, Viognier
appellations.summary: Costières de Nîmes lies on a plateau between Nîmes and the Camargue, the southernmost outpost of the Rhône Valley vineyards. Its galets roulés, laid down by the ancient Rhône and Durance, are the same type as Châteauneuf's, and its Grenache and Syrah reds are ripe and spicy, with sea breezes keeping them fresh. Promoted to AOC in 1986 as Costières du Gard, renamed in 1989, it moved from Languedoc's interprofession to Inter Rhône in 2004. Its area has fallen sharply, to 2,145 ha in 2025 from 2,844 ha in 2020.
appellations.terroir: A plateau of quartzite pebbles over red clay and sand, at 20 to 140 m; Mediterranean breezes from the Camargue.
appellations.nerd_note: The Mas des Tourelles at Beaucaire makes wine with Roman methods in a reconstructed Gallo-Roman cellar.

appellations.name: Clairette de Bellegarde
appellations.summary: Clairette de Bellegarde is a tiny white-only AOC in the commune of Bellegarde in the Costières, south of Nîmes, for dry wines made solely from Clairette. Only about 10 ha (2025) remain, making it one of France's smallest appellations by planted area.
appellations.terroir: Pebbly and sandy terraces of the Costières.
appellations.nerd_note: Its delimited area of about 2,460 ha in INAO's file dwarfs the handful of hectares actually declared.

appellations.name: Duché d'Uzès
appellations.grapes: Syrah (min 40%) and Grenache (min 20%) for red; Viognier (min 40%) and Grenache Blanc for white
appellations.summary: Duché d'Uzès became an AOC in July 2013 after a campaign that began in 1989, covering garrigue hills around the old ducal town of Uzès, between Nîmes and Alès. All its wines are blends: reds based on Syrah and Grenache, rosés, and whites led by Viognier. Its 285 ha (2025) produced 9,089 hl at only 32 hl/ha. The appellation celebrates the 'royal vines' of Arpaillargues-et-Aureilhac.
appellations.terroir: Limestone garrigue, marls and sandstones on low hills at the foot of the Cévennes.
appellations.nerd_note: Uzès is not in INAO's parcel delimitation file of October 2026, so its boundary on the map may be drawn from communes.

appellations.name: Côtes du Vivarais
appellations.summary: Côtes du Vivarais lies in the southern Ardèche around the Gorges de l'Ardèche and Vallon-Pont-d'Arc, near the Chauvet Cave. Its light, fruity Grenache and Syrah reds and rosés come from limestone plateaux; the area has fallen to only 120 ha (2025).
appellations.terroir: Limestone plateaux and garrigue around the Ardèche gorges.
appellations.nerd_note: Domaine Gallety makes the appellation's best-known age-worthy reds.

appellations.name: Clairette de Die
appellations.grapes: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains (min 75% for Tradition), Clairette
appellations.summary: Clairette de Die is the Diois's flagship: a lightly sweet, low-alcohol (about 7 to 8 percent) sparkling wine made mostly from Muscat by the méthode dioise ancestrale, in which fermentation starts in tank, is chilled to pause it, and finishes in bottle without added sugar or yeast. The result is grapey, floral and fresh. Dry traditional-method sparkling wine from the Diois is sold as Crémant de Die. The Cave de Die Jaillance co-operative dominates, but growers such as Achard-Vincent show what organic Muscat can do.
appellations.terroir: Limestone scree, marl and clay at 200 to 700 m along the Drôme valley; cool nights preserve Muscat's aroma.
appellations.nerd_note: The méthode dioise is related to the ancestral method of Limoux and Gaillac and predates Champagne's.

appellations.name: Crémant de Die
appellations.summary: Crémant de Die, created in 1993, is the dry, traditional-method sparkling wine of the Diois, made mostly from Clairette with Aligoté and a little Muscat. It is crisp and lightly floral, and with only 64 ha (2025) it is one of the smaller crémant appellations.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl slopes in the Drôme valley.

appellations.name: Coteaux de Die
appellations.summary: Coteaux de Die is a still, dry white from Clairette grown in the Diois. With about 3 ha declared in 2025, it is one of France's rarest appellations.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl in the Drôme valley.
appellations.nerd_note: It shares its delimited area with Clairette de Die and Crémant de Die.

appellations.name: Châtillon-en-Diois
appellations.grapes: Gamay, Pinot Noir, Syrah; Aligoté and Chardonnay for white
appellations.summary: Châtillon-en-Diois covers mountain vineyards east of Die at up to 700 m, where Gamay, Pinot Noir and Syrah make light, fresh reds and Aligoté and Chardonnay make crisp whites. About 40 ha (2025) are declared.
appellations.terroir: Limestone scree and marl at altitude in the upper Drôme valley.

appellations.name: Alsace
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Muscat, Pinot Blanc, Auxerrois, Sylvaner, Chasselas, Pinot Noir, Klevener de Heiligenstein
appellations.summary:
AOC Alsace, also called Vin d'Alsace, covers the whole Alsace vineyard (about 15,500 ha planted, about 20,000 ha delimited across 117 communes in INAO's file) and most of its production. Its wines are usually labelled by grape: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Muscat, Pinot Blanc, Sylvaner and Pinot Noir. Pinot Blanc on a label may contain Auxerrois, and Edelzwicker or Gentil denote blends.

Since 2011 the label may add one of 13 dénominations géographiques complémentaires: Bergheim, Blienschwiller, Coteaux du Haut-Koenigsbourg, Côte de Rouffach, Côtes de Barr, Klevener de Heiligenstein, Ottrott, Rodern, Saint-Hippolyte, Scherwiller, Val Saint-Grégoire, Vallée Noble and Wolxheim, each with its own grape rules, or the name of a lieu-dit, with a lower maximum yield (68 hl/ha for whites). These are the closest Alsace comes to village and premier cru wines. Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles may be made from the four noble grapes. Since the 2021 vintage, still Alsace wines must show a sweetness indication (sec, demi-sec, moelleux or doux) on the label.
appellations.terroir: The full mosaic of Alsace soils, from the Rhine plain's alluvium and loess to the granite, limestone, marl and sandstone foothills of the Vosges.
appellations.nerd_note: The 1972 law that requires all Alsace AOC wine to be bottled in the region and in the tall flûte d'Alsace bottle makes Alsace one of the few French appellations with a compulsory bottle shape.

appellations.name: Crémant d'Alsace
appellations.grapes: Pinot Blanc, Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir, Riesling, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: Crémant d'Alsace, recognised by decree on 24 August 1976, is traditional-method sparkling wine made with a second fermentation in bottle, at least 9 months on the lees and no release until 12 months after bottling. Mostly based on Pinot Blanc and Auxerrois, with Chardonnay, Riesling and Pinot Gris, it is fresh, creamy and apple-scented; rosé is made only from Pinot Noir. Grapes for crémant are earmarked in the vineyard before harvest and picked earlier. It has been Alsace's growth category in the 2020s while still-wine sales declined, and producers such as Pierre Sparr, Wolfberger, Dopff au Moulin (which pioneered it in the early twentieth century), Lucien Albrecht and Cave de Turckheim make large volumes.
appellations.terroir: Grown across the whole Alsace AOC area; cooler sites and earlier picking give the necessary acidity.
appellations.nerd_note: Julien Dopff learned the Champagne method in Épernay and began making sparkling wine in Riquewihr in 1900, 76 years before the crémant appellation existed.

appellations.name: Alsace Bergheim
appellations.summary: Wines from the town of Bergheim, home to the Altenberg de Bergheim and Kanzlerberg grands crus; limestone and marl give rich, structured whites. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

appellations.name: Alsace Blienschwiller
appellations.summary: A Bas-Rhin village south of Dambach-la-Ville on granite and sandstone, home to the Winzenberg grand cru; Sylvaner and Riesling are local specialities. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

appellations.name: Alsace Coteaux du Haut Koenigsbourg
appellations.summary: Granite and gneiss slopes below the castle of Haut-Koenigsbourg around Orschwiller, Kintzheim and Saint-Hippolyte; crisp Riesling and Pinot Gris. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

appellations.name: Alsace Côte de Rouffach
appellations.summary: The limestone and sandstone hills of Rouffach, Pfaffenheim and Westhalten in the Haut-Rhin, including some of the warmest, driest sites in Alsace; known for Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

appellations.name: Alsace Côtes de Barr
appellations.summary: The slopes around Barr, Mittelbergheim, Gertwiller and Heiligenstein in the Bas-Rhin, on limestone and marl; known for Sylvaner. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

appellations.name: Alsace Klevener de Heiligenstein
appellations.summary: A unique name for wine from Savagnin Rose (Klevener), a non-aromatic relative of Gewurztraminer, planted at Heiligenstein in the eighteenth century by mayor Ehret Wantz; also grown in four neighbouring communes. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

appellations.name: Alsace Ottrott
appellations.summary: A red-wine enclave below Mont Sainte-Odile, where Pinot Noir (the Rouge d'Ottrott) has been made for centuries; the name is reserved for Pinot Noir. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

appellations.name: Alsace Rodern
appellations.summary: A village between Ribeauvillé and Saint-Hippolyte on granite and sandstone, with a long tradition of Pinot Noir; the name is used for red wine. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

appellations.name: Alsace Saint-Hippolyte
appellations.summary: The village below the Haut-Koenigsbourg, known for Pinot Noir on granite and sandstone; the name is used for red wine. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

appellations.name: Alsace Scherwiller
appellations.summary: A Bas-Rhin village on granite and alluvial soils at the mouth of the Val de Villé, known for Riesling. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

appellations.name: Alsace Val Saint Grégoire
appellations.summary: The Munster valley villages around Turckheim, Ingersheim and Wintzenheim, on granite and sandstone; the name applies to Pinot Blanc, Auxerrois and Pinot Gris. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

appellations.name: Alsace Vallée Noble
appellations.summary: A side valley above Soultzmatt in the Haut-Rhin with limestone and sandstone, known for Riesling, Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris; the Zinnkoepflé grand cru lies here. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

appellations.name: Alsace Wolxheim
appellations.summary: A village west of Strasbourg on limestone and marl, famed for Riesling; Napoleon is said to have favoured its wine. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Altenberg de Bergbieten
match: Alsace grand cru Altenberg de Bergbieten
Alsace Grand Cru Altenberg de Bergbieten
appellations.summary: Altenberg de Bergbieten, in the northern Bas-Rhin, gives broad, spicy Riesling and Gewurztraminer from a sunny southeast slope of marl, limestone and gypsum. One of the northernmost grands crus, it ripens surprisingly well thanks to shelter from the Vosges.
appellations.terroir: Marl and limestone with gypsum on a southeast-facing slope west of Strasbourg. Communes: Bergbieten (Bas-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Altenberg (old hill) is the commonest grand cru name in Alsace: there are three, at Bergbieten, Bergheim and Wolxheim.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Altenberg de Bergheim
match: Alsace grand cru Altenberg de Bergheim
Alsace Grand Cru Altenberg de Bergheim
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Muscat (blends permitted)
appellations.summary: Altenberg de Bergheim is one of Alsace's historic vineyards and one of the two grands crus that may make blends of several grapes, a privilege won by Marcel Deiss, who planted it as a field blend. Its limestone gives powerful, mineral wines; Deiss's Altenberg is sometimes partly botrytised.
appellations.terroir: Jurassic limestone and marl on a south-facing slope above the walled town of Bergheim. Communes: Bergheim (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Varietal labelling is not allowed for blends here; the wine must be a complantation of noble grapes.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Altenberg de Wolxheim
match: Alsace grand cru Altenberg de Wolxheim
Alsace Grand Cru Altenberg de Wolxheim
appellations.summary: Altenberg de Wolxheim is a limestone hill on the edge of the Bruche valley west of Strasbourg, long the city's favourite source of Riesling and reputedly a favourite of Napoleon. Its limestone and marl give firm, mineral, slow-ageing Riesling and structured Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris, with the cooler, more northern profile of the Bas-Rhin.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl on a southeast-facing hill west of Strasbourg. Communes: Wolxheim (Bas-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Wolxheim is also one of Alsace's 13 dénominations géographiques complémentaires.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Brand
appellations.summary: Brand, meaning fire or burn, is one of the great Riesling sites of Alsace: a steep granite slope that heats up fast in the sun. Legend says the sun burned a dragon living in a cave on the hill. Its Rieslings are taut, smoky and floral, and its Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer are rich but precise.
appellations.terroir: Two-mica granite on a steep slope facing south and southeast above Turckheim, at the mouth of the Munster valley. Communes: Turckheim (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Brand was enlarged from a few hectares to about 57 ha when the grand cru was delimited, a sore point for purists.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Bruderthal
appellations.summary: Bruderthal, the brothers' valley, was named after the monks who farmed it. It gives fleshy, aromatic Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris and firm Riesling in the northern Bas-Rhin.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl with sandstone on a southeast slope above Molsheim. Communes: Molsheim (Bas-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Molsheim was a Jesuit university town, and its monks were important early vineyard owners.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Eichberg
appellations.summary: Eichberg (oak hill), above the round medieval village of Eguisheim, is one of the driest and warmest sites in Alsace. It gives rich, spicy Gewurztraminer and ripe Pinot Gris and Riesling.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl with sandstone scree on a southeast slope. Communes: Eguisheim (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Eguisheim claims to be the birthplace of Alsace viticulture, and its concentric medieval streets surround the castle of Pope Leo IX, born here in 1002.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Engelberg
appellations.summary: Engelberg, the angels' hill, straddles Dahlenheim and Scharrachbergheim at the northern end of the Route des Vins, among the northernmost grands crus. Its pale limestone and marl give taut, mineral Riesling and fresh, spicy Gewurztraminer with a cool-climate line, and it ripens later than the sites of the Haut-Rhin.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl at the northern end of the Route des Vins. Communes: Dahlenheim, Scharrachbergheim (Bas-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Engelberg lies on the line where the Vosges foothills meet the Kochersberg plateau.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Florimont
appellations.summary: Florimont, the hill of flowers, rises just west of Colmar between Ingersheim and Katzenthal, on limestone and marl with a sunny southern exposure. It gives aromatic, spicy Gewurztraminer and supple, ripe Riesling and Pinot Gris, and its proximity to Colmar, the driest town in France's north, makes it one of the warmest grands crus.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl on a south-facing hill west of Colmar. Communes: Ingersheim, Katzenthal (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Its Latinised name is unusual among Alsace's mostly German-language grand cru names.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Frankstein
appellations.summary: Frankstein is made up of four separate granite hillsides around Dambach-la-Ville, the largest wine commune of the Bas-Rhin. It gives delicate, floral, mineral Riesling and Gewurztraminer.
appellations.terroir: Two-mica granite in four separate parcels on the slopes above Dambach-la-Ville. Communes: Dambach-la-Ville (Bas-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: The granite here is the same that crops out at the nearby chapel of Saint-Sébastien.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Froehn
appellations.summary: Froehn is a compact grand cru of about 14 ha wrapped around the hilltop village of Zellenberg, between Riquewihr and Ribeauvillé. Its marl and clay, with some schist, give rich, ripe Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat, and it is one of the few grands crus where Muscat is a speciality.
appellations.terroir: Marl and clay with schist on a south-facing hill. Communes: Zellenberg (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Zellenberg sits on a hilltop between Riquewihr and Ribeauvillé with views over the plain.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Furstentum
appellations.summary: Furstentum, the principality, is a warm, sheltered amphitheatre between Kientzheim and Sigolsheim that ripens Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris to great richness, and gives powerful Riesling.
appellations.terroir: Limestone with marl and sandstone on a steep south-facing slope. Communes: Kientzheim, Sigolsheim (Kaysersberg Vignoble).
appellations.nerd_note: Its name recalls ownership by the prince-abbots of Kientzheim.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Geisberg
appellations.summary: Geisberg, the goat hill, is one of the smallest grands crus, about 8 ha of steep terraces above Ribeauvillé, documented since 1308. It is one of Alsace's great Riesling sites: firm, mineral and long-lived.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl with sandstone on steep terraces. Communes: Ribeauvillé (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Trimbach's famous Riesling Cuvée Frédéric Émile comes from parcels in Geisberg and Osterberg but does not carry a grand cru name.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Gloeckelberg
appellations.summary: Gloeckelberg, the bell hill, sits between Rodern and Saint-Hippolyte below the Haut-Koenigsbourg, on granite with sand and clay. Its wines are delicate and floral rather than powerful: fragrant Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris and fine Riesling, in two villages better known for their Pinot Noir.
appellations.terroir: Granite with sand and clay on a southeast slope. Communes: Rodern, Saint-Hippolyte (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Rodern and Saint-Hippolyte are also traditional Pinot Noir villages with their own dénominations.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Goldert
appellations.summary: Goldert, golden garden, owes its name to the golden colour of its wines. It is famous for Muscat and Gewurztraminer of great richness, as well as fine Riesling.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl with sandstone on an east and southeast slope. Communes: Gueberschwihr (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Ernest Burn's Clos Saint-Imer, a walled vineyard within Goldert, was documented in the eighth century.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Hatschbourg
appellations.summary: Hatschbourg spreads over a warm, sunny slope above Hattstatt and Voegtlinshoffen south of Colmar, on limestone and marl covered with loess. It gives powerful, honeyed Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris, often with some residual sugar, and broad, ripe Riesling; the Cattin family is its best-known producer.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl with loess on a southeast slope. Communes: Hattstatt, Voegtlinshoffen (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: The Cattin family, based at Voegtlinshoffen, is one of the largest owners.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Hengst
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Muscat; Pinot Noir for red (since 2022)
appellations.summary: Hengst, the stallion, is one of the most powerful grands crus: its calcareous marl gives dense, spicy Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris and firm, long-lived Riesling. Since 2022 it is one of three grands crus where Pinot Noir is permitted, recognising a long local tradition.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl with sandstone on a steep southeast-facing hill. Communes: Wintzenheim (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Albert Mann and Josmeyer made celebrated Pinot Noirs from Hengst for years before they could carry the grand cru name.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Kaefferkopf
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Muscat (blends permitted)
appellations.summary: Kaefferkopf, the beetle's head, was the 51st grand cru, added in 2007 after decades of argument over its delimitation and rules. It is one of the two grands crus allowed to make blends, and its varied soils give rich, complex wines. The Kaefferkopf name was already used on labels in the 1930s, after a 1932 court ruling.
appellations.terroir: Granite, sandstone and limestone in a single 74 ha grand cru. Communes: Ammerschwihr (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Kaefferkopf's grand cru rules allow Gewurztraminer-led blends with Riesling and Pinot Gris, a nod to its history of field blends.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Kanzlerberg
appellations.summary: Kanzlerberg, the chancellor's hill, is the smallest grand cru of Alsace, a little over 3 ha next to Altenberg de Bergheim. Its gypsum-rich marl gives dense, powerful Riesling and Gewurztraminer.
appellations.terroir: Gypsum-rich marl and limestone; the smallest grand cru at about 3 ha. Communes: Bergheim (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: With barely 3.3 ha delimited, a whole vintage of Kanzlerberg rarely exceeds about 20,000 bottles across all its owners.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Kastelberg
appellations.summary: Kastelberg, castle hill, is a steep slope of black Steiger schist above Andlau, and it is one of the great Riesling sites of the Bas-Rhin: austere, smoky and slow-ageing. Roman remains have been found here.
appellations.terroir: Steiger schist (dark, slaty) on a steep hill above Andlau. Communes: Andlau (Bas-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Kastelberg's schist is unique among the grands crus and gives Rieslings often compared with the Mosel.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Kessler
appellations.summary: Kessler, the cauldron, is a bowl-shaped valley on the slopes above Guebwiller, where red sandstone gives silky, spicy Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris. Domaine Schlumberger, the largest grand cru owner in Alsace, farms much of it on terraces worked by horse.
appellations.terroir: Pink Vosges sandstone with clay on terraced slopes in a sheltered valley. Communes: Guebwiller (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Guebwiller has four grands crus (Kessler, Kitterlé, Saering and Spiegel), more than any other commune.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Kirchberg de Barr
match: Alsace grand cru Kirchberg de Barr
Alsace Grand Cru Kirchberg de Barr
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Muscat; Pinot Noir for red (since 2022)
appellations.summary: Kirchberg de Barr, the church hill, rises above the town of Barr and gives structured Riesling and rich Gewurztraminer. Since 2022 it is one of three grands crus allowed to make Pinot Noir.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl on a hill above the town of Barr. Communes: Barr (Bas-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Barr hosts Alsace's oldest wine fair, held in July since the nineteenth century.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Kirchberg de Ribeauvillé
match: Alsace grand cru Kirchberg de Ribeauvillé
Alsace Grand Cru Kirchberg de Ribeauvillé
appellations.summary: Kirchberg de Ribeauvillé, the church hill, lies on a steep, sunny slope west of Ribeauvillé below the town's three ruined castles. Its limestone, marl and sandstone scree give fine, mineral, citrus-scented Riesling and some of Alsace's best dry Muscat, with Louis Sipp, Jean Sipp and André Kientzler as leading growers.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl with sandstone scree on a south-facing slope. Communes: Ribeauvillé (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Ribeauvillé has three grands crus: Geisberg, Kirchberg and Osterberg.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Kitterlé
appellations.summary: Kitterlé is one of the steepest grands crus, on volcanic sandstone above Guebwiller, and gives powerful, spicy Riesling and Gewurztraminer. Domaine Schlumberger farms most of it.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic sandstone with spilite on a very steep terraced slope. Communes: Guebwiller (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Its slopes are so steep that the terraces must be maintained by hand and horse.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Mambourg
appellations.summary: Mambourg is a long, warm, south-facing hill above Sigolsheim with a near-Mediterranean flora, giving rich Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris and powerful Riesling. Sigolsheim was destroyed in the fighting of 1944 to 1945; a national military cemetery crowns the hill.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl on a long south-facing hill. Communes: Sigolsheim (Kaysersberg Vignoble).
appellations.nerd_note: Vines on Mambourg were recorded as early as 783.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Mandelberg
appellations.summary: Mandelberg, almond hill, is named for the almond trees that grow in its mild microclimate between Mittelwihr and Beblenheim. It gives rich, aromatic Gewurztraminer and Riesling.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl on a south-facing slope. Communes: Mittelwihr, Beblenheim (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Mittelwihr's mild climate is shown by the almond trees, which flower in March.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Marckrain
appellations.summary: Marckrain, the boundary slope, faces east above Bennwihr and Sigolsheim, on marl and limestone that hold water and give rich, spicy Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris, often with late-harvest sweetness. Much of it is made by the Bestheim co-operative, founded in Bennwihr after the village was destroyed in 1944.
appellations.terroir: Marl and limestone on an east-facing slope. Communes: Bennwihr, Sigolsheim (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Bennwihr was almost entirely destroyed in December 1944 and rebuilt around its co-operative.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Moenchberg
appellations.summary: Moenchberg, the monks' hill, lies between Andlau and Eichhoffen on a south-facing slope of marl, limestone and colluvium. It was church land for centuries, and today it gives aromatic, elegant Riesling and ripe Pinot Gris, softer and earlier-drinking than neighbouring Kastelberg.
appellations.terroir: Marl and limestone with colluvium on a south-facing slope. Communes: Andlau, Eichhoffen (Bas-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Not to be confused with Muenchberg at Nothalten, whose name also means monks' hill.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Muenchberg
appellations.summary: Muenchberg, another monks' hill, was planted by the Cistercians of Baumgarten abbey in the twelfth century. Its horseshoe-shaped bowl of volcanic sandstone gives intense, mineral Riesling, made famous by André Ostertag.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic sandstone and pebbles in a natural amphitheatre. Communes: Nothalten (Bas-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: André Ostertag's Muenchberg Riesling is one of the reference grand cru Rieslings of the Bas-Rhin.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Ollwiller
appellations.summary: Ollwiller lies below the Hartmannswillerkopf (Vieil Armand), a First World War battlefield, near the southern end of the Alsace vineyard. It gives fresh Riesling and Gewurztraminer.
appellations.terroir: Sandstone and clay at the southern end of the vineyard below the Vieil Armand. Communes: Wuenheim (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: The Hartmannswillerkopf above the vineyard was one of the deadliest battlefields of the Vosges in 1915.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Osterberg
appellations.summary: Osterberg, the eastern hill, lies next to Geisberg on the slopes north of Ribeauvillé, on marl and limestone that give more weight than its neighbour. It gives fine, powerful Riesling and rich Gewurztraminer, and Trimbach's Cuvée Frédéric Émile Riesling draws partly on its parcels.
appellations.terroir: Marl and limestone on a southeast slope. Communes: Ribeauvillé (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Osterberg's marl gives more weight than neighbouring Geisberg's limestone.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Pfersigberg
appellations.summary: Pfersigberg, the peach hill, is a large grand cru of about 71 ha above Eguisheim and Wettolsheim, on warm limestone and marl facing southeast. It gives aromatic Gewurztraminer and broad, peachy Riesling and Pinot Gris, with Kuentz-Bas, Paul Ginglinger, Bruno Sorg and Léon Beyer among its leading growers.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl on a long southeast slope. Communes: Eguisheim, Wettolsheim (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Peach trees once grew among the vines, giving the hill its name.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Pfingstberg
appellations.summary: Pfingstberg, Pentecost hill, rises above Orschwihr in the southern Haut-Rhin on a steep southeast slope of sandstone, limestone and marl. It gives fine, racy Riesling and aromatic Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer, and the biodynamic Zusslin family and Lucien Albrecht are its best-known producers.
appellations.terroir: Sandstone and limestone on a steep southeast slope. Communes: Orschwihr (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Zusslin, a biodynamic estate, also owns the Clos Liebenberg monopole nearby.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Praelatenberg
appellations.summary: Praelatenberg, the prelates' hill, was owned by the monks of Ebersmunster abbey. Its granite and gneiss slopes below the Haut-Koenigsbourg castle give fresh, mineral Riesling and fine Pinot Gris.
appellations.terroir: Granite and gneiss below the castle of Haut-Koenigsbourg. Communes: Kintzheim (Bas-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Praelatenberg is the only grand cru of the Bas-Rhin on the Haut-Koenigsbourg massif.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Rangen
appellations.summary: Rangen is the southernmost grand cru and one of the most extraordinary vineyards in France: a very steep, south-facing wall of volcanic rock above the Thur river at Thann. Its wines, smoky, powerful and deeply mineral, were famous in the sixteenth century. Zind-Humbrecht's Clos Saint-Urbain, around the chapel of Saint-Urbain, and Schoffit's Clos Saint-Théobald are its references.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic rock (andesite, tuffs and greywacke) on an extremely steep south-facing slope. Communes: Thann, Vieux-Thann (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Thanks to its volcanic soil and steepness, the Rangen ripens late despite its south-facing slope; local lore says its wine 'makes your head spin'.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Rosacker
appellations.summary: Rosacker, the field of roses, above Hunawihr and its fortified church, gives taut, mineral, long-lived Riesling. Trimbach's Clos Sainte Hune, a 1.67 ha parcel owned for more than 200 years, lies entirely within it but is sold without the grand cru name.
appellations.terroir: Dolomitic limestone and marl on an east-facing slope. Communes: Hunawihr (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Clos Sainte Hune, often called Alsace's greatest Riesling, has never carried the Rosacker name on its label.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Saering
appellations.summary: Saering is the most northerly of Guebwiller's four grands crus, on terraced slopes of limestone, marl and sandstone facing east and southeast. It gives fine, citrusy, early-approachable Riesling and aromatic Gewurztraminer and Muscat; Domaine Schlumberger and Dirler-Cadé are the main owners.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl with sandstone on terraced slopes. Communes: Guebwiller (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Saering, Kessler, Kitterlé and Spiegel make Guebwiller the commune with the most grands crus.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Schlossberg
appellations.summary: Schlossberg, castle hill, was the first Alsace grand cru, created by decree in 1975. Its steep granite terraces below the ruined castle of Kaysersberg give some of the most elegant, floral and mineral Rieslings of Alsace. It covers about 80 ha.
appellations.terroir: Granite with sand on steep terraces. Communes: Kientzheim, Kaysersberg (Kaysersberg Vignoble).
appellations.nerd_note: Schlossberg's terraces were rebuilt after the war; its first grand cru vintage was 1975.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Schoenenbourg
appellations.summary: Schoenenbourg, the beautiful castle, rises behind the medieval walls of Riquewihr and was famous across Europe in the sixteenth century. Its gypsum-rich marl gives rich, long-lived Riesling, and its Vendanges Tardives and Sélections de Grains Nobles are among Alsace's greatest. Hugel, Dopff au Moulin, Marcel Deiss and Bott-Geyl own parcels.
appellations.terroir: Keuper marl with gypsum, sandstone and dolomite on a north and northeast-facing amphitheatre above Riquewihr. Communes: Riquewihr, Zellenberg (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Hugel long refused to use grand cru names on its labels; it now marks wines from its best sites, including Schoenenbourg, as Grossi Laüe, Alsatian for great growths.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Sommerberg
appellations.summary: Sommerberg, summer hill, is a steep granite slope above Niedermorschwihr that gives some of the most precise, mineral Rieslings in Alsace, notably from Albert Boxler.
appellations.terroir: Granite on extremely steep terraces. Communes: Niedermorschwihr, Katzenthal (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Boxler bottles separate Sommerberg cuvées from different parts of the hill.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Sonnenglanz
appellations.summary: Sonnenglanz, sunshine glow, is a warm, sheltered slope above Beblenheim known for rich Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris and for botrytised sweet wines. It was among the first sites in Alsace to be marketed by name.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl on a gentle southeast slope. Communes: Beblenheim (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Beblenheim is home to the Bott-Geyl family, one of the biodynamic leaders of the central Haut-Rhin.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Spiegel
appellations.summary: Spiegel, the mirror, lies between Bergholtz and Guebwiller on sandstone and marl facing east and southeast. It gives fine, spicy Riesling and supple Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris, and it shares the village of Bergholtz with Domaine Eugène Meyer, the first wine estate in France to farm biodynamically (1969).
appellations.terroir: Sandstone and marl on a southeast slope. Communes: Bergholtz, Guebwiller (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Bergholtz is home to Domaine Eugène Meyer, France's first biodynamic wine estate (1969).

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Sporen
appellations.summary: Sporen, next to Schoenenbourg, is traditionally planted with Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris and was once used for a famous field blend (Gentil). Its clay gives rich, powerful wines.
appellations.terroir: Clay and marl with stones on a gentle slope east of Riquewihr. Communes: Riquewihr (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Hugel's Gewurztraminer Grossi Laüe comes largely from Sporen.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Steinert
appellations.summary: Steinert, the stony one, is a hot, steep limestone slope above Pfaffenheim and Westhalten, so stony that the soil warms quickly in spring. It gives powerful, smoky Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer and fine, mineral Riesling, and the biodynamic pioneer Pierre Frick makes some of its most distinctive wines.
appellations.terroir: Limestone on a steep, stony slope. Communes: Pfaffenheim, Westhalten (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Pierre Frick, a biodynamic pioneer since 1981, is known for sulphur-free wines from Steinert.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Steingrubler
appellations.summary: Steingrubler, the stone quarry, lies above Wettolsheim on a mixed soil of limestone, sandstone and granite, a reflection of the faulting that shattered the Vosges foothills here. It gives spicy Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris and fine Riesling; Albert Mann and Barmès-Buecher are its best-known growers.
appellations.terroir: Limestone, sandstone and granite in a mixed soil. Communes: Wettolsheim (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Its name refers to old stone quarries on the hill.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Steinklotz
appellations.summary: Steinklotz, block of stone, is the northernmost grand cru, above Marlenheim, where the Merovingian kings had a royal estate. Its limestone gives powerful Pinot Gris and Riesling; Pinot Noir from here is renowned locally.
appellations.terroir: Limestone with marl at the northern gateway of the Route des Vins. Communes: Marlenheim (Bas-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Marlenheim's Merovingian royal villa is mentioned by Gregory of Tours in the sixth century.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Vorbourg
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Muscat; Pinot Noir for red (since 2022)
appellations.summary: Vorbourg is a large, warm grand cru between Rouffach and Westhalten. Its limestone gives rich Pinot Gris, Gewurztraminer and Riesling, and since 2022 it may also make Pinot Noir. René Muré's Clos Saint Landelin, a walled monopole within it, is its best-known wine.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and sandstone on a sunny, south-facing hill. Communes: Rouffach, Westhalten (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Clos Saint Landelin belonged to the bishops of Strasbourg before the Revolution.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Wiebelsberg
appellations.summary: Wiebelsberg rises above Andlau on light, quartz-rich sandstone facing southeast, in contrast to neighbouring Kastelberg's black schist. It gives delicate, floral and saline Riesling that is approachable younger than Kastelberg's, from growers such as Marc Kreydenweiss and Guy Wach.
appellations.terroir: Quartz-rich sandstone on a southeast slope above Andlau. Communes: Andlau (Bas-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Andlau has three grands crus: Kastelberg, Moenchberg and Wiebelsberg.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Wineck-Schlossberg
appellations.summary: Wineck-Schlossberg lies below the ruined tower of the Wineck castle at Katzenthal and Ammerschwihr, on a steep granite slope in a side valley west of Colmar. Its granite gives precise, floral, finely mineral Riesling and delicate Gewurztraminer, with Meyer-Fonné and Klur among its growers.
appellations.terroir: Granite below the ruined castle of Wineck. Communes: Katzenthal, Ammerschwihr (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: The Wineck castle tower stands among the vines above Katzenthal.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Winzenberg
appellations.summary: Winzenberg, the winegrowers' hill, rises above Blienschwiller in the Bas-Rhin on two-mica granite facing south. Its light, quick-draining soils give fresh, floral Riesling and Gewurztraminer with a fine mineral edge, and the village is also one of Alsace's 13 dénominations géographiques complémentaires.
appellations.terroir: Granite on a south-facing slope. Communes: Blienschwiller (Bas-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Blienschwiller is one of Alsace's 13 dénominations géographiques complémentaires.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Zinnkoepflé
appellations.summary: Zinnkoepflé is one of the highest and driest grands crus, a steep south-facing hill above the Vallée Noble where wild orchids and Mediterranean plants grow. It gives powerful, spicy Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris and taut Riesling.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and sandstone on a high, hot, south-facing slope up to about 420 m. Communes: Soultzmatt, Westhalten (Haut-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Its microclimate is so dry that a protected steppe-like flora, unusual in northern France, grows on the hillside.

appellations.name: Alsace grand cru Zotzenberg
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Muscat, Sylvaner
appellations.summary: Zotzenberg, above Mittelbergheim, is the only grand cru allowed to make Sylvaner (since 2006), a tribute to a local grape long prized here. Its limestone also gives fine Riesling and Gewurztraminer.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl on a southeast slope above Mittelbergheim. Communes: Mittelbergheim (Bas-Rhin).
appellations.nerd_note: Albert Seltz led the campaign that won Sylvaner grand cru status in Zotzenberg.

appellations.name: Arbois
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Savagnin, Poulsard, Trousseau, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Arbois was among the very first AOCs decreed in France, on 15 May 1936, and it is the Jura's most important appellation by name, covering about 800 ha in production around the town of Arbois and 12 surrounding communes. It makes every Jura style: Trousseau and Poulsard reds (it is the heartland of Trousseau), Chardonnay and Savagnin whites, ouillé and sous voile, vin jaune and vin de paille. The village of Pupillin, the 'world capital of Ploussard', may add its name (Arbois-Pupillin).

Arbois is also the town where Louis Pasteur grew up and did much of his research on wine fermentation; his family house is a museum. Producers range from the Fruitière Vinicole d'Arbois, founded in 1906 as one of France's first wine co-operatives, to Stéphane Tissot, Jacques Puffeney (retired 2014), Domaine de la Tournelle, Domaine Rolet and Lucien Aviet.
appellations.terroir: Triassic red and grey marls and Liassic marls, with limestone scree; vines at 250 to 450 m around the Cuisance valley.
appellations.nerd_note: Arbois's AOC decree is dated 15 May 1936, in the first batch of French appellations; Arbois-Pupillin is the only village name allowed on an Arbois label.

appellations.name: Château-Chalon
appellations.summary: Château-Chalon is the grand cru of vin jaune: an appellation of about 50 ha in production (94 ha delimited) on steep marl slopes below a village perched on a rocky spur, where only vin jaune may be made. The Benedictine abbey of Château-Chalon, whose abbesses were drawn from the nobility, developed the wine from the Middle Ages. In poor years growers release no Château-Chalon at all, as happened in 1974, 1980 and 1984. The wines, from Savagnin aged at least six years and three months under the voile, are more intense and long-lived than other vins jaunes: walnut, curry, saffron and salt, lasting a century.
appellations.terroir: Grey and black Liassic marls on steep, south and southwest-facing slopes below the village, at 250 to 400 m; the cliffs above shelter the vines.
appellations.nerd_note: The village of Château-Chalon is one of the Plus Beaux Villages de France and its Belvédère Sainte-Anne overlooks the whole appellation.

appellations.name: Côtes du Jura
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Savagnin, Poulsard, Trousseau, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Côtes du Jura is the regional appellation, covering the whole Jura vineyard (about 640 ha in production) from Salins-les-Bains in the north to Saint-Amour in the south. It makes every Jura style. The south of the region, the Sud Revermont around Rotalier and Lons-le-Saunier, has become famous through Jean-François Ganevat, the Labet family and Domaine Pignier, who make single-site Chardonnay of Burgundian finesse.
appellations.terroir: Grey, blue and red marls with limestone; the Revermont in the south has warmer slopes and more limestone.
appellations.nerd_note: Château d'Arlay claims to be the oldest wine estate in France still in operation by the same lineage of owners, documented since the eleventh century.

appellations.name: L'Etoile
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Savagnin, Poulsard (for vin de paille)
appellations.summary: L'Étoile is a small white-wine appellation around the village of L'Étoile near Lons-le-Saunier. Its name, the star, may refer to the five hills around the village or to the star-shaped fossils of crinoids (pentacrines) in its limestone. It makes Chardonnay and Savagnin, vin jaune and vin de paille, and its crisp, mineral whites are some of the finest in the Jura.
appellations.terroir: Marl and limestone with star-shaped crinoid fossils; five small hills around the village.
appellations.nerd_note: L'Étoile and Château-Chalon (vin jaune only) are the two Jura appellations with no red wine.

appellations.name: Crémant du Jura
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Poulsard, Trousseau, Savagnin
appellations.summary: Crémant du Jura, created in the mid-1990s, is the traditional-method sparkling wine of the Jura, mostly from Chardonnay, and now accounts for about a quarter of the region's production. It is crisp and fine, and the Jura has made sparkling wine since the nineteenth century.
appellations.terroir: Grown across the Jura AOC area.

appellations.name: Macvin du Jura
appellations.grapes: Grape must from Jura varieties fortified with Marc du Jura
appellations.summary: Macvin du Jura, an AOC since 1991, is a vin de liqueur: unfermented grape must blended with Marc du Jura aged at least 14 months, then aged in oak for a year. It may be white, red or rosé and is served chilled as an aperitif or with dessert. The Jura claims it dates from the fourteenth century, when it was made by the abbesses of Château-Chalon.
appellations.terroir: Grown across the Jura AOC area.
appellations.nerd_note: The name may derive from vin maqué (crushed) or from 'mac', the local word for marc.

appellations.name: Marc du Jura
appellations.summary: Marc du Jura is the Jura's grape-pomace brandy, aged at least two years in oak, which became an AOC in 2015. It is also the spirit used to fortify Macvin. It is listed here for completeness; it is a spirit appellation rather than a wine.

appellations.name: Vin de Savoie
appellations.grapes: Jacquère, Altesse, Roussanne (Bergeron), Chasselas, Gringet, Chardonnay; Mondeuse, Gamay, Pinot Noir, Persan
appellations.summary: Vin de Savoie (or Savoie) covers the whole Savoie vineyard across 56 communes and makes mostly crisp, light whites from Jacquère, plus reds from Mondeuse, Gamay and Pinot Noir. Recognised in 1957 and confirmed as an AOC in 1973, it may add one of 16 cru names: Abymes, Apremont, Arbin, Ayze, Chautagne, Chignin, Chignin-Bergeron, Cruet, Crépy, Jongieux, Marignan, Marin, Montmélian, Ripaille, Saint-Jean-de-la-Porte and Saint-Jeoire-Prieuré.
