Since 2015 its traditional-method sparkling wines may be labelled Crémant de Savoie, with at least 40 percent Jacquère and Altesse.
appellations.terroir: Glacial moraines, limestone scree and molasse on south and southeast-facing Alpine slopes at 250 to 500 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Mondeuse from Arbin was so valued in the nineteenth century that it was shipped to Paris and Lyon as a rival to Burgundy.

appellations.name: Vin de Savoie Abymes
match: Vin de Savoie Abymes ou Les Abymes
appellations.summary: Les Abymes (the abysses) is the chaotic field of limestone boulders left by the collapse of Mont Granier in November 1248, now planted with Jacquère that gives light, flinty whites. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

appellations.name: Vin de Savoie Apremont
appellations.summary: Apremont lies on the same Mont Granier landslide as Les Abymes, at Apremont and neighbouring communes; its Jacquère whites are crisp, floral and mineral, the best-known wine of Savoie. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

appellations.name: Vin de Savoie Arbin
appellations.summary: Arbin, on the steep slopes of the Combe de Savoie near Montmélian, is the home of Mondeuse, whose red here is dark, peppery and able to age. Louis Magnin made it famous. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

appellations.name: Vin de Savoie Ayze
appellations.summary: Ayze in the Arve valley of Haute-Savoie makes still and sparkling wine from Gringet, a grape found only here; Domaine Belluard rescued it. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

appellations.name: Vin de Savoie Chautagne
appellations.summary: Chautagne, on the slopes north of the Lac du Bourget, is known for light reds from Gamay, Pinot Noir and Mondeuse. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

appellations.name: Vin de Savoie Chignin
appellations.summary: Chignin, below the ruined towers of Chignin southeast of Chambéry, makes Jacquère whites and Mondeuse reds on limestone scree. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

appellations.name: Vin de Savoie Chignin-Bergeron
appellations.summary: Chignin-Bergeron is Savoie's richest white, made from Roussanne (locally Bergeron) on the warm, stony slopes of Chignin, Francin and Montmélian; apricot and honey with Alpine freshness. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

appellations.name: Vin de Savoie Cruet
appellations.summary: Cruet, in the Combe de Savoie, makes fresh Jacquère and Mondeuse from south-facing scree slopes. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

appellations.name: Vin de Savoie Crépy
appellations.summary: Crépy, near Lake Geneva at Ballaison, makes Chasselas whites, light and often slightly sparkling; it was a separate AOC (1948) before becoming a Vin de Savoie cru. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

appellations.name: Vin de Savoie Jongieux
appellations.summary: Jongieux, on the steep slopes above the Rhône west of the Lac du Bourget, makes whites and reds; the Marestel Roussette cru is in the same village. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

appellations.name: Vin de Savoie Marignan
appellations.summary: Marignan, on the shores of Lake Geneva at Sciez, makes light Chasselas whites. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

appellations.name: Vin de Savoie Marin
appellations.summary: Marin, near Thonon-les-Bains on Lake Geneva, makes Chasselas whites from glacial soils. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

appellations.name: Vin de Savoie Montmélian
appellations.summary: Montmélian, below the site of a great Savoyard fortress demolished by Louis XIV, makes Jacquère and Mondeuse. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

appellations.name: Vin de Savoie Ripaille
appellations.summary: Ripaille is the vineyard of the Château de Ripaille near Thonon-les-Bains on Lake Geneva, a single-estate cru of Chasselas. Its château belonged to Amadeus VIII of Savoy, who became antipope Felix V. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

appellations.name: Vin de Savoie Saint-Jean-de-la-Porte
appellations.summary: Saint-Jean-de-la-Porte, in the Combe de Savoie, is a cru for Mondeuse reds. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

appellations.name: Vin de Savoie Saint-Jeoire-Prieuré
appellations.summary: Saint-Jeoire-Prieuré, on the slopes southeast of Chambéry toward the Combe de Savoie, makes crisp Jacquère whites on limestone scree around an old Benedictine priory. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

appellations.name: Roussette de Savoie
appellations.summary: Roussette de Savoie is the appellation for Altesse, Savoie's finest white grape, legendarily brought back from Cyprus by a princess of Savoy. The wines are aromatic, with bergamot, quince and honey, and age well. Roussette de Savoie is now made entirely from Altesse. Four crus may add their name: Frangy, Marestel, Monterminod and Monthoux.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl slopes; the crus lie on steep sites near the Rhône and above Chambéry.
appellations.nerd_note: Marestel, a very steep slope at Jongieux, is often called the grand cru of Altesse.

appellations.name: Roussette de Savoie Frangy
appellations.summary: Frangy in Haute-Savoie, on the Usses river near the Rhône north of Seyssel, is the northernmost Roussette cru. Its molasse and glacial slopes give fresh, floral Altesse with notes of bergamot and almond, lighter than Marestel's. It is one of four crus of Roussette de Savoie.

appellations.name: Roussette de Savoie Marestel
appellations.summary: Marestel, a very steep slope at Jongieux above the Rhône, is the most famous Roussette cru, giving rich, long-lived Altesse; Domaine Dupasquier is the reference. It is one of four crus of Roussette de Savoie.

appellations.name: Roussette de Savoie Monterminod
appellations.summary: Monterminod, on a steep limestone slope above Chambéry at Saint-Alban-Leysse, is the southernmost and smallest Roussette cru, about 16 ha delimited. Its Altesse is rich and honeyed, and suburban housing presses on its edges. It is one of four crus of Roussette de Savoie.

appellations.name: Roussette de Savoie Monthoux
appellations.summary: Monthoux is a small Roussette cru of about 23 ha on a sheltered limestone slope near the Lac du Bourget. Its Altesse is fine and aromatic, with quince and white flowers, and benefits from the lake's moderating influence. It is one of four crus of Roussette de Savoie.

appellations.name: Seyssel
appellations.summary: Seyssel, on both banks of the Rhône at Seyssel (Ain and Haute-Savoie), was one of the first appellations of the Alps, recognised in 1942. It makes still Altesse whites and a traditional-method sparkling wine based on the local Molette grape with Altesse, a speciality made famous by the house of Varichon et Clerc.
appellations.terroir: Molasse, sand and glacial deposits on slopes above the Rhône gorge.
appellations.nerd_note: Seyssel's sparkling wine was a nineteenth-century speciality of the Savoie and still uses the rare Molette grape.

appellations.name: Bugey
appellations.grapes: Gamay, Poulsard, Pinot Noir, Mondeuse; Chardonnay, Jacquère, Altesse
appellations.summary: Bugey became an AOC in 2009 after decades as a VDQS. It makes still whites (at least half Chardonnay), reds and rosés, traditional-method sparkling, and three named crus. Bugey Cerdon is a pink, off-dry ancestral-method sparkler from Gamay and Poulsard, with strawberry and raspberry fruit and only about 8 percent alcohol: the fermentation starts in tank and finishes in bottle, without added sugar. Bugey Manicle (Chardonnay white or Pinot Noir red) and Bugey Montagnieu (Mondeuse red or Altesse-based sparkling) are smaller crus.
appellations.terroir: Limestone scree and marl in valleys of the southern Jura massif; Cerdon in the Ain valley in the north, Montagnieu and Manicle along the Rhône in the south.
appellations.nerd_note: Raphaël Bartucci's Cerdon was one of the first natural wines from Bugey to reach Paris wine bars in the early 2000s.

appellations.name: Roussette du Bugey
appellations.summary: Roussette du Bugey is the Bugey appellation for Altesse whites, with two crus that may add their name, Montagnieu and Virieu-le-Grand. The wines are floral and honeyed, similar to Roussette de Savoie.
appellations.terroir: Limestone scree on slopes along the Rhône.

appellations.name: Bugey Manicle
appellations.summary: A steep, south-facing limestone lieu-dit at Cheignieu-la-Balme and Pugieu near Belley, about 24 ha delimited, reserved for Chardonnay whites and Pinot Noir reds. It is the most Burgundian of Bugey's crus, giving taut, mineral whites and light, fragrant reds.

appellations.name: Bugey Montagnieu
appellations.summary: Steep limestone slopes above the Rhône at Montagnieu, Briord and Seillonnaz, about 124 ha delimited. The cru is known for dark, peppery Mondeuse reds and for traditional-method sparkling wine based on Altesse, Chardonnay and Mondeuse; Altesse whites are sold as Roussette du Bugey Montagnieu.

appellations.name: Roussette du Bugey Virieu-le-Grand
appellations.summary: A small cru of Roussette du Bugey of about 35 ha around the village of Virieu-le-Grand in the Furans valley, for pure Altesse whites that are floral, honeyed and fresh from limestone scree.

appellations.name: Bugey Cerdon
appellations.summary: Bugey Cerdon is a pink, off-dry, low-alcohol sparkling wine made by the ancestral method from Gamay and Poulsard in the Cerdon valley and nine other communes. Fermentation stops partway in tank (by chilling and filtering) and finishes in bottle, so the bubbles and sweetness come only from the grapes. It is fresh, fruity and about 8 percent alcohol.
appellations.terroir: Limestone scree and marl in the Ain valley.

appellations.name: Côtes de Toul
appellations.summary: Côtes de Toul, promoted from VDQS (1951) to AOC on 31 March 1998, covers about 110 ha in eight communes west of Toul: Blénod-lès-Toul, Bruley, Bulligny, Charmes-la-Côte, Domgermain, Lucey, Mont-le-Vignoble and Pagney-derrière-Barine. Its speciality is vin gris, a pale, fresh rosé made by pressing red grapes immediately, mostly from Gamay with at least 10 percent Pinot Noir. Pinot Noir makes the red wine and Auxerrois the white.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and Jurassic marl on an east-facing escarpment above the Moselle valley, at 200 to 380 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Vin gris must blend at least two grape varieties, with no single variety above 85 percent.

appellations.name: Moselle
appellations.grapes: Auxerrois, Müller-Thurgau, Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc, Riesling, Gewurztraminer; Pinot Noir, Gamay
appellations.summary: The French Moselle AOC, a VDQS from 1995 to 2010, covers scattered vineyards in three zones of the Moselle department: south of Metz along the Moselle (Ancy-Dornot, Scy-Chazelles), around Sierck-les-Bains and Contz-les-Bains near the Luxembourg border, and the Seille valley around Vic-sur-Seille. Production is tiny, about 1,500 hl a year, mostly crisp whites from Auxerrois and Müller-Thurgau, with some Pinot Noir. It is the upstream French end of the same river that becomes the Mosel in Germany and the Moselle in Luxembourg.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl in the Metz area, Keuper marl and limestone near Sierck, marl around Vic-sur-Seille.
appellations.nerd_note: Château de Vaux, a restored estate on the slopes west of Metz run by the Molozay family, led the revival of Moselle wine in the 1990s.

sites.name: Les Clos
sites.class: Grand Cru climat (Chablis Grand Cru AOC 1938)
sites.text: The largest (about 26 ha in production, 29 ha delimited) and most celebrated of the seven Chablis grand crus, on a steep southwest slope in the middle of the hill. Les Clos gives the most powerful and slow-developing Chablis, with a smoky, almost iodine intensity that can need a decade. Its name recalls a vineyard walled by monks.

sites.name: Blanchot
sites.class: Grand Cru climat (Chablis Grand Cru AOC 1938)
sites.text: At the eastern end of the grand cru hill, Blanchot faces southeast rather than southwest, so it gets morning rather than afternoon sun. Its whiter, marlier soil gives the most floral and delicate wine of the seven.

sites.name: Valmur
sites.class: Grand Cru climat (Chablis Grand Cru AOC 1938)
sites.text: Valmur lies in a fold between Les Clos and Vaudésir, with two exposures on either side of a small valley. Its wines combine the depth of Les Clos with a lifted, aromatic finesse.

sites.name: Vaudésir
sites.class: Grand Cru climat (Chablis Grand Cru AOC 1938)
sites.text: Vaudésir sits in a sheltered side valley with steep slopes facing both southeast and southwest. Its wines are spicy and intense, and most of La Moutonne, Domaine Long-Depaquit's monopole, lies here.

sites.name: Grenouilles
sites.class: Grand Cru climat (Chablis Grand Cru AOC 1938)
sites.text: The smallest grand cru (about 9 ha), at the bottom of the slope near the Serein. Named after the frogs of the riverbank, it gives aromatic, supple wines. About 7 ha belong to the La Chablisienne co-operative, which sells them as Château Grenouilles.

sites.name: Preuses
sites.class: Grand Cru climat (Chablis Grand Cru AOC 1938)
sites.text: Preuses sits high on the western side of the hill with a gentler slope and southeast exposure. It produces round, generous and early-approachable grand cru, and its upper edge touches La Moutonne.

sites.name: Bougros
sites.class: Grand Cru climat (Chablis Grand Cru AOC 1938)
sites.text: The westernmost grand cru, on lower slopes facing west-southwest. Bougros is often the most rustic and earthy of the seven, but William Fèvre's steep Côte Bouguerots parcel is one of the region's most mineral wines.

sites.name: La Moutonne
sites.class: Monopole within Chablis Grand Cru (Vaudésir and Preuses)
sites.text: A 2.35 ha amphitheatre of vines mostly within Vaudésir, with a strip in Preuses, owned by Domaine Long-Depaquit (Albert Bichot). It once belonged to the monks of Pontigny and is sometimes called the unofficial eighth grand cru. Its steep, enclosed bowl gives a dense, honeyed Chablis.

sites.name: Montée de Tonnerre
sites.text: The most admired premier cru of Chablis, on the right bank just east of the grand cru hill and on the same Kimmeridgian slope, facing southwest. It groups Montée de Tonnerre, Chapelot and Pied d'Aloup. The wines approach grand cru in depth while keeping a sharp, saline line; Raveneau's is legendary.

sites.name: Mont de Milieu
sites.text: A long southeast-facing slope east of Montée de Tonnerre, on the old border between Burgundy and Champagne, which may explain the name 'middle hill'. Its warm exposure gives ripe, broad Chablis with a firm chalky core.

sites.name: Fourchaume
sites.text: The largest right-bank premier cru (about 100 ha delimited), stretching north from the grand crus toward La Chapelle-Vaupelteigne and Maligny. Including Vaulorent, which touches Preuses, it gives generous, round wines.

sites.name: Vaillons
sites.text: The best-known left-bank premier cru, a southeast-facing slope above the village of Chablis. Vaillons groups several climats (Châtains, Séchet, Beugnons, Les Lys, Mélinots) and gives fine, elegant, mineral wines that are often the first premier cru drinkers meet.

sites.name: Montmains
sites.text: A left-bank premier cru on thin, stony Kimmeridgian soil facing southeast. It includes Butteaux and Forêts (Forest), whose wines from Raveneau and Dauvissat are among the most mineral and long-lived in Chablis.

sites.name: Les Forêts
sites.text: A climat within Montmains, spelled Forest on Vincent Dauvissat's labels. Higher and cooler than most of the left bank, it gives taut, stony and deeply flavoured wines that need years in bottle.

sites.name: Côte de Léchet
sites.text: A steep slope above the village of Milly on the left bank, facing southeast, with very thin soils over Kimmeridgian rock. Its wines are lean, salty and tightly wound.

sites.name: Vosgros
sites.text: A small left-bank premier cru in a side valley south of Chablis near Chichée, on a steep southwest slope. It gives taut, rather austere wine with a long saline finish.

sites.name: Chambertin
sites.text: The heart of Gevrey's grand cru slope, about 12.9 ha facing east above the Route des Grands Crus, between Clos de Bèze to the north and Latricières to the south. Its brown limestone soil gives deep, firm, long-lived Pinot Noir.

sites.name: Chambertin-Clos de Bèze
sites.text: The walled vineyard first given to the monks of Bèze in 630, about 15.4 ha immediately north of Chambertin. It gives perfumed, silky and very long red wine.

sites.name: Chapelle-Chambertin
sites.text: About 5.5 ha below Clos de Bèze, named after a twelfth-century chapel of the monks of Bèze. Thin soils give a lighter, perfumed grand cru.

sites.name: Charmes-Chambertin
sites.text: About 12.2 ha below Chambertin and Latricières; with Mazoyères, about 31 ha may use the Charmes name. Soft, round and approachable grand cru.

sites.name: Mazoyères-Chambertin
sites.text: The southern grand cru of Gevrey, about 18.6 ha next to the Morey border. Its wine is usually sold as Charmes-Chambertin.

sites.name: Griotte-Chambertin
sites.text: The smallest Gevrey grand cru, about 2.7 ha in a warm stony hollow below Chambertin. Fragrant, cherry-scented wine.

sites.name: Latricières-Chambertin
sites.text: About 7.4 ha south of Chambertin, cooled by the Combe Grisard; a fresh, mineral grand cru.

sites.name: Mazis-Chambertin
sites.text: About 9.1 ha at the northern end of the grand cru belt below Ruchottes; dense, dark and gamey wine.

sites.name: Ruchottes-Chambertin
sites.text: About 3.3 ha above Mazis-Chambertin, the highest and stoniest Gevrey grand cru; lean and mineral.

sites.name: Clos de la Roche
sites.text: The largest grand cru of Morey-Saint-Denis, about 16.9 ha of stony limestone; deep, firm and savoury wine.

sites.name: Clos Saint-Denis
sites.text: About 6.6 ha between Clos de la Roche and Clos des Lambrays; fragrant, elegant wine.

sites.name: Clos des Lambrays
sites.text: About 8.8 ha, a near-monopole of Domaine des Lambrays promoted to grand cru in 1981; silky and aromatic.

sites.name: Clos de Tart
sites.text: A walled monopole of 7.5 ha owned by Artémis since 2017, with rows running across the slope; deep, spicy grand cru.

sites.name: Bonnes-Mares
sites.text: About 15 ha astride the Chambolle and Morey border, with red and white soils; the most powerful wine of Chambolle.

sites.name: Musigny
sites.text: About 10.9 ha above Clos de Vougeot at the southern end of Chambolle; silky, perfumed red and the rare Musigny blanc.

sites.name: Clos de Vougeot
sites.text: The 50 ha walled vineyard created by the monks of Cîteaux, now split among about 80 owners, with the château of the Chevaliers du Tastevin at its centre.

sites.name: Echezeaux
sites.text: About 37.7 ha in Flagey-Échezeaux, made of 11 lieux-dits; spicy, fragrant grand cru of variable style.

sites.name: Grands-Echezeaux
sites.text: About 9.1 ha beside the upper wall of Clos de Vougeot; dense and consistent grand cru.

sites.name: Richebourg
sites.text: About 8 ha north of Romanée-Conti and above Romanée-Saint-Vivant; the most opulent Vosne grand cru.

sites.name: Romanée-Conti
sites.text: The 1.81 ha monopole of Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, marked by a stone cross at the top of the vineyard; the world's most famous red wine vineyard.

sites.name: La Romanée
sites.text: France's smallest appellation, 0.85 ha directly upslope of Romanée-Conti, owned by the Liger-Belair family since 1815.

sites.name: La Tâche
sites.text: The 6 ha monopole of Domaine de la Romanée-Conti south of La Grande Rue; dark, spicy, exuberant grand cru.

sites.name: Romanée-Saint-Vivant
sites.text: About 9.4 ha below Romanée-Conti, once owned by the priory of Saint-Vivant de Vergy; silky and fragrant.

sites.name: La Grande Rue
sites.text: A 1.65 ha monopole of Domaine Lamarche between Romanée-Conti and La Tâche, promoted to grand cru in 1992.

sites.name: Clos Saint-Jacques
sites.text: A 6.7 ha southwest-facing slope on the Côte Saint-Jacques, considered a grand cru in all but name and priced like one. Only five owners share it: Armand Rousseau (2.2 ha), Esmonin, Fourrier, Bruno Clair and Louis Jadot. It ripens later than the grand crus but gives wines of exceptional purity and length.

sites.name: Lavaut Saint-Jacques
sites.text: Next to Clos Saint-Jacques at the mouth of the Combe de Lavaux, on stony scree. Cooler air from the combe gives a tense, aromatic wine with firm structure.

sites.name: Les Cazetiers
sites.text: North of Clos Saint-Jacques on the same southeast-facing Côte Saint-Jacques. Rich, spicy wine often compared to Chambertin; Faiveley and Bruno Clair have large holdings.

sites.name: Combe au Moine
sites.text: High on the Côte Saint-Jacques at the edge of the woods, a cool, stony site whose late-ripening wines gain value in warm years.

sites.name: Aux Combottes
sites.text: A premier cru surrounded by grand crus (Latricières, Mazoyères and Clos de la Roche) at the Morey border. Cold air pooling in a slight depression is the usual explanation for its lower rank.

sites.name: Estournelles-Saint-Jacques
sites.text: A small, steep climat above Lavaut Saint-Jacques on thin stony soil; precise, high-toned wines from Denis Mortet and Frédéric Esmonin.

sites.name: Petite Chapelle
sites.text: Just south of Chapelle-Chambertin, below the grand crus, giving supple, perfumed Gevrey close to grand cru style.

sites.name: Clos de la Bussière
sites.text: A walled 2.6 ha monopole of Domaine Georges Roumier, below Bonnes-Mares at the Chambolle end of Morey. Roumier's version is firm and savoury.

sites.name: Les Ruchots
sites.text: Below Clos des Lambrays and next to Clos de Tart, stony soil gives an aromatic, finely structured Morey.

sites.name: Les Monts Luisants
sites.text: Above Clos de la Roche, high and stony. Ponsot's white Clos des Monts Luisants, planted with Aligoté in 1911, is one of Burgundy's curiosities; reds come from the lower part.

sites.name: Clos Sorbè
sites.text: A small premier cru just below Clos des Lambrays; rich, dark Morey with a spicy edge.

sites.name: Les Amoureuses
sites.text: The lovers, 5.3 ha below Musigny and across the road from Clos de Vougeot, on thin soil over hard limestone. Often priced above grand crus, its wine is pure perfume and silk. Roumier, Mugnier, de Vogüé, Robert Groffier and Joseph Drouhin make it.

sites.name: Les Charmes
sites.text: One of Chambolle's largest premier crus (9.4 ha), below the village, giving rounder, fleshier Chambolle.

sites.name: Les Cras
sites.text: High above the village on thin, stony soil with little clay; tense and mineral wines, famous from Ghislaine Barthod and Georges Roumier.

sites.name: Les Sentiers
sites.text: Next to Bonnes-Mares at the northern end of the village; firmer, darker Chambolle with grand cru character.

sites.name: Les Fuées
sites.text: Just below Bonnes-Mares; aromatic yet firm wine, with Mugnier's version among the best.

sites.name: La Combe d'Orveau
sites.text: At the southern edge of Chambolle beside Musigny, partly classified as grand cru. Anne Gros and Perrot-Minot make prized versions.

sites.name: Le Clos Blanc
sites.text: The white-wine clos planted by the monks of Cîteaux in 1110, a 2.3 ha monopole of Domaine de la Vougeraie, making one of the few great whites of the Côte de Nuits.

sites.name: Les Petits Vougeots
sites.text: Just north of the Clos and below Musigny; light, fragrant reds from a few growers.

sites.name: Cros Parantoux
sites.text: A cold, rocky 1 ha site above Richebourg that Henri Jayer replanted after the Second World War, blasting rock with dynamite. His wines from it became legends; today Méo-Camuzet and Emmanuel Rouget share it.

sites.name: Aux Malconsorts
sites.text: Adjoining La Tâche at the southern end of Vosne, this 5.9 ha climat is regarded as the closest premier cru to grand cru quality. Cathiard, Dujac and de Montille make celebrated versions.

sites.name: Les Suchots
sites.text: About 13 ha between Romanée-Saint-Vivant and Échezeaux; rich, spicy wine from a long list of good growers.

sites.name: Les Beaux Monts
sites.text: High above Échezeaux toward the woods, about 12 ha; cooler and more aromatic, increasingly valued in warm years.

sites.name: Aux Brûlées
sites.text: Next to Richebourg; dense, spicy and generous wines, Méo-Camuzet's being the most famous.

sites.name: Aux Reignots
sites.text: A steep strip directly above Romanée-Conti and La Romanée. Comte Liger-Belair and Sylvain Cathiard make fine, mineral wines from it.

sites.name: Les Chaumes
sites.text: Below La Tâche and Malconsorts on the lower slope; fleshy, round wines for earlier drinking.

sites.name: Clos des Réas
sites.text: A walled 2.1 ha monopole of Domaine Michel Gros below the village, in the family since 1860.

sites.name: Les Saints-Georges
sites.text: The town's flagship vineyard, about 7.5 ha on the southern slope, whose name Nuits added in 1892. Growers have applied for grand cru status. Its wines are deep, firm and long-lived.

sites.name: Les Vaucrains
sites.text: Above Les Saints-Georges on stony soil; powerful, tannic wine that needs years in bottle.

sites.name: Les Cailles
sites.text: About 3.8 ha on the southern slope of Nuits below Les Porrets, on stony limestone; it gives fine-grained, elegant Nuits-Saint-Georges, notably from Robert Chevillon.

sites.name: Les Pruliers
sites.text: Just south of the town on stony limestone; firm, spicy wines with fine structure.

sites.name: Aux Boudots
sites.text: Next to Vosne's Malconsorts at the northern end of Nuits; the most Vosne-like premier cru, silky and perfumed.

sites.name: Aux Murgers
sites.text: North of the town, its name refers to the piles of stones (murgers) cleared from the vines. Méo-Camuzet's version is a classic.

sites.name: Clos de la Maréchale
sites.text: A 9.6 ha monopole in Premeaux, run by Domaine J.F. Mugnier from 2004 after a long lease to Faiveley ended. Mugnier also makes a white from it.

sites.name: Clos des Forêts Saint-Georges
sites.text: A 7.2 ha monopole of Domaine de l'Arlot in Premeaux; firm, dark Nuits from a cool, stony slope.

sites.name: Clos de l'Arlot
sites.text: The walled park and terraced vineyard around Domaine de l'Arlot's house in Premeaux, about 4 ha; red and a rare, fine white.

sites.name: Clos Napoléon
sites.text: A 1.8 ha monopole of Domaine Pierre Gelin next to the Parc Noisot, named after the Napoleon statue that Claude Noisot commissioned nearby.

sites.name: Clos de la Perrière
sites.text: A 5.9 ha walled monopole of the Joliet family on the site of an old quarry, once ranked alongside Chambertin.

sites.name: Corton
sites.text: The red grand cru hill of the Côte de Beaune, about 160 ha delimited across three communes, with 28 named climats from Bressandes to Le Clos du Roi.

sites.name: Corton-Charlemagne
sites.text: About 72 ha on the upper, southwest and west-facing slopes of the hill of Corton; a powerful, mineral white grand cru.

sites.name: Charlemagne
sites.text: The lieu-dit En Charlemagne in Pernand-Vergelesses, heart of the Charlemagne grand cru, whose wines are sold as Corton-Charlemagne.

sites.name: Montrachet
sites.text: About 8 ha split between Puligny and Chassagne, on a gently sloping, sun-catching strip of thin limestone soil; the world's most famous white wine vineyard.

sites.name: Chevalier-Montrachet
sites.text: About 7.6 ha directly above Le Montrachet on steep, stony limestone; lean, mineral and long-lived.

sites.name: Bâtard-Montrachet
sites.text: About 11.9 ha below Le Montrachet, astride Puligny and Chassagne; the richest and most opulent of the Montrachet family.

sites.name: Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet
sites.text: About 3.7 ha in the Puligny corner of Bâtard-Montrachet; elegant and approachable.

sites.name: Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet
sites.text: About 1.6 ha in Chassagne south of Bâtard; the smallest Montrachet grand cru.

sites.name: Corton Les Bressandes
sites.text: About 17 ha on the southeast-facing middle slope above Aloxe, with red, iron-rich soil; generous, fine-grained and perhaps the most consistent red Corton.

sites.name: Corton Le Clos du Roi
sites.text: About 11 ha high on the southeast slope; once property of the dukes of Burgundy and then the French crown. Firm, deep, long-lived red, often considered the finest Corton.

sites.name: Corton Les Renardes
sites.text: About 14 ha on the eastern flank toward Ladoix; gamey, wild-scented and powerful red Corton.

sites.name: Corton Le Corton
sites.text: About 12 ha at the crown of the hill below the woods, the site that gave the whole hill its name; Bouchard and Bonneau du Martray make it.

sites.name: Corton Les Pougets
sites.text: About 10 ha on the southwest-facing slope between the reds and the whites; Louis Jadot's red and white Pougets are classics.

sites.name: Corton Le Rognet et Corton
sites.text: About 12 ha in Ladoix on the eastern flank; contains Faiveley's Clos des Cortons Faiveley monopole, a walled 3 ha parcel.

sites.name: Clos des Mouches
sites.text: About 25 ha at the southern end of Beaune toward Pommard. Joseph Drouhin built its fame from the 1920s with both a red and one of the best white wines in Beaune. The name refers to bees (mouches à miel).

sites.name: Les Grèves
sites.text: About 31 ha of gravelly soil in the middle of the Beaune slope; Bouchard's Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus lies within it. Deep, perfumed reds.

sites.name: Les Bressandes
sites.text: About 17 ha north of the town on stony limestone, giving fine, aromatic Beaune with good structure.

sites.name: Clos des Ursules
sites.text: Louis Jadot's walled monopole of about 2 ha inside Les Vignes Franches, bought in 1826 by the founder of the house; Jadot's flagship Beaune.

sites.name: Les Teurons
sites.text: About 21 ha in the heart of the Beaune slope; rich and rounded reds, with Domaine Rossignol-Trapet and Bouchard as key owners.

sites.name: Les Marconnets
sites.text: At the northern edge of Beaune next to Savigny; firm, dark Beaune that ages well.

sites.name: Les Rugiens Bas
sites.text: The lower half of Les Rugiens next to Volnay, about 5.8 ha of red iron-rich soil; Pommard's most celebrated wine, deep and structured. The 2025 Pièce des Présidents was a Rugiens.

sites.name: Les Grands Épenots
sites.text: About 10 ha toward Beaune, on deeper soil; elegant, aromatic Pommard. Domaine de Courcel's Grand Clos des Épenots is the reference.

sites.name: Clos des Épeneaux
sites.text: A 5.2 ha walled monopole of Domaine du Comte Armand, within Les Grands and Petits Épenots; powerful, long-lived Pommard.

sites.name: Les Pézerolles
sites.text: About 6 ha on the upper slope toward Beaune; finer, more perfumed Pommard.

sites.name: Clos des Ducs
sites.text: A 2.4 ha walled monopole of Domaine Marquis d'Angerville, beside the family house above the village; it once belonged to the dukes of Burgundy. Pure, perfumed and long-lived Volnay.

sites.name: Les Caillerets
sites.text: About 12 ha at the southern end of Volnay next to Meursault's Santenots; stony, fine and deep. Pousse d'Or's Clos des 60 Ouvrées lies within it.

sites.name: Taillepieds
sites.text: About 7 ha on a steep slope below the village; the name means foot-cutter, after the steepness. Fine, mineral Volnay.

sites.name: Clos des Chênes
sites.text: About 15 ha high on the slope toward Monthélie; firm, spicy and long-lived. Michel Lafarge's version is a classic.

sites.name: Champans
sites.text: About 11 ha in the middle of the slope; balanced, aromatic wines with good depth.

sites.name: Santenots
sites.text: About 29 ha of Meursault land sold as Volnay when red. Lafon's Santenots-du-Milieu and the Hospices de Beaune's Volnay-Santenots are among the best.

sites.name: Les Perrières
sites.text: About 13 ha high in the south of Meursault on stony soil over limestone quarries (perrières). The most mineral and finest of Meursault's premier crus, regarded as grand cru quality.

sites.name: Les Genevrières
sites.text: About 16.5 ha north of Perrières; floral, elegant Meursault named after the juniper bushes that once grew there.

sites.name: Les Charmes
sites.text: The largest Meursault premier cru, about 31 ha on the lower slope toward Puligny; round, generous and approachable.

sites.name: Les Gouttes d'Or
sites.text: About 5.3 ha north of the village, 'drops of gold'; rich, nutty Meursault.

sites.name: Les Pucelles
sites.text: About 6.8 ha immediately north of Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet; floral, refined wine, Domaine Leflaive's top premier cru.

sites.name: Le Cailleret
sites.text: About 3.3 ha directly north of Le Montrachet; the most grand cru-like of Puligny's premier crus. De Montille's Clos du Cailleret and Domaine des Lambrays share it.

sites.name: Les Combettes
sites.text: About 6.8 ha against Meursault's Charmes; rich yet mineral, a meeting point of the two villages' styles.

sites.name: Les Folatières
sites.text: The largest Puligny premier cru, about 17.7 ha on the upper slope; floral, mineral wine, with Henri Boillot and Leflaive among many owners.

sites.name: Clavaillon
sites.text: About 5.6 ha below Les Pucelles; Domaine Leflaive owns most of it and makes a supple, early-drinking premier cru.

sites.name: Champ Canet
sites.text: About 4.7 ha high toward Blagny on stony soil; aromatic and mineral wines from Sauzet and Carillon.

sites.name: Les Caillerets
sites.text: About 5.6 ha above the village on stony limestone; Chassagne's finest white premier cru, mineral and long.

sites.name: Morgeot
sites.text: A large grouping (about 56 ha) south of the village toward Santenay, named after the abbey cellar of the Cistercians of Maizières. Red and white; rich, broad wines.

sites.name: La Romanée
sites.text: About 3.4 ha high on the slope next to Les Grandes Ruchottes; precise, mineral whites from Moreau and Morey.

sites.name: Les Grandes Ruchottes
sites.text: About 2.1 ha high on the slope with very thin, stony soil; Ramonet's Ruchottes is a cult wine.

sites.name: En Remilly
sites.text: About 29.5 ha on a steep slope touching the Montrachet hill and Chassagne; the best-known Saint-Aubin premier cru, taut and stony.

sites.name: Les Murgers des Dents de Chien
sites.text: About 16 ha above Chevalier-Montrachet; the 'dog's teeth' are the sharp stones that cover it. Pure, mineral Chardonnay.

sites.name: Les Lavières
sites.text: About 18 ha on the north side of the Rhoin valley next to Pernand; stony, fine and aromatic Savigny.

sites.name: Île des Vergelesses
sites.text: About 9.4 ha on a gentle slope facing Savigny, the best red climat of Pernand: fine, spicy and fragrant.

sites.name: Les Gravières
sites.text: About 29 ha of gravelly soil next to Chassagne; Santenay's most refined red and some white.

sites.name: Hospices de Beaune (Hôtel-Dieu)
sites.class: Historic hospital, wine estate and auction (founded 1443)
sites.text: The medieval hospital founded in 1443 by Nicolas Rolin and Guigone de Salins, famous for its glazed polychrome roof. Its roughly 60 ha domaine of donated vineyards is sold each November at the world's best-known charity wine auction, run by Sotheby's since 2021. The 165th sale on 16 November 2025 raised about 18.8 million euros.

sites.name: Cité des Climats et vins de Bourgogne (Beaune)
sites.text: The Beaune site of the Cité des Climats et vins de Bourgogne, a network of three wine centres (with Chablis and Mâcon) opened in 2023. Its spiral building evokes a vine tendril and explains the UNESCO-listed climats.

sites.name: Château de Beaune (Bouchard Père et Fils)
sites.text: The fifteenth-century bastion of Beaune's ramparts, bought by Bouchard Père et Fils in 1820, where the house ages its wines in vaulted cellars. Bouchard is one of the Côte d'Or's largest vineyard owners, with about 130 ha including 12 ha of grand crus.

sites.name: Château de Meursault
sites.text: A château with cellars dating from the eleventh to fourteenth centuries and one of the largest estates of the Côte de Beaune, owned since 2012 by the Halley family.

sites.name: Château de Pommard
sites.text: An eighteenth-century château with a walled vineyard, the 20 ha Clos Marey-Monge, one of the largest monopoles in Burgundy; owned since 2014 by Michael Baum.

sites.name: Château Corton C (Corton-André)
sites.text: The château at the foot of the Corton hill with its turrets roofed in glazed Burgundian tiles, one of the most photographed buildings of the Côte de Beaune.

sites.name: Château de Santenay
sites.text: The former residence of Philip the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, with a glazed-tile roof and a large vineyard estate across the Côte de Beaune and the Côte Chalonnaise.

sites.name: Domaine Leflaive
sites.text: The reference domaine of Puligny-Montrachet, on the Place des Marronniers. Founded by Joseph Leflaive in the early twentieth century, it converted to biodynamics under Anne-Claude Leflaive in the 1990s and owns parcels of Montrachet, Chevalier, Bâtard and Bienvenues.

sites.name: Domaine Coche-Dury
sites.text: Jean-François Coche-Dury's tiny domaine in Meursault, now run by his son Raphaël, makes some of the most sought-after white Burgundies, especially Corton-Charlemagne and Meursault Perrières, with a style of tension and reductive struck-match.

sites.name: Domaine des Comtes Lafon
sites.text: Based at the Clos de la Barre in Meursault, the Lafon domaine was turned into a superstar by Dominique Lafon from 1984, with biodynamic farming and famous Meursault premier crus and Montrachet. Count Jules Lafon revived the Paulée de Meursault in 1923.

sites.name: Domaine Roulot
sites.text: Jean-Marc Roulot, also an actor, has made this family domaine one of the most admired in Meursault, with pure, mineral wines from village lieux-dits such as Les Luchets and Les Tessons and the premier cru Clos des Bouchères.

sites.name: Domaine Ramonet
sites.text: The great name of Chassagne-Montrachet, run by Noël and Jean-Claude Ramonet, with Montrachet, Bâtard and the premier cru Ruchottes, as well as fine Chassagne reds.

sites.name: Domaine Marquis d'Angerville
sites.text: The Volnay domaine of the d'Angerville family, beside its monopole Clos des Ducs. Marquis Jacques d'Angerville was an early champion of estate bottling and fought fraud in the 1930s; Guillaume d'Angerville, in charge since 2003, converted it to biodynamic farming.

sites.name: Domaine d'Auvenay
sites.text: Lalou Bize-Leroy's private estate at a farmhouse in the hills above Saint-Romain, producing tiny quantities of Chevalier-Montrachet, Mazis-Chambertin, Bonnes-Mares and Puligny that are among the world's most expensive wines.

sites.name: Sur la Roche
sites.text: About 15 ha on the steep scree slopes under the Roche de Vergisson, among the highest vineyards of Pouilly-Fuissé. Cool and stony, it gives taut, mineral Chardonnay.

sites.name: Les Crays
sites.text: About 10.8 ha at Vergisson on limestone and marl, the Château de Fuissé's Les Combettes neighbour; fine, chalky wines.

sites.name: Le Clos de Solutré
sites.text: A walled 4.4 ha clos below the Roche de Solutré; rich and mineral.

sites.name: Les Ménétrières
sites.text: About 5.2 ha at Fuissé on stony limestone; known for J.A. Ferret's 'Tête de Cru' Ménétrières.

sites.name: Le Clos
sites.text: The 2.7 ha walled clos of the Château de Fuissé, a monopole of the Vincent family whose wines put Pouilly-Fuissé on the map.

sites.name: Les Brûlés
sites.text: A tiny 0.8 ha climat at Fuissé, burnt by the sun on a south-facing slope; Château de Fuissé makes a single-vineyard bottling.

sites.name: Aux Quarts
sites.text: About 11 ha at Chaintré on clay and limestone; broad, powerful whites, the southern heart of the appellation.

sites.name: Le Clos Reyssier
sites.text: About 8.7 ha at Chaintré, a warm, clay-rich site giving rich, ripe wines.

sites.name: Vers Cras
sites.text: About 23 ha around Pouilly and Fuissé; one of the larger premier crus, with stony red clay over limestone.

sites.name: Les Quarts
sites.text: About 12.5 ha on the same slope as Pouilly-Fuissé's Aux Quarts, promoted to premier cru from the 2024 vintage.

sites.name: Les Mûres
sites.text: The only Pouilly-Loché premier cru, about 7 ha, recognised from the 2024 vintage.

sites.name: Clos des Myglands
sites.text: A 6.3 ha monopole of Faiveley on the slope north of Mercurey; structured, dark Pinot Noir.

sites.name: Clos du Roy
sites.text: About 10.8 ha high on the slope; one of Mercurey's most structured red premier crus.

sites.name: Clos Salomon
sites.text: A 7 ha monopole of Domaine du Clos Salomon, named after a fourteenth-century owner; fine, perfumed red.

sites.name: Clos du Cellier aux Moines
sites.text: A 13 ha walled vineyard planted by the Cistercian monks of La Ferté in the twelfth century; the stone cellar survives.

sites.name: Grésigny
sites.text: About 6.4 ha on stony limestone in the south of Rully; fine, mineral Chardonnay.

sites.name: Roche de Solutré
sites.text: A limestone cliff rising 493 m over the Pouilly-Fuissé vineyards and gave its name to the Solutrean culture of the Upper Palaeolithic. Its scree feeds the vineyards below, and President Mitterrand made an annual pilgrimage to its summit.

sites.name: Roche de Vergisson
sites.text: Solutré's twin cliff, 485 m, above the village of Vergisson, whose steep scree slopes hold the premier cru Sur la Roche.

sites.name: Château de Fuissé
sites.text: The fifteenth and seventeenth-century château of the Vincent family, whose single-vineyard bottlings (Le Clos, Les Brûlés, Les Combettes) helped establish Pouilly-Fuissé's reputation for climat wines.

sites.name: Domaine Guffens-Heynen
sites.text: A tiny domaine in Vergisson founded by Belgian couple Jean-Marie Guffens and Maine Heynen in 1976, whose intense Pouilly-Fuissé and Mâcon-Pierreclos inspired a generation of Mâconnais growers. Guffens also runs the Verget négociant.

sites.name: Abbaye de Cluny
sites.text: Founded in 910, Cluny became the centre of an order of more than a thousand monasteries and owned vineyards across Burgundy. Its great church, the largest in Christendom until Saint Peter's in Rome, was mostly demolished after the Revolution.

sites.name: Domaine A. et P. de Villaine
sites.text: Founded in 1973 by Aubert and Pamela de Villaine in Bouzeron; now run by Pierre de Benoist. Its Aligoté campaign won Bouzeron its village appellation in 1997.
producers: Domaine A. et P. de Villaine

sites.name: Château de Chamirey
sites.text: An eighteenth-century château and one of Mercurey's largest estates, owned by the Devillard family, who also own the Domaine des Perdrix in Nuits-Saint-Georges.

sites.name: Abbaye de Pontigny
sites.text: The second daughter house of Cîteaux, whose monks developed the Chablis vineyard in the twelfth century. Its abbey church, one of the largest Cistercian churches still standing, overlooks the Serein valley north of Chablis.

sites.name: Domaine François Raveneau
sites.text: On the Rue de Chichée in Chablis, the Raveneau family makes the most sought-after Chablis, notably Les Clos, Valmur, Blanchot and the premier crus Montée de Tonnerre, Butteaux and Chapelot. Old oak barrels and a refusal to chase ripeness make the wines famously long-lived.

sites.name: Domaine Vincent Dauvissat
sites.text: Vincent Dauvissat, now his son Ghislain, makes Chablis grand and premier crus (Les Clos, Preuses, La Forest, Séchet) that rival Raveneau's in reputation, with organic and biodynamic farming and old oak.

sites.name: Château du Clos de Vougeot
sites.text: In the middle of the Clos de Vougeot, the Cistercians built a cellar and press house in the twelfth century, still holding four huge medieval presses, and a Renaissance château in 1551. Since 1945 it has belonged to the Confrérie des Chevaliers du Tastevin, whose banquets and tastevinage are famous.

sites.name: Abbaye de Cîteaux
sites.text: The mother house of the Cistercian order, founded in 1098 in the marshes east of Nuits-Saint-Georges. Its monks built the Clos de Vougeot and, by observing their vines plot by plot, laid foundations for the idea of the climat. Trappist monks still live here.

sites.name: Domaine de la Romanée-Conti
sites.text: The cellars and offices of the world's most famous wine estate, in the village of Vosne-Romanée. It owns the monopoles Romanée-Conti and La Tâche, holds parcels of Richebourg, Romanée-Saint-Vivant, Grands-Échezeaux, Échezeaux, Corton, Montrachet and Bâtard-Montrachet, and is co-owned by the de Villaine family and the heirs of the Leroy family.

sites.name: Domaine Leroy
sites.text: Lalou Bize-Leroy, former co-director of the DRC, created this biodynamic domaine in 1988 by buying the Charles Noëllat estate in Vosne. It owns parcels of nine grand crus and is renowned for very low yields.

sites.name: Domaine Armand Rousseau
sites.text: Founded by Armand Rousseau in the early twentieth century and one of Burgundy's estate-bottling pioneers in the 1930s, the domaine is now run by Cyrielle Rousseau and her father Éric. Its Chambertin, Clos de Bèze and Clos Saint-Jacques are benchmarks.

sites.name: Domaine Georges Roumier
sites.text: Christophe Roumier's family domaine in Chambolle-Musigny, with Les Amoureuses, Bonnes-Mares, Musigny, Ruchottes-Chambertin and Corton-Charlemagne. Its wines are among the most sought-after reds in Burgundy.

sites.name: Château de Chambolle-Musigny (Domaine J.F. Mugnier)
sites.text: The family château of Frédéric Mugnier, a former airline pilot who took over the domaine in 1985. He makes transparent, delicate Musigny, Bonnes-Mares, Les Amoureuses and the Clos de la Maréchale.

sites.name: Domaine Comte Georges de Vogüé
sites.text: In the hands of the same family since 1450, the domaine owns about 7.1 ha of Musigny, two thirds of the grand cru, plus Bonnes-Mares and Les Amoureuses.

sites.name: Clos de Tart (estate)
sites.text: The domaine buildings and deep cellars of Clos de Tart, the walled grand cru monopole owned by Artémis since 2017.

sites.name: Château de Gevrey-Chambertin
sites.text: A thirteenth-century fortified house built by the abbots of Cluny to protect their vineyards and cellars, overlooking the village.

sites.name: Pressoirs des Ducs de Bourgogne
sites.text: In Chenôve, the dukes' press house holds two giant thirteenth-century oak presses, each able to press grapes from several hectares at once.

sites.name: Parc Noisot
sites.text: A park created by Claude Noisot, a captain of Napoleon's Imperial Guard, with the bronze 'Réveil de Napoléon' by François Rude (1847) overlooking the vines of Fixin.

sites.name: Montagne de Corton
sites.text: The wooded hill rising between Aloxe-Corton, Ladoix-Serrigny and Pernand-Vergelesses, ringed with the grand cru vineyards of Corton (red) and Corton-Charlemagne (white). It is the only Côte d'Or hill with grand crus on three sides.

sites.name: Saint-Amour
sites.text: The northernmost of the ten crus, around the village of Saint-Amour-Bellevue on the border with the Mâconnais.

sites.name: Juliénas
sites.text: Hill village named after Julius Caesar; firm, spicy Gamay from granite and schist.

sites.name: Chénas
sites.text: The smallest cru, once covered by oak forests; deep, spicy wines often good value.

sites.name: Moulin-à-Vent
sites.text: The sixteenth-century windmill on a hilltop at Romanèche-Thorins that gave its name to the cru, now a listed historic monument surrounded by vines. The pink granite here carries veins of manganese.

sites.name: Fleurie
sites.text: The nineteenth-century chapel of La Madone on the hill above Fleurie village, overlooking the cru's pink granite slopes.

sites.name: Chiroubles
sites.text: The highest cru, an amphitheatre of steep granite slopes; light, fragrant Gamay.

sites.name: Morgon
sites.text: The village of Villié-Morgon and the cru that surrounds it, cradle of the natural wine movement.

sites.name: Régnié
sites.text: The newest cru (1988), on rolling granite hills between Morgon and Brouilly.

sites.name: Brouilly
sites.text: The largest cru, encircling Mont Brouilly on six communes; generous, fruity Gamay.

sites.name: Côte de Brouilly
sites.text: Mont Brouilly, the extinct volcano whose steep diorite slopes hold the cru and whose summit chapel was built in 1857.

sites.name: Côte du Py
sites.text: An extinct volcanic hill east of Villié-Morgon, the most famous climat of Morgon. Its blue schist and pyrite-rich roche pourrie give powerful, deeply mineral Gamay that can age like fine Burgundy; Jean Foillard's Côte du Py is the classic.

sites.name: Corcelette
sites.text: A sandy granite climat in the northwest of Morgon, giving lighter, perfumed wines; Foillard and Mee Godard make admired versions.

sites.name: Grand Cras
sites.text: A climat in the south of Morgon with clay, gravel and granite; Marcel Lapierre's family vineyards include parcels here.

sites.name: Domaine Marcel Lapierre
sites.text: Marcel Lapierre (1950 to 2010) began making unsulphured, wild-yeast Morgon in 1981 with Jules Chauvet's advice and became the father figure of natural wine. His children Mathieu and Camille continue the domaine in Villié-Morgon.

sites.name: Domaine Jean Foillard
sites.text: One of the Gang of Four, Jean Foillard has made Morgon from the Côte du Py since the 1980s with natural methods and is famous for his Cuvée Corcelette and Côte du Py.

sites.name: Les Thorins
sites.text: A climat just north of the windmill, considered one of the finest of Moulin-à-Vent; it gave its name to the commune of Romanèche-Thorins.

sites.name: Champ de Cour
sites.text: A south-facing climat below the windmill; its wines are rich and deep, notably from Château des Jacques and Richard Rottiers.

sites.name: Château des Jacques
sites.text: Bought by Louis Jadot in 1996, Château des Jacques makes Moulin-à-Vent in Burgundian style with destemming and oak, bottling climats such as Clos du Grand Carquelin, Champ de Cour and La Roche.

sites.name: La Madone (Fleurie)
sites.text: The granite hill crowned by the chapel of La Madone above Fleurie, one of the seven lieux-dits in the cru's premier cru application.

sites.name: Poncié
sites.text: A high, granitic lieu-dit in the north of Fleurie near Moulin-à-Vent, and one of the seven proposed premier crus.

sites.name: La Roilette
sites.text: A clay-rich lieu-dit bordering Moulin-à-Vent, known for the Coudert family's Clos de la Roilette, whose fuller, firmer wine was long sold under the Fleurie name.

sites.name: Château Thivin
sites.text: The oldest estate on Mont Brouilly, in the Geoffray family since 1877, making benchmark Côte de Brouilly from diorite slopes.

sites.name: Hameau Duboeuf
sites.text: The wine theme park and museum created by négociant Georges Duboeuf (1933 to 2020), the 'king of Beaujolais' who turned Nouveau into a global event, at the old railway station of Romanèche-Thorins.

sites.name: Château de Pizay
sites.text: A château with fifteenth-century origins and a large Morgon and Beaujolais-Villages estate, now also a hotel.

sites.name: Chusclan
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.text: Gard-bank villages around Chusclan and Bagnols-sur-Cèze north of Laudun, long known for rosé; a named village since 1967.

sites.name: Gadagne
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.text: Five communes east of Avignon around Châteauneuf-de-Gadagne, on pebble terraces like Châteauneuf's; a named village since 2012.

sites.name: Massif d'Uchaux
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.appellation: Côtes du Rhône Villages Massif d'Uchaux
sites.text: A wooded massif of sandstone and sand north of Orange, recognised in 2005; red only, known for fine, perfumed Grenache from estates such as Château Saint-Estève and Domaine de la Guicharde.

sites.name: Nyons
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.text: Olive capital of the Drôme provençale, recognised in 2020, with limestone hills at altitude giving fresh reds.

sites.name: Plan de Dieu
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.appellation: Côtes du Rhône Villages Plan de Dieu
sites.text: A flat plateau of pebble-strewn garrigue between Orange and Vaison, once Templar land, making ripe, powerful Grenache-based reds.

sites.name: Puyméras
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.text: Hill vineyards in Puyméras, Faucon and Mérindol-les-Oliviers near Vaison-la-Romaine at up to 400 m, giving fresh, spicy reds.

sites.name: Roaix
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.text: A small village between Rasteau and Séguret with limestone and marl slopes; a named village since 1967.

sites.name: Rochegude
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.text: A village with a medieval château north of Orange, on pebble and sand terraces.

sites.name: Rousset-les-Vignes
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.text: A high village in the Drôme provençale on limestone, recognised in 1969, making fresh reds.

sites.name: Sablet
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.text: A village below the Dentelles near Gigondas on sandy soils (its name means sand), known for fine reds and some of the best whites of the Villages.

sites.name: Saint-Andéol
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.text: Four Ardèche communes around Saint-Marcel-d'Ardèche and Bourg-Saint-Andéol on the right bank, the only named village in the Ardèche.

sites.name: Saint-Gervais
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.text: A Gard village on a terrace above the Cèze, recognised in 1974; Domaine Sainte-Anne put it on the map.

sites.name: Saint-Maurice
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.text: Saint-Maurice-sur-Eygues in the Drôme, recognised in 1967, with pebble terraces along the Eygues.

sites.name: Saint-Pantaléon-les-Vignes
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.text: A Drôme village near Valréas, recognised in 1969, with sandy and limestone soils.

sites.name: Sainte-Cécile
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.text: Sainte-Cécile-les-Vignes and neighbours north of Orange, recognised in 2016, on pebble and sand terraces.

sites.name: Séguret
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.text: A perched medieval village below the Dentelles, with limestone slopes giving structured reds and fine whites.

sites.name: Signargues
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.text: Four Gard communes west of Avignon on pebble terraces, recognised in 2005; red only.

sites.name: Suze-la-Rousse
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.text: Villages around the castle of Suze-la-Rousse, home of the Université du Vin, recognised in 2016.

sites.name: Vaison-la-Romaine
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.text: Vineyards in Buisson and Villedieu near the Roman town of Vaison, recognised in 2016.

sites.name: Valréas
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.text: The largest named village, in the papal enclave (Enclave des Papes) of the Vaucluse surrounded by the Drôme, recognised in 1967.

sites.name: Visan
sites.class: Côtes du Rhône Villages named village
sites.text: A hilltop village beside the Enclave des Papes, a named village of the Côtes du Rhône Villages since the 1960s.

sites.name: Côte Brune
sites.text: The dark, iron-rich mica-schist slope north of Ampuis that gives the most structured, tannic Côte Rôtie. The lieu-dit itself is small; Jamet's Côte Brune and Gentaz-Dervieux's old bottlings are legendary.

sites.name: Côte Blonde
sites.text: The paler granite and gneiss slope south of the Reynard stream at Ampuis, giving softer, more perfumed Côte Rôtie, often with more Viognier. The legend says the names come from a lord of Ampuis's two daughters, one brunette, one blonde.

sites.name: La Landonne
sites.text: A steep southeast slope on dark schist in the Côte Brune sector, assembled by Guigal from many owners in the 1970s; its first vintage, 1978, launched the second of Guigal's La La wines. Dense, black-fruited, long-lived pure Syrah. Rostaing also makes a Landonne.

sites.name: La Mouline
sites.text: Guigal's 1 ha amphitheatre of terraces in the Côte Blonde, first bottled separately in 1966. Co-fermented with about 10 percent Viognier, it is the most perfumed and silky of the three La La's.

sites.name: La Turque
sites.text: A 1 ha vineyard in the Côte Brune replanted by Guigal from 1980; first vintage 1985. It combines Côte Brune structure with Côte Blonde perfume.

sites.name: La Viallière
sites.text: A lieu-dit at Vérenay in the north of Côte Rôtie, on schist; prized by growers such as Jean-Michel Stephan and Benetière.

sites.name: Château d'Ampuis
sites.text: A Renaissance château on the Rhône at Ampuis, bought and restored by the Guigal family in 1995, and the name of Guigal's Château d'Ampuis Côte Rôtie, blended from seven lieux-dits.

sites.name: E. Guigal
sites.text: Founded in 1946 by Étienne Guigal, the house is now run by Marcel and Philippe Guigal. It owns Vidal-Fleury, Jean-Louis Grippat, Domaine de Bonserine and Château de Nalys in Châteauneuf, and is the largest producer of Côte Rôtie.

sites.name: Coteau de Vernon
sites.text: A steep granite slope above Condrieu, the source of Georges Vernay's most famous Viognier, from vines planted in the 1930s and 1940s; mineral and long-lived.

sites.name: Chéry
sites.text: One of the top Condrieu slopes, south of the town, on granite with arzelle topsoil; André Perret's Chéry is a reference.

sites.name: Château-Grillet
sites.text: The château and its amphitheatre of Viognier terraces above the Rhône at Vérin, one of France's few single-estate AOCs, owned by Artémis since 2011.

sites.name: Les Bessards
sites.text: The steep western end of the hill, on granite, giving the backbone of red Hermitage: dark, firm and long-lived. Chave, Chapoutier (Le Pavillon) and Jaboulet (La Chapelle) draw heavily on it.

sites.name: L'Hermite
sites.text: The top of the hill around the chapel, with thinner, sandy granite soils; gives perfumed red and fine white. Chapoutier's L'Ermite is a single-site red and white.

sites.name: Le Méal
sites.text: In the middle of the hill, on limestone-rich pebbles and loess over granite; warm and rich, giving ripe, sumptuous red and white. Chapoutier bottles Le Méal separately.

sites.name: Les Greffieux
sites.text: At the bottom of the hill below Le Méal and Les Bessards, on silty alluvium and scree; gives supple, aromatic reds. Marc Sorrel and Chapoutier make single-site versions.

sites.name: Chante-Alouette
sites.text: A name traditionally linked to the eastern, loess-covered part of the hill around Les Murets, best known through Chapoutier's white Hermitage Chante-Alouette, made from Marsanne since the nineteenth century.

sites.name: Les Rocoules
sites.text: A lieu-dit in the east of the hill (spelled Roucoule in the land register) on loess and limestone, famous for white Hermitage from Marsanne and Roussanne; Chave and Sorrel use it.

sites.name: Chapelle Saint-Christophe (Hermitage)
sites.text: The small chapel at the top of the Hermitage hill, associated with the hermit-knight Gaspard de Stérimberg. Jaboulet owns it and named its flagship Hermitage La Chapelle after it; the 1961 vintage is one of the most celebrated wines of the twentieth century.

sites.name: Domaine Jean-Louis Chave
sites.text: Based at Mauves on the Saint-Joseph bank, the Chave family have made wine since 1481. Jean-Louis Chave blends Hermitage from up to nine lieux-dits; the rare Cuvée Cathelin is made only in exceptional years.

sites.name: Domaine Auguste Clape
sites.text: The Clape family domaine on the main road through Cornas, whose traditional, unoaked Cornas kept the appellation's reputation alive through lean decades. Pierre-Marie and Olivier Clape now run it.

sites.name: Reynard (Cornas)
sites.text: A steep granite terrace above the village, made famous by Thierry Allemand's Cornas Reynard; also used by Clape.

sites.name: Chaillot (Cornas)
sites.text: A lieu-dit at the northern edge of Cornas, source of Thierry Allemand's Chaillot and Franck Balthazar's Chaillot.

sites.name: Paul Jaboulet Aîné (Vineum)
sites.text: Founded in 1834 and owned by the Frey family since 2006, Jaboulet makes Hermitage La Chapelle and Crozes-Hermitage Domaine de Thalabert; its Vineum tasting room is in Tain.

sites.name: Crête de Brézème
sites.text: The terraced hill of Brézème at Livron-sur-Drôme, where Syrah grows on limestone marl halfway between Valence and Montélimar.

sites.name: Château des Papes (ruins)
sites.text: The ruined summer castle of Pope John XXII on the hill above the village. Its keep was blown up by retreating German troops in 1944, leaving one tall wall that is the symbol of Châteauneuf-du-Pape.

sites.name: Palais des Papes
sites.text: The Gothic palace in Avignon built for the popes during their exile from Rome (1309 to 1377), whose court spurred the vineyards of the southern Rhône. It is part of a UNESCO World Heritage site.

sites.name: Château Fortia
sites.text: Home of Baron Pierre Le Roy de Boiseaumarié, who drew up the 1923 rules for Châteauneuf-du-Pape and co-founded the national appellation system. The estate still produces Châteauneuf.

sites.name: Château Rayas
sites.text: Emmanuel Reynaud's mythical estate in a wooded clearing on sandy soil in the north of the appellation, making pure Grenache from low-yielding old vines. Its unusual, ethereal, almost Burgundian Châteauneuf is one of the world's most sought-after wines.

sites.name: Château de Beaucastel
sites.text: The Perrin family estate at Courthézon, on galets roulés in the northeast of the appellation, known for using all 13 traditional grape varieties with a high share of Mourvèdre, organic farming since the 1950s and flash-heating the grapes before fermentation. Its Hommage à Jacques Perrin is a cult wine.

sites.name: Domaine du Vieux Télégraphe
sites.text: The Brunier family estate on the plateau of La Crau, named after a Chappe semaphore telegraph tower that stood here from 1821. Its vines grow in deep layers of galets roulés, giving structured, spicy, long-lived Châteauneuf.

sites.name: La Crau plateau
sites.text: The highest, most exposed plateau of Châteauneuf, covered with a thick layer of galets roulés over red clay. Vieux Télégraphe, Pegau and Henri Bonneau's Réserve des Célestins draw from it.

sites.name: Château La Nerthe
sites.text: One of the oldest estates of Châteauneuf, documented since 1560, whose wines were among the first to be bottled with the estate name in the eighteenth century. Commandeur Joseph Ducos experimented with grape varieties here in the 1880s.

sites.name: Domaine Henri Bonneau
sites.text: The tiny cellar in the village of the late Henri Bonneau (died 2016), whose Réserve des Célestins, from old Grenache on La Crau aged for years in old barrels, became a legend. His son Marcel continues.

sites.name: Clos des Papes
sites.text: The Avril family estate, making wine since the eighteenth century, with vines scattered across 24 parcels. Paul-Vincent Avril's Clos des Papes was Wine Spectator's Wine of the Year for the 2005 vintage.

sites.name: Château Mont-Redon
sites.text: One of the largest single estates of Châteauneuf, on the northwestern plateau of Mont-Redon covered in galets roulés, owned by the Abeille and Fabre families.

sites.name: Domaine du Pegau
sites.text: Laurence Féraud's family estate, famous for the traditional Cuvée Réservée and the rare Cuvée da Capo.

sites.name: Château de Fonsalette
sites.text: Owned by the Reynaud family of Château Rayas at Lagarde-Paréol, Fonsalette makes Côtes du Rhône of Châteauneuf quality, including a famous pure Syrah.

sites.name: Dentelles de Montmirail
sites.text: A jagged ridge of Jurassic limestone 'lace' rising to 734 m between Gigondas, Vacqueyras, Beaumes-de-Venise and Séguret. Its slopes hold some of the highest and freshest vineyards of the Southern Rhône.

sites.name: Château de Saint-Cosme
sites.text: Louis Barruol's family estate, owned since 1490, with Gallo-Roman vats cut in the rock and single-site Gigondas such as Le Claux, Hominis Fides and Valbelle.

sites.name: Domaine Marcel Richaud
sites.text: Marcel Richaud began bottling in the 1970s and campaigned for Cairanne's promotion; his L'Ebrescade is one of the Southern Rhône's great reds.

sites.name: Château d'Aquéria
sites.text: A seventeenth-century château and 98 ha estate on the road from Tavel to Pujaut, one of the best-known producers of Tavel and Lirac.

sites.name: Pujaut (phylloxera first found)
sites.text: The Gard village just west of Avignon where dying vines in 1863 marked the first recorded appearance of phylloxera in France. Within three decades it had devastated nearly every French vineyard.

sites.name: Mont Ventoux
sites.text: The Giant of Provence, whose foothills hold the Ventoux appellation. Cool air from its slopes gives freshness to the vineyards below.

sites.name: Mas des Tourelles
sites.text: An estate at Beaucaire built on the site of a Gallo-Roman pottery that reconstructed a Roman wine cellar and makes wines from Roman recipes (mulsum, turriculae) each autumn.

sites.name: Altenberg de Bergbieten
sites.appellation: Alsace grand cru Altenberg de Bergbieten
sites.text: Altenberg de Bergbieten, in the northern Bas-Rhin, gives broad, spicy Riesling and Gewurztraminer from a sunny southeast slope of marl, limestone and gypsum. Marl and limestone with gypsum on a southeast-facing slope west of Strasbourg.

sites.name: Altenberg de Bergheim
sites.appellation: Alsace grand cru Altenberg de Bergheim
sites.text: Altenberg de Bergheim is one of Alsace's historic vineyards and one of the two grands crus that may make blends of several grapes, a privilege won by Marcel Deiss, who planted it as a field blend. Jurassic limestone and marl on a south-facing slope above the walled town of Bergheim.

sites.name: Altenberg de Wolxheim
sites.appellation: Alsace grand cru Altenberg de Wolxheim
sites.text: Altenberg de Wolxheim is a limestone hill on the edge of the Bruche valley west of Strasbourg, long the city's favourite source of Riesling and reputedly a favourite of Napoleon. Limestone and marl on a southeast-facing hill west of Strasbourg.

sites.name: Brand
sites.text: Brand, meaning fire or burn, is one of the great Riesling sites of Alsace: a steep granite slope that heats up fast in the sun. Two-mica granite on a steep slope facing south and southeast above Turckheim, at the mouth of the Munster valley.

sites.name: Bruderthal
sites.text: Bruderthal, the brothers' valley, was named after the monks who farmed it. Limestone and marl with sandstone on a southeast slope above Molsheim.

sites.name: Eichberg
sites.text: Eichberg (oak hill), above the round medieval village of Eguisheim, is one of the driest and warmest sites in Alsace. Limestone and marl with sandstone scree on a southeast slope.

sites.name: Engelberg
sites.text: Engelberg, the angels' hill, straddles Dahlenheim and Scharrachbergheim at the northern end of the Route des Vins, among the northernmost grands crus. Limestone and marl at the northern end of the Route des Vins.

sites.name: Florimont
sites.text: Florimont, the hill of flowers, rises just west of Colmar between Ingersheim and Katzenthal, on limestone and marl with a sunny southern exposure. Limestone and marl on a south-facing hill west of Colmar.

sites.name: Frankstein
sites.text: Frankstein is made up of four separate granite hillsides around Dambach-la-Ville, the largest wine commune of the Bas-Rhin. Two-mica granite in four separate parcels on the slopes above Dambach-la-Ville.

sites.name: Froehn
sites.text: Froehn is a compact grand cru of about 14 ha wrapped around the hilltop village of Zellenberg, between Riquewihr and Ribeauvillé. Marl and clay with schist on a south-facing hill.

sites.name: Furstentum
sites.text: Furstentum, the principality, is a warm, sheltered amphitheatre between Kientzheim and Sigolsheim that ripens Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris to great richness, and gives powerful Riesling.. Limestone with marl and sandstone on a steep south-facing slope.

sites.name: Geisberg
sites.text: Geisberg, the goat hill, is one of the smallest grands crus, about 8 ha of steep terraces above Ribeauvillé, documented since 1308. Limestone and marl with sandstone on steep terraces.

sites.name: Gloeckelberg
sites.text: Gloeckelberg, the bell hill, sits between Rodern and Saint-Hippolyte below the Haut-Koenigsbourg, on granite with sand and clay. Granite with sand and clay on a southeast slope.

sites.name: Goldert
sites.text: Goldert, golden garden, owes its name to the golden colour of its wines. Limestone and marl with sandstone on an east and southeast slope.

sites.name: Hatschbourg
sites.text: Hatschbourg spreads over a warm, sunny slope above Hattstatt and Voegtlinshoffen south of Colmar, on limestone and marl covered with loess. Limestone and marl with loess on a southeast slope.

sites.name: Hengst
sites.text: Hengst, the stallion, is one of the most powerful grands crus: its calcareous marl gives dense, spicy Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris and firm, long-lived Riesling. Limestone and marl with sandstone on a steep southeast-facing hill.

sites.name: Kaefferkopf
sites.text: Kaefferkopf, the beetle's head, was the 51st grand cru, added in 2007 after decades of argument over its delimitation and rules. Granite, sandstone and limestone in a single 74 ha grand cru.

sites.name: Kanzlerberg
sites.text: Kanzlerberg, the chancellor's hill, is the smallest grand cru of Alsace, a little over 3 ha next to Altenberg de Bergheim. Gypsum-rich marl and limestone; the smallest grand cru at about 3 ha.

sites.name: Kastelberg
sites.text: Kastelberg, castle hill, is a steep slope of black Steiger schist above Andlau, and it is one of the great Riesling sites of the Bas-Rhin: austere, smoky and slow-ageing. Steiger schist (dark, slaty) on a steep hill above Andlau.

sites.name: Kessler
sites.text: Kessler, the cauldron, is a bowl-shaped valley on the slopes above Guebwiller, where red sandstone gives silky, spicy Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris. Pink Vosges sandstone with clay on terraced slopes in a sheltered valley.

sites.name: Kirchberg de Barr
sites.appellation: Alsace grand cru Kirchberg de Barr
sites.text: Kirchberg de Barr, the church hill, rises above the town of Barr and gives structured Riesling and rich Gewurztraminer. Limestone and marl on a hill above the town of Barr.

sites.name: Kirchberg de Ribeauvillé
sites.appellation: Alsace grand cru Kirchberg de Ribeauvillé
sites.text: Kirchberg de Ribeauvillé, the church hill, lies on a steep, sunny slope west of Ribeauvillé below the town's three ruined castles. Limestone and marl with sandstone scree on a south-facing slope.

sites.name: Kitterlé
sites.text: Kitterlé is one of the steepest grands crus, on volcanic sandstone above Guebwiller, and gives powerful, spicy Riesling and Gewurztraminer. Volcanic sandstone with spilite on a very steep terraced slope.

sites.name: Mambourg
sites.text: Mambourg is a long, warm, south-facing hill above Sigolsheim with a near-Mediterranean flora, giving rich Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris and powerful Riesling. Limestone and marl on a long south-facing hill.

sites.name: Mandelberg
sites.text: Mandelberg, almond hill, is named for the almond trees that grow in its mild microclimate between Mittelwihr and Beblenheim. Limestone and marl on a south-facing slope.

sites.name: Marckrain
sites.text: Marckrain, the boundary slope, faces east above Bennwihr and Sigolsheim, on marl and limestone that hold water and give rich, spicy Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris, often with late-harvest sweetness. Marl and limestone on an east-facing slope.

sites.name: Moenchberg
sites.text: Moenchberg, the monks' hill, lies between Andlau and Eichhoffen on a south-facing slope of marl, limestone and colluvium. Marl and limestone with colluvium on a south-facing slope.

sites.name: Muenchberg
sites.text: Muenchberg, another monks' hill, was planted by the Cistercians of Baumgarten abbey in the twelfth century. Volcanic sandstone and pebbles in a natural amphitheatre.

sites.name: Ollwiller
sites.text: Ollwiller lies below the Hartmannswillerkopf (Vieil Armand), a First World War battlefield, near the southern end of the Alsace vineyard. Sandstone and clay at the southern end of the vineyard below the Vieil Armand.

sites.name: Osterberg
sites.text: Osterberg, the eastern hill, lies next to Geisberg on the slopes north of Ribeauvillé, on marl and limestone that give more weight than its neighbour. Marl and limestone on a southeast slope.

sites.name: Pfersigberg
sites.text: Pfersigberg, the peach hill, is a large grand cru of about 71 ha above Eguisheim and Wettolsheim, on warm limestone and marl facing southeast. Limestone and marl on a long southeast slope.

sites.name: Pfingstberg
sites.text: Pfingstberg, Pentecost hill, rises above Orschwihr in the southern Haut-Rhin on a steep southeast slope of sandstone, limestone and marl. Sandstone and limestone on a steep southeast slope.

sites.name: Praelatenberg
sites.text: Praelatenberg, the prelates' hill, was owned by the monks of Ebersmunster abbey. Granite and gneiss below the castle of Haut-Koenigsbourg.

sites.name: Rangen
sites.text: Rangen is the southernmost grand cru and one of the most extraordinary vineyards in France: a very steep, south-facing wall of volcanic rock above the Thur river at Thann. Volcanic rock (andesite, tuffs and greywacke) on an extremely steep south-facing slope.

sites.name: Rosacker
sites.text: Rosacker, the field of roses, above Hunawihr and its fortified church, gives taut, mineral, long-lived Riesling. Dolomitic limestone and marl on an east-facing slope.

sites.name: Saering
sites.text: Saering is the most northerly of Guebwiller's four grands crus, on terraced slopes of limestone, marl and sandstone facing east and southeast. Limestone and marl with sandstone on terraced slopes.

sites.name: Schlossberg
sites.text: Schlossberg, castle hill, was the first Alsace grand cru, created by decree in 1975. Granite with sand on steep terraces.

sites.name: Schoenenbourg
sites.text: Schoenenbourg, the beautiful castle, rises behind the medieval walls of Riquewihr and was famous across Europe in the sixteenth century. Keuper marl with gypsum, sandstone and dolomite on a north and northeast-facing amphitheatre above Riquewihr.

sites.name: Sommerberg
sites.text: Sommerberg, summer hill, is a steep granite slope above Niedermorschwihr that gives some of the most precise, mineral Rieslings in Alsace, notably from Albert Boxler.. Granite on extremely steep terraces.

sites.name: Sonnenglanz
sites.text: Sonnenglanz, sunshine glow, is a warm, sheltered slope above Beblenheim known for rich Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris and for botrytised sweet wines. Limestone and marl on a gentle southeast slope.

sites.name: Spiegel
sites.text: Spiegel, the mirror, lies between Bergholtz and Guebwiller on sandstone and marl facing east and southeast. Sandstone and marl on a southeast slope.

sites.name: Sporen
sites.text: Sporen, next to Schoenenbourg, is traditionally planted with Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris and was once used for a famous field blend (Gentil). Clay and marl with stones on a gentle slope east of Riquewihr.

sites.name: Steinert
sites.text: Steinert, the stony one, is a hot, steep limestone slope above Pfaffenheim and Westhalten, so stony that the soil warms quickly in spring. Limestone on a steep, stony slope.

sites.name: Steingrubler
sites.text: Steingrubler, the stone quarry, lies above Wettolsheim on a mixed soil of limestone, sandstone and granite, a reflection of the faulting that shattered the Vosges foothills here. Limestone, sandstone and granite in a mixed soil.

sites.name: Steinklotz
sites.text: Steinklotz, block of stone, is the northernmost grand cru, above Marlenheim, where the Merovingian kings had a royal estate. Limestone with marl at the northern gateway of the Route des Vins.

sites.name: Vorbourg
sites.text: Vorbourg is a large, warm grand cru between Rouffach and Westhalten. Limestone and sandstone on a sunny, south-facing hill.

sites.name: Wiebelsberg
sites.text: Wiebelsberg rises above Andlau on light, quartz-rich sandstone facing southeast, in contrast to neighbouring Kastelberg's black schist. Quartz-rich sandstone on a southeast slope above Andlau.

sites.name: Wineck-Schlossberg
sites.text: Wineck-Schlossberg lies below the ruined tower of the Wineck castle at Katzenthal and Ammerschwihr, on a steep granite slope in a side valley west of Colmar. Granite below the ruined castle of Wineck.

sites.name: Winzenberg
sites.text: Winzenberg, the winegrowers' hill, rises above Blienschwiller in the Bas-Rhin on two-mica granite facing south. Granite on a south-facing slope.

sites.name: Zinnkoepflé
sites.text: Zinnkoepflé is one of the highest and driest grands crus, a steep south-facing hill above the Vallée Noble where wild orchids and Mediterranean plants grow. Limestone and sandstone on a high, hot, south-facing slope up to about 420 m.

sites.name: Zotzenberg
sites.text: Zotzenberg, above Mittelbergheim, is the only grand cru allowed to make Sylvaner (since 2006), a tribute to a local grape long prized here. Limestone and marl on a southeast slope above Mittelbergheim.

sites.name: Famille Hugel
sites.text: In Riquewihr since 1639, Hugel is one of Alsace's best-known names. Jean Hugel was instrumental in creating the Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles rules of 1984. The family owns parcels of Schoenenbourg and Sporen but refuses to use grand cru names.

sites.name: Maison Trimbach
sites.text: Based in Ribeauvillé, the Trimbach family has made wine since 1626. Its Riesling Clos Sainte Hune (in Rosacker) and Cuvée Frédéric Émile (Geisberg and Osterberg) are benchmark dry Rieslings.

sites.name: Clos Sainte Hune
sites.class: Monopole within Alsace grand cru Rosacker
sites.text: A 1.67 ha parcel of Riesling within the Rosacker grand cru above Hunawihr, owned by the Trimbach family for more than 200 years. Austere and very long-lived, it is often called Alsace's greatest Riesling.

sites.name: Domaine Zind-Humbrecht
sites.text: The Humbrecht family estate at Turckheim, run by Olivier Humbrecht MW, the first French Master of Wine (1989), and farmed biodynamically since the late 1990s. It owns parcels in Rangen (Clos Saint-Urbain), Brand, Hengst and Goldert.

sites.name: Clos Saint-Urbain (Rangen)
sites.class: Monopole within Alsace grand cru Rangen
sites.text: Zind-Humbrecht's parcel around the chapel of Saint-Urbain on the volcanic Rangen above Thann, source of some of Alsace's most powerful Riesling and Pinot Gris.

sites.name: Domaine Weinbach
sites.text: The walled Clos des Capucins at the foot of the Schlossberg in Kientzheim, founded by Capuchin monks in 1612 and owned by the Faller family since 1898. Run by Catherine Faller and her children, it makes famous Schlossberg Riesling and Furstentum Gewurztraminer.

sites.name: Domaine Ostertag
